## Open items — MOSTLY RESOLVED 2026-08-10 via official MRT platform docs

User supplied `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/mrt-overview.md` + `mrt-administration.md` (official
Salesforce Managed Runtime docs). These resolve almost everything that previously required a
Gideon/platform conversation:

**Multi-app support — CONFIRMED YES.** "An organization can contain multiple projects for
multiple storefronts and each project can contain multiple environments" (mrt-overview.md
"Projects and Organizations"). Platform-architecturally, Option B is fully supported — this was
the single biggest open unknown and it's now closed.

**Numeric platform limits — CONFIRMED, and this is a real constraint on Option B's *shape*.**
Org-wide cap: **max 100 total environments, max 10 production environments** (raisable only by
contacting Salesforce Support). Zimmermann today uses 6 environments (dev/test/sit/uat/staging/
prod) in one project. A literal "one MRT app per integration" reading of Option B (~18 systems ×
6 tiers = 108 environments) **exceeds the 100-environment org cap on its own** and would need a
Support-ticket limit increase for production count too. A **domain-grouped** version (e.g. 3-5
apps clustering related integrations — payments, CMS-proxy, CRM/order-data, etc.) stays
comfortably under both caps (~24-36 total environments). This is the first hard, quantified
argument for why Option B, if chosen, should group by domain rather than by individual
integration — feed directly into §2.1 Constraints and §3 Options Analysis.

**Cost model — PARTIALLY resolved, nuance matters.** "Because environments run on highly
efficient microservices that automatically scale up and down, you can create as many
environments as you need **at no additional cost**" (up to the caps above). This answers the
*platform-mechanics* half (environments aren't individually metered) but is generic Salesforce
product documentation, not a Zimmermann-specific commercial statement — it does **not** confirm
whether Zimmermann's actual contract caps or charges for an *additional project* (as opposed to
additional environments within an existing project). **Narrowed remaining open item:** confirm
with account team/Gideon whether provisioning a wholly new MRT *project* (not just an
environment) has any commercial implication under Zimmermann's specific agreement.

**MRT execution/concurrency model — CONFIRMED.** App Server = Node.js + Express, "serverless,"
auto-scaling ("massive scaling capacity"). Critically: **"Unhandled promise rejections break app
rendering"** (mrt-overview.md, Rendering constraints) — this is the concrete platform-level
mechanism behind the failure-isolation argument: under Option A, one integration's unhandled
rejection can break rendering for a request that also needed a *different*, otherwise-healthy
integration, because they share the same Node process/request lifecycle. Hard execution-time
ceiling: **20s production / 16s non-production**, then HTTP 502 — a real ceiling regardless of
topology, and a concrete reason the still-inert undici per-pool timeouts (`connectionPools.ts`,
see Discrepancy #2) matter independent of which option wins.

**Deploy/rollback granularity — CONFIRMED, directly answers the ticket's named dimension.**
"Each project can have multiple bundles, but each environment can have only one bundle designated
as deployed" — a bundle is the *entire* built app, immutable. **Under Option A, any change to any
one integration requires deploying (and, if bad, rolling back) the single shared bundle
containing all integrations' code** — a bad change to Integration X forces a rollback that also
reverts unrelated Integration Y's code if it shipped in the same bundle. Option B gives each
domain-app its own independent bundle lineage — true deploy/rollback isolation. This is the
clearest, most concrete win for Option B of everything found so far.

**Architectural catch for Option B — new insight, important for §3 Options Analysis.** MRT
environments are hostname-bound HTTP-serving units ("A hostname can be set as the External
Hostname for only one environment at a time"). Zimmermann's architecture.md §"Cross-Storefront
Session & Basket Scope" depends on **all 8 storefronts sharing one first-party domain** for
session-cookie sharing. A literal per-integration-app split would need either (a) each
integration-app treated as an **internal backend microservice** that the one customer-facing
"front door" app calls server-to-server (exactly the pattern the still-inert `connectionPools.ts`
undici pools were designed for — this becomes the actual wiring mechanism, not just a nice-to-have),
or (b) CDN/edge-level path routing across multiple MRT origins (heavier — Zimmermann's CDN is
Akamai/SFCC-default per architecture.md, not something MRT's own per-project edge covers across
projects). **This means "per-integration app" in practice is a backend-microservices-behind-one-
front-door pattern, not a literal request-routing split** — worth stating explicitly in the TSD
so Option B isn't misread as "split the storefront itself into 18 sites."

**Certificates — a non-issue either way.** TLS certs are **org-scoped**, usable by any environment
in the same org (not per-project) — Option B's extra projects would share the same wildcard cert
with no additional certificate-provisioning overhead.

**Project-level role granularity — a concrete secrets/ownership-blast-radius argument for Option
B.** Each MRT project has its own Admin/Developer/Marketer/Viewer role assignments (env-var
visibility, deploy access, log access are all project-scoped, one role per user per project).
Under Option A everyone who needs deploy/env-var access to *any* integration necessarily has it
for *all* integrations (one shared project). Option B lets access be scoped per domain-app —
directly answers the ticket's "secrets & security blast radius" and "ownership" dimensions with a
platform-verified mechanism, not a hypothetical.

**Collateral finding (out of SFCC-237's scope — one-TSD-one-problem — but worth flagging
separately):** "Server-Side Cookie Access is enabled by default for new projects. **Existing
projects continue to have server-side cookies turned off by default**" (mrt-administration.md).
Zimmermann's `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie architecture (architecture.md §"Cross-Storefront
Session") is load-bearing on server-side cookie access being *on*. Worth an independent Runtime
Admin check (project settings) that this is actually enabled on the existing `zimmermann` project
— not something derivable from the codebase, and not something to fold into this TSD.

**Now genuinely narrow remaining opens (all "check Runtime Admin," not "unknowable platform
questions"):** (1) Zimmermann's actual commercial cost for an *additional project* specifically;
(2) current environment/production-count usage against the 100/10 org caps, to know real headroom;
(3) whether the existing `zimmermann` project runs ARM or x86 (x86 retires 2027-01-31; ARM is
default for anything created after its introduction); (4) the server-side-cookie collateral check
above. None of these require Claude — they're one-glance-at-Runtime-Admin facts for whoever has
access (the user has Managed Runtime access per role, presumably).

content.text:
## Analysis: mrt-overview.md + mrt-administration.md

These are the official Salesforce Managed Runtime platform docs, and they resolve nearly everything that was previously blocking on Gideon/platform.

### The big unlock — multi-app support: **confirmed YES**
"An organization can contain multiple projects for multiple storefronts and each project can contain multiple environments." Platform-architecturally, Option B is fully supported. This was the single biggest unknown from the previous pass.

### A hard, quantified constraint that shapes Option B's *shape*
Org-wide caps: **max 100 total environments, max 10 production environments** (raisable only via a Salesforce Support ticket). Zimmermann today uses 6 (dev/test/sit/uat/staging/prod) in one project. A literal "one MRT app per integration" reading of Option B (~18 systems × 6 tiers = 108 environments) **blows past the 100-environment cap by itself**. A domain-grouped version (e.g. 3-5 apps clustering related integrations — payments, CMS-proxy, CRM/order-data) stays comfortably under both caps. This is a concrete, doc-sourced reason Option B, if chosen, should never mean literally-one-app-per-system.

### Cost model — half-resolved
"You can create as many environments as you need at no additional cost" — this confirms environments aren't individually metered, but it's generic Salesforce product doc, not Zimmermann's commercial terms. **Narrowed to one specific remaining question:** does an additional *project* (not environment) carry any cost under Zimmermann's actual agreement — that still needs the account team/Gideon.

### Concurrency/blast-radius model — confirmed
Node.js + Express, serverless, auto-scaling. Critically: **"Unhandled promise rejections break app rendering"** — the concrete mechanism behind the failure-isolation argument (one integration's bug can break a render that only needed a different, healthy integration, because they share a process). Hard execution ceiling: 20s prod / 16s non-prod → HTTP 502.

### Deploy/rollback — the clearest concrete win for Option B
Each environment has exactly one deployed bundle at a time, and a bundle is the *entire* app, immutable. Under Option A, a bad change to one integration forces rolling back the whole shared bundle — including unrelated integrations that shipped fine in the same release. Option B gives each domain-app an independent bundle lineage. This directly answers the ticket's named "deploy/rollback" dimension with a platform fact, not a guess.

### New architectural insight for the Options Analysis
MRT environments are hostname-bound (one External Hostname per environment). Zimmermann's architecture depends on all 8 storefronts sharing one first-party domain for session-cookie sharing. So a literal per-integration split can't mean "split storefront routing across apps" — it has to mean **backend microservices behind one front-door app**, calling out server-to-server. That's exactly the pattern the still-inert `connectionPools.ts` undici pools were built for — wiring them stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the actual mechanism Option B would depend on.

### Secondary confirmations
Certificates are org-scoped (shared across projects — no extra overhead for Option B). Project-level roles (Admin/Developer/Marketer/Viewer, one per user per project) give a platform-verified mechanism for the "secrets & ownership blast radius" dimension: Option A means anyone touching any integration has access to all of them; Option B lets that be scoped per domain-app.

### Collateral finding (separate from this TSD — flagging, not folding in)
"Existing projects continue to have server-side cookies turned off by default" unless explicitly enabled — Zimmermann's `httpOnly` SLAS cookie architecture is load-bearing on this being *on*. Worth an independent Runtime Admin check on the existing `zimmermann` project; not something I can verify from the repo, and out of scope for a one-TSD-one-problem document about app topology.

### What's left (now much narrower — all "look at Runtime Admin," not "unknowable")
1. Commercial cost of an additional project specifically
2. Current org env/production-count usage against the 100/10 caps
3. ARM vs x86 on the existing project
4. The server-side-cookie check above

Memory and task list updated (#2 and #3 now resolved; new task #8 captures the narrowed residual). Given how much just unblocked, want me to proceed toward drafting the TSD now, or hold for the remaining Runtime Admin checks first?

additional information:

* as per the former Integration Lead, Mani - "you cannot run multiple separate or independent Node.js application processes (like auxiliary microservices or distinct integration apps) inside a single Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT) environment. MRT is strictly designed to host one unified application bundle generated from an official PWA Kit template."


we did quick searches and arrived with quick answers:

* question: is it possible to run multi-MRT node apps (for integrations) for SFCC PWA Kit, specifically to "Dedicated MRT node application per integration"
   * No, running a dedicated, separate Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT) Node.js application per integration is not natively supported or how MRT is architected for the SFCC PWA Kit. Salesforce Managed Runtime is strictly designed to host unified PWA Kit storefront projects (combining React, Node, and Express into a single SSR app server per environment/project) rather than serving as a general-purpose, multi-app microservices hosting platform. [[1](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/pwa-kit-managed-runtime/guide/mrt-overview.html)]
Understanding MRT Constraints
      * Single App Model: Each MRT project/environment maps to one deployed bundle running a unified Express server designed to render your storefront. [[1](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/pwa-kit-managed-runtime/guide/mrt-overview.html)]
      * Not a PaaS for Microservices: You cannot spin up isolated, concurrent Node worker apps or independent sidecars inside MRT just for back-end integrations.
      * Alternative Hosting: Heavy integration logic, middleware layers, or third-party connectors should reside on an external cloud platform (like AWS, Heroku, or Google Cloud). Your PWA Kit's Express server proxies or calls these services via secure APIs.
Recommended Architectural Approaches
      * Unified Custom Server: Extend the PWA Kit's built-in Express server (`app.js` / server bundle) to include custom API routes or proxy middleware if your integrations are lightweight. [[1](https://rhino-inquisitor.com/lag-to-riches-a-pwa-kit-developers-guide/)]
      * External Integration Layer: Offload dedicated integration apps to a separate traditional Node.js hosting environment, keeping MRT strictly focused on the frontend rendering and shopper requests.
* question: is it possible to run multi-MRT node apps (for integrations) for SFCC PWA Kit, specifically to "Dedicated MRT node application per integration/domain"
   * No, you cannot host multiple dedicated, independent Managed Runtime (MRT) node applications for a single PWA Kit project/domain split by integration. Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT) expects a single, unified Express/React server bundle per MRT environment, meaning all server-side integration logic must live inside that single Node process. [[1](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/pwa-kit-managed-runtime/guide/mrt-overview.html), [2](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/pwa-kit-managed-runtime/guide/mrt-overview.html)]
How MRT Architecture Works
      * Single Node Server: MRT runs a single unified Express server instance (`ssr.js`) per environment to handle server-side rendering (SSR) and proxy requests. [[1](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/sfra/guide/sfnext-pwa-overview.html), [2](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/pwa-kit-managed-runtime/guide/mrt-overview.html), [3](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/pwa-kit-managed-runtime/guide/sfnext-pwa-overview.html)]
      * One Bundle per Deploy: The deployment model relies on uploading a single compiled bundle (`bundle.zip`) via the [Managed Runtime Admin Tool](https://www.google.com/url?sa=i&source=web&rct=j&url=https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/pwa-kit-managed-runtime/guide/mrt-overview.html&ved=2ahUKEwiy6Zzm3JWWAxVsh68BHXumCRMQy_kOegoIAggACAAIDhAJ&opi=89978449&cd&psig=AOvVaw2SWPhjd8zW4kmyZKGnYGlK&ust=1786439748457000) or B2C CLI. [[1](https://medium.com/@imunesh.kumar5/mrt-deployments-in-salesforce-commerce-cloud-using-b2c-cli-d6b37d89bb03), [2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zxE1SD3FuzM)]
      * Domain Mapping: You can map multiple distinct domains to multiple separate MRT environments or projects (e.g., `brand-us.com` vs `brand-uk.com`), but each environment still runs just one application codebase. [[1](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/commerce-solutions/guide/managed-runtime-administration.html), [2](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/pwa-kit-managed-runtime/guide/multiple-sites.html), [3](https://www.dreamfactory.com/resources/whitepapers/implementing-the-twelve-factor-app-methodology)]

4	Audience: B2C Commerce ISV Partners
5	What is Headless Commerce?
6	Headless Commerce is an API-first implementation pattern that decouples ecommerce frontend and backend which gives developers more flexibility to create an extraordinary user experience with their storefront and UI layer. We are already seeing some Salesforce B2C Commerce customers are leveraging APIs to assemble their entire commerce technology stack. Such customers use Commerce APIs, along with the Composable Storefront, which is made up of the PWA Kit and the Managed Runtime (MRT).
7	
8	Solución
9	Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
10	
11	What is PWA Kit?
12	The Progressive Web App (PWA) Kit is a new storefront technology for headless commerce using Salesforce Commerce APIs and our commerce-react-sdk. It provides our customers with a more flexible and agile approach to building and maintaining modern shopping experiences. PWA kit allows merchants to quickly spin up fully functioning headless storefronts that are connected to their Salesforce Commerce Cloud instance.
13	
14	
15	Headless Commerce Integration Patterns
16	B2C Commerce Headless integrations come in a variety of flavors. Integrations will follow several patterns, depending on whether they include front-end and back-end modifications. The table below provides guidance on what customers should expect for different patterns.
17	 
18	
19	Integration Type	Integration Sub-type	Use Case	Assets	Resources	Is this a Composable Storefront listing on the AgentExchange?
20	B2C Commerce Cartridge
21	
22	(Available under Package Listing type in the AgentExchange publishing console)	SFRA Back-end + Front-end	A cartridge focuses on customizing B2C Commerce behavior. The cartridge is tasked with B2C modification, achieved through the use of SFRA hooks, jobs, and/or controllers.
23	
24	The cartridge can contain forms, templates and scripts for manipulation of the front end within the cartridge.	B2C Commerce Cartridge - ISV Partners are responsible for hosting the file location. + metadata required.Instructions for installing and setting up the cartridge	B2C Commerce Cartridgefor ISV'sDeveloper with B2C Commerce CartridgeB2C Commerce API GuideB2C Commerce API ReferenceB2C Commerce API Release Notes	No
25	B2C Commerce Headless Integration
26	
27	(Available under API Listing type in the AgentExchange publishing console)	B2C Commerce Cartridge with SCAPI hooks	A cartridge focuses on customizing B2C Commerce behavior. The cartridge is tasked with B2C modification, achieved through the use of SCAPI hooks, jobs, and/or controllers.
28	
29	This cartridge cannot have any type of scripts or templates to manipulate the front end. The data gets injected to the composable storefront through components.	B2C Commerce Cartridge - ISV Partners are responsible for hosting the file location. + metadata required.Instructions for installing and setting up the cartridge	B2C Commerce Cartridgefor ISV'sDeveloper with B2C Commerce CartridgeB2C Commerce API GuideB2C Commerce API ReferenceB2C Commerce API Release Notes	Yes, if the cartridge can be installed and used with Composable Storefronts (uses SCAPI hooks to insert custom logic), otherwise no
30	Composable Storefront (Font-end)	Reusable, modular react components that can be used in the PWA Kit composable storefronts that runs on Salesforce MRT. Available to merchants via NPM packages.

NPM PackageInstructions on how to install and use components and/or modifications to code in Composable Storefront.	The complete guide to publishing a React package to npmCreating Node.js modules	Yes
33	Composable Storefront (Front-end + Back-End)	The combo integration requires both a back-end and front-end integration. This solution type is utilized for more complex use cases. B2C Commerce Cartridgefor ISV'sDeveloper with B2C Commerce CartridgeB2C Commerce API GuideB2C Commerce API ReferenceB2C Commerce API Release NotesThe complete guide to publishing a React package to npmCreating Node.js modules	Yes

For data consumption and injection integrations	Headless Integration guide	Guide for Headless Integrations (B2C Commerce ISV Partners)	Yes, only if the instructions include integrating with the composable storefront, otherwise no.

39	Are there any prerequisites that an ISV must have to start developing a composable storefront solution?
40	You must be an active B2C Commerce (ISV) Partner - check out our B2C Commerce ISV Partner Onboarding Guide if you are not yet an ISV Partner
41	You must have access to Account Manager

44	Developer experience with B2C Commerce Cartridges

48	Composable Storefront back-end integrations and SFRA cartridges are B2C cartridges. The main difference is that a back-end integration for a composable storefront is strictly focused on backend behavior. This integration is tasked with handling any back-end logic that cannot be completed in the front end. The integration is connected to a front-end component via APIs. Whereas an SFRA cartridge has both backend and front-end manipulation. These integrations are completely coupled and follow our architecture patterns that can be web services-based or file-based.

52	Every Composable Storefront must have a project created in Runtime Admin for managing deployments. Managed Runtime (MRT) provides the infrastructure to deploy, host, and monitor your Composable Storefront. Here, the storefront code that runs in an environment is called a bundle. You can manage multiple environments from MRT such as production, development, or testing environments to better manage and maintain your storefronts.

54	From each MRT environment, we use a combination of React, Node, and Express frameworks to run the App Server to create these dynamic and fast websites. For more information on setting up and using Managed Runtime refer this guide on Managed Runtime Overview.

60	B2C Commerce ISV Partners can list their integration is the AgentExchange either as B2C Commerce Headless Integration if your integration satisfies the requirements listed in the above table.

64	Composable Storefront - Your integration should qualify either one of the integration sub-types listed under B2C Commerce Headless Integration in the table above.
65	Sample AgentExchange listing name: Appy Enterprises Payment Composable Storefront for B2C Commerce
66	Headless Integration (API-only) - Your integration is a Connect Apps (API-only) sub-types listed under B2C Commerce Headless Integration in the table above.
67	Sample AgentExchange listing name: Appy Enterprises Payment Headless Integration for B2C Commerce

70	To meet the needs of our customers’ developers and architects, we’re looking for the following to be listed as Headless capable.
71	
72	The ISV Partner must have a publicly available REST API or SDK for facilitating integrations.
73	The ISV Partner must have an integration guide on how to implement the solution with Salesforce Commerce APIs.
74	Any resources of significant value to the developer can be included part of the headless integration, but are not required. Assets such as React components that work with our Composable Storefront or a sample app that demonstrates how the various bits come together are encouraged. ISV Partners are advised to host these assets in their website.
75	
76	Why should I provide a B2C Commerce Headless Integration listing?
77	B2C Commerce is a clear leader in the enterprise eCommerce market and we see trends develop quickly. While mostly sophisticated customers are adopting Headless, just about every customer and prospect is looking at Headless to reap the benefits it offers. Consider this projection from Gartner: By 2023, 50% of new commerce capabilities will be incorporated as API-centric SaaS services.
78	
79	
80	What resources I will need to develop a B2C Commerce Headless Integration?
81	ISV partners who will be integrating with Composable Storefront, they will need access to Managed Runtime to deploy any example PWA Kit integrations.
82	
83	Requirements:
84	
85	The ISV Partner must be an active B2C Commerce (ISV) Partner
86	The ISV Partner must have access to Account Manager
87	The ISV Partner must complete the course: Get Started with Headless Development (Provisions Version) in the Partner Learning Camp.
88	Partners must complete PWA Kit & Managed Runtime workshop training before being fully provisioned.
89	SI partners need to sign up their team for upcoming live workshop for PWA Kit and Managed Runtime, via the Enablement Calendar here: https://salesforce.quip.com/RdSPATbTdy4i
90	If you have completed the workshop and the Managed Runtime access has not been provisioned yet, please log a case via the Help Portal:
91	
92	Select your Partner Org in the top-right dropdown menu.
93	Select ‘Create a Case’ > Inquiry Type: ‘Partner Program Support’
94	In the Product field, select 'Partner Programs & Benefits'.
95	In the Topic field, select 'B2C Commerce ISV Partners'.
96	In the Subject, add 'B2C Commerce Partner Managed Runtime Request'
97	In the Description, add the URL for the Environment in Managed Runtime where the bundles created during completion of the PLC Curriculum were deployed (format should be https://<project>-<environment>.mobify-storefront.com)
98	The ISV partner will then be responsible for adding users in Account Manager with the Managed Runtime User role, which will allow them to log into https://runtime.commercecloud.com for access.
99	
100	
101	How do I submit my Listing?
102	An AgentExchange listing is the storefront for your solution and is the best way to close new business. Publishing your listing is the first step to acquiring new customers and generating user reviews. Publishing your listing is an easy, self-guided experience every step of the way.
103	
104	Access the B2C Commerce ISV Partner Onboarding Guide for steps on how to create and publish your listing.
105	
106	
107	Does a B2C Commerce Headless Integration listing require certification?
108	B2C Commerce Headless Integration must adhere to applicable security guidelines as defined in the updated AgentExchange Partner Security Guidelines. In addition, Salesforce reserves the right to perform a security review of any solution at our sole discretion.
109	
110	Keep in mind, the AgentExchange Partner Security Guidelines are not exhaustive. To secure your solutions, we encourage partners to follow all applicable enterprise security standards including Open Web Application Security Project (http://www.owasp.org/) (OWASP) guidance.
111	
112	However, the Commerce Cloud Product Management team will be reviewing the integration guide for completeness. Also, Partners are required to include security best practices in their documentation.
113	
114	As noted above, there is no requirement to use a Commerce Cloud Certified Developer. In most cases a Consulting partner will not be necessary to deliver a B2C Commerce Headless Integration listing.
115	
116	
117	Will a B2C Commerce Headless Integration listing cost me anything?
118	At this time, there is no additional cost nor additional contract terms for this listing type as it’s a discretionary program benefit. Exceptions apply for the On-Demand Sandbox usage - access the B2C Commerce ISV Partner Onboarding Guide for more details on the On-Demand Sandbox Pricing Policy.
119	
120	
121	Where will the B2C Commerce Headless Integration listing be published?
122	The B2C Commerce Headless Integration listings will be published on the AgentExchange Marketplace.
123	
124	
125	Are there more resources available for B2C Commerce Headless Integration listings?
126	Yes, there are additional resources.
127	
128	A guide template can be found here.
129	An example documentation for all levels of implementation as well as the type of React components that are helpful can be seen at Algolia.
130	Our friends over at Magnolia have posted a video in support of their integration guide and sample project with React component.
131	For more about the Commerce APIs - visit the Salesforce Developer Center for B2C Commerce.
132	For more about the PWA-Kit and Managed RunTime - take a look at the Trail that introduces PWA-Kit and Managed RunTime. There is also more detail available on the Salesforce Developer Center for B2C Commerce.
133	Partners can sign-up and attend the virtual workshops on PWA Kit & Managed Runtime. 
134	
135	How can I get a demo Composable Storefront and demo-managed runtime environment?
136	Check out our Get Started resources for the Composable Storefront. This documentation provides the instructions for setting up a brand new composable storefront by using our PWA Kit app generator.
137	
138	Note: you will have to complete the ‘Get Started with Headless Development’ course on Partner Learning camp to gain access to Managed Runtime.

ISV partners who will be integrating with Composable Storefront, they will need access to Managed Runtime to deploy any example PWA Kit integrations.

The ISV Partner must be an active B2C Commerce (ISV) Partner
The ISV Partner must have access to Account Manager
The ISV Partner must complete the course: Get Started with Headless Development (Provisions Version) in the Partner Learning Camp.
Partners must complete PWA Kit & Managed Runtime workshop training before being fully provisioned.
SI partners need to sign up their team for upcoming live workshop for PWA Kit and Managed Runtime, via the Enablement Calendar here: https://salesforce.quip.com/RdSPATbTdy4i
If you have completed the workshop and the Managed Runtime access has not been provisioned yet, please log a case via the Help Portal:

Select your Partner Org in the top-right dropdown menu.
Select ‘Create a Case’ > Inquiry Type: ‘Partner Program Support’
In the Product field, select 'Partner Programs & Benefits'.
In the Topic field, select 'B2C Commerce ISV Partners'.
In the Subject, add 'B2C Commerce Partner Managed Runtime Request'
In the Description, add the URL for the Environment in Managed Runtime where the bundles created during completion of the PLC Curriculum were deployed (format should be https://<project>-<environment>.mobify-storefront.com)

An AgentExchange listing is the storefront for your solution and is the best way to close new business. Publishing your listing is the first step to acquiring new customers and generating user reviews. Publishing your listing is an easy, self-guided experience every step of the way.

Access the B2C Commerce ISV Partner Onboarding Guide for steps on how to create and publish your listing.


Does a B2C Commerce Headless Integration listing require certification?
B2C Commerce Headless Integration must adhere to applicable security guidelines as defined in the updated AgentExchange Partner Security Guidelines. In addition, Salesforce reserves the right to perform a security review of any solution at our sole discretion.

Keep in mind, the AgentExchange Partner Security Guidelines are not exhaustive. To secure your solutions, we encourage partners to follow all applicable enterprise security standards including Open Web Application Security Project (http://www.owasp.org/) (OWASP) guidance.

However, the Commerce Cloud Product Management team will be reviewing the integration guide for completeness. Also, Partners are required to include security best practices in their documentation.

As noted above, there is no requirement to use a Commerce Cloud Certified Developer. In most cases a Consulting partner will not be necessary to deliver a B2C Commerce Headless Integration listing.

At this time, there is no additional cost nor additional contract terms for this listing type as it’s a discretionary program benefit. Exceptions apply for the On-Demand Sandbox usage - access the B2C Commerce ISV Partner Onboarding Guide for more details on the On-Demand Sandbox Pricing Policy.

The B2C Commerce Headless Integration listings will be published on the AgentExchange Marketplace.

Yes, there are additional resources.

A guide template can be found here.
An example documentation for all levels of implementation as well as the type of React components that are helpful can be seen at Algolia.
Our friends over at Magnolia have posted a video in support of their integration guide and sample project with React component.
For more about the Commerce APIs - visit the Salesforce Developer Center for B2C Commerce.
For more about the PWA-Kit and Managed RunTime - take a look at the Trail that introduces PWA-Kit and Managed RunTime. There is also more detail available on the Salesforce Developer Center for B2C Commerce.
Partners can sign-up and attend the virtual workshops on PWA Kit & Managed Runtime.

Check out our Get Started resources for the Composable Storefront. This documentation provides the instructions for setting up a brand new composable storefront by using our PWA Kit app generator.

Note: you will have to complete the ‘Get Started with Headless Development’ course on Partner Learning camp to gain access to Managed Runtime.

# Development Workflow Differences with PWA Kit

PWA Kit uses a traditional Webpack-based development server with configuration spread across multiple files. Storefront Next leverages Vite for faster development with native ESM, instant HMR, and type-safe configuration. The shift to Vite provides a more modern developer experience with faster feedback loops and better tooling integration.

## Key Differences

| Aspect        | PWA Kit             | Storefront Next              |
| ------------- | ------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Dev Server    | Webpack Dev Server  | Vite Dev Server              |
| CLI Tool      | `pwa-kit-dev start` | `sfnext dev`                 |
| HMR           | Webpack HMR         | Vite native HMR              |
| Config Format | JavaScript          | TypeScript                   |
| Env Vars      | Standard .env       | Typed with `PUBLIC__` prefix |
| Testing       | Jest                | Vitest                       |
| Type Safety   | Optional            | Required                     |

## Key Similarities

1. Port conventions: Both can run on any port.
2. API proxy pattern: Both use `/mobify/proxy/` path.
3. Environment variables: Both support .env files.
4. Node.js debugging: Both support `--inspect` flag.
5. Express-based: Both use Express for SSR.

## Storefront Conversion Considerations

1. Port Change

   - Update any hardcoded port references from 3000 to 5173.
   - Or configure Vite to use port 3000.

2. Environment Variables

   - Convert standard env vars to `PUBLIC__` prefix format.
   - Update .env files with new naming convention.

3. Config Migration

   - Convert `config/default.js` to `config.server.ts`.
   - Add TypeScript types for configuration.

4. Testing Migration
   - Convert Jest tests to Vitest.
   - Update test configuration files.

opening `:::important` callout, read in full earlier the same day: "Managed Runtime only supports
applications created from a PWA Kit template." I had this fact already but under-weighted its
implication. It means MRT is not general-purpose Node/container hosting (unlike AWS/Heroku/GCP) —

rendering/routing system), never a lightweight generic API service.

  delivered as *one of*: (a) a B2C Commerce Cartridge running inside **SFCC itself**, not MRT; (b)
  a **Node module / NPM package that extends the same PWA Kit Express server** — "PWA Kit ships

integration's backend on its own Managed-Runtime-hosted project*, is **not a supported pattern**

the one-sentence discard reason), and the real comparison becomes Option A vs. the modular-app
middle option** — flag this restructure to the user before drafting, since it changes what the
ticket's own Option A/B framing means.

+Scope" depends on **all 8 storefronts sharing one first-party domain** for session-cookie sharing.
+This part still holds. What does NOT hold — see the correction immediately below — is the
+mechanism originally proposed here (hosting per-integration backends as *sibling MRT projects*
+called server-to-server).
+## CORRECTION (later 2026-08-10): Option B as literally stated is not platform-supported
+User supplied a direct quote from **Mani (former Integration Lead)** plus two more docs

+offering, no topology content). This meaningfully corrects the architectural mechanism proposed

+**Mani's statement (verbatim, as relayed by the user):** "you cannot run multiple separate or
+independent Node.js application processes (like auxiliary microservices or distinct integration
+apps) inside a single Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT) environment. MRT is strictly designed to
+host one unified application bundle generated from an official PWA Kit template."
+**Independently corroborated by a primary source already in hand** — mrt-overview.md's own
+opening `:::important` callout, read in full earlier the same day: "Managed Runtime only supports
+applications created from a PWA Kit template." I had this fact already but under-weighted its
+implication. It means MRT is not general-purpose Node/container hosting (unlike AWS/Heroku/GCP) —

+  with a slim server that forwards requests to the React rendering pipeline but **can be extended
+  to take arbitrary action on incoming HTTP requests**"; or (c) a **Connected App** — an

+integration's backend on its own Managed-Runtime-hosted project*, is **not a supported pattern**

## Correction to my last analysis — literal Option B isn't platform-supported

This new input meaningfully corrects one piece of what I reported last turn. I need to walk that back clearly rather than bury it.

**Mani's statement is confirmed by primary sources, not just asserted.** I already had the fact that backs it up — `mrt-overview.md`'s own opening callout says "Managed Runtime only supports applications created from a PWA Kit template" — but I under-weighted what that means: MRT isn't general-purpose Node hosting. Every MRT project must be a full PWA-Kit-shaped bundle (React + Express + PWA Kit's rendering pipeline), never a lightweight generic API service. `b2c-commerce-integration.md` (Salesforce's own ISV integration FAQ — a primary source, not a search summary) confirms this directly: **"Every Composable Storefront must have a project created in Runtime Admin"** — one project per storefront — and its integration-pattern table shows backend logic for a Composable Storefront only ever ships as one of: an SFCC cartridge (runs in Business Manager, not MRT), a **Node module extending the same PWA Kit Express server**, or an externally-hosted "Connected App" API. There's no fourth pattern of "a second MRT project as one integration's backend."

**What I got wrong last turn:** I proposed that "per-integration app" could work as sibling MRT projects called server-to-server via the existing undici pools. That mechanism is wrong for MRT specifically — MRT's multi-project support is real (confirmed again by the user's search results' "map multiple distinct domains to multiple separate MRT environments or projects, e.g. brand-us.com vs brand-uk.com"), but it's for **multi-brand/multi-domain separation**, not for splitting one storefront's integration code. The undici-pool mechanism itself is still right — it's just for calling **external, non-MRT services**, not sibling MRT apps.

**What this means for the TSD:** the ticket's literal Option B ("dedicated MRT application per integration/domain") isn't viable as stated — not because of Zimmermann's config or org limits, but because the platform doesn't run that shape of thing at all. The real comparison narrows to **Option A (single app, today's default) vs. the ticket's own "middle option" (single modular app** — one project, integration code organised into separated modules each with its own undici pool/timeout/error boundary). A third path — hosting one specific high-risk integration's proxy layer on genuinely external infrastructure (AWS/GCP/Heroku, or an ISV's own API) — is architecturally sound per Salesforce's own guidance, but it's a materially bigger, separate decision (new hosting target, new CI/CD, new on-call) that probably belongs in the discarded-option slot or a forward-looking §7 Risks note, not as a real contender in this TSD.

`development-workflows-difference-with-pwa-kit.md` turned out unrelated to this ticket — it's a dev-tooling comparison (Webpack vs. Vite) against a separate, newer Salesforce offering called "Storefront Next," with no MRT-topology content. Read in full, nothing to carry forward here.

Memory updated with the full correction and sourcing. This changes the shape of §3 Options Analysis meaningfully — worth restructuring so the ticket's Option A/B framing maps onto "single app vs. modular app," with literal per-integration hosting explicitly named and discarded with reasons, rather than presenting it as a live contender.

## Testing strategy for the SFCC-237 TSD

For a feature TSD, "testing" means new functional tests. For an architecture-decision spike like this, the deliverable is a *decision*, not new code — so proving the case means three different kinds of evidence, not one test suite. Breaking it down by what actually needs proving:

### 1. Prove Option B is truly unsupported — empirical, not just documentary
Right now the invalidation rests on Mani's statement + Salesforce's own docs — strong, but secondhand relative to Zimmermann's actual account. The rigorous version: someone with Runtime Admin access (you) spends ~10 minutes attempting to create a second lightweight project via `b2c mrt project list` / the Runtime Admin UI's "New Project" flow, and confirms it still demands a full PWA Kit bundle — no "lightweight service" option anywhere in the flow. This converts a cited claim into a first-hand-verified one before it goes in front of Tim.

### 2. Prove today's isolation is actually zero — and that wiring the pools fixes it
This is the one genuinely worth writing as real code, because it's cheap and it's the single most concrete piece of evidence for the whole recommendation. Per [testing.md](.claude/rules/testing.md), this is a Vitest-layer "integration boundary" test, not E2E:
- **Before fix:** mock one integration's `fetch` (e.g. `marketingCloud.ts`) to reject, call it alongside an unrelated call (e.g. `slasTokens.ts`) in the same request context, and show the unrelated call also fails/hangs — empirically demonstrating "unhandled rejection breaks rendering" against Zimmermann's actual code, not just the MRT doc's general claim.
- **After fix:** once `connectionPools.ts`'s dispatchers are actually wired with per-pool timeouts, re-run the same test and show the unrelated call now succeeds independently.
- This doubles as a permanent regression test once merged — not disposable spike scaffolding.

### 3. Tie to validation that's already planned, don't duplicate it
- **LCP/performance at scale** — architecture.md §9.3 already commits to a Stage load-test pass measuring per-pool queue-depth once traffic exists. The TSD should reference this as the mechanism, not invent a new one.
- **Bundle-size headroom** — already covered by the existing `bundlesize` CI gate; note the 400MB/249MB MRT ceiling is so far above current sizes (~100KB/515KB) that this is a non-issue, not a new test to write.

### 4. Cheap audits that back §4.3 Trade-offs Accepted with real numbers
- **Secrets/ownership blast radius:** a 5-minute look at the existing project's Users & Permissions page in Runtime Admin — how many people currently hold Developer/Admin role (= access to every integration's env vars/deploy), turning "accepted trade-off" into a concrete number.

## What holds up as-is
- **Performance/LCP** — tying to the already-planned Stage load test is correct, no change needed.
- **Ownership** — the quick Runtime Admin access-count audit is correct, no change needed.
- **Cost** — not a "test" at all, stays informational (task #8), no change needed.

## What's a real gap — the biggest finding
The ticket explicitly says failure isolation means **"event loop / memory / process, not just sockets."** My original plan (one test: break integration A's promise, watch it break integration B) only proves *one* of those three failure shapes — a rejected promise. It says nothing about:
- **Event loop blocking** — a heavy, *synchronous* piece of work in one integration's code (a big JSON parse, a slow regex) freezes the *entire* Node process for every concurrent request, not just the request that triggered it. This is actually the more classic Node.js isolation failure than a rejected promise, and it's the one the ticket names first. **Need to add this as a second scenario.**

## The hands-on testing plan, walked through step by step

Same kitchen picture as before — one shared kitchen, several chefs (integrations), all in one room. Here's literally what we're going to do to prove where the danger is and whether our fix actually works.

### Test 1: "One burnt pan shouldn't ruin the whole order" (the rejection test)
**What we do:** Write a test that plays out one customer's order needing food from two chefs at once — say, Chef Marketing-Cloud and Chef SLAS-login. We deliberately make Chef Marketing-Cloud's pan catch fire (force that one `fetch` call to fail) while Chef SLAS-login's dish is completely fine.
**What we watch:** Does SLAS-login's dish still reach the customer, or does the whole order get cancelled because of the *other* chef's fire?
**Before the fix:** we expect to see the whole order cancelled — proving today, one broken integration really can take down a page that didn't even need it.
**After the fix:** we wire in the safety wall (the connection-pool code that already exists but isn't switched on) and run the exact same test — now SLAS-login's dish comes out fine even though Marketing-Cloud's still burned. Same test, two runs, before-and-after — that's the proof, not our say-so.

### Test 2: "One slow chef shouldn't freeze the whole kitchen" (the event-loop test)
**What we do:** This is a different kind of danger. Instead of a fire (a rejected promise), imagine a chef who plants themselves in the middle of the kitchen doing something slow *by hand* instead of putting it in the oven and walking away — nobody else can move past them while they're doing it. In code terms: one integration doing a heavy, blocking calculation instead of properly `await`-ing it. We run a fast, simple request alongside a deliberately slow blocking one and time how long the fast one takes.
**What we watch:** Does the fast request's time balloon just because the slow one happened to be running at the same moment?
**Important honesty point:** unlike Test 1, there's no "wire in a wall" fix for this one — the connection pools are about *network* traffic, not about one chef physically blocking the room. This risk doesn't get engineered away; it gets *managed* by a coding rule (never write blocking code in integration handlers). So this test's job isn't "prove we fixed it" — it's "prove this danger is real, so it goes in the TSD as an accepted trade-off with a rule attached, not swept under the rug."

### Test 3: "A fire in the US kitchen section shouldn't burn AU's food" (the multi-region test)
**What we do:** Simulate two customers at once — one ordering off the AU menu (which never touches, say, Avalara tax lookups), one ordering off the US menu (which does). We break the Avalara-style call for the US order only.
**What we watch:** Does the AU order — which has *nothing to do with* that integration — still come out fine, or does it get caught in the blast too, purely because both orders are being cooked in the same room?
**Why this matters:** "AU doesn't use that integration" sounds safe, but it isn't, if AU and US share one kitchen. This test makes that concrete instead of theoretical, which is exactly what the ticket means by "multi-region" — it's not a separate concern, it's the same fire risk wearing a different hat.

### The three quick Runtime Admin look-arounds (5-15 minutes each, done by you, not code)
1. **"Try to rent half a kitchen"** — open Runtime Admin, click New Project, and see firsthand whether it ever offers "just a backend service" or always assumes a full storefront. Also glance at the deploy commands — do they only ever accept a full built storefront, never a lighter package? This is us checking the landlord's actual counter, not just the brochure.
2. **"Count the master keys"** — open the existing project's Users & Permissions page and count how many people currently hold Developer or Admin role (both mean "can see every integration's secrets and deploy the app"). Turns "lots of people can see everything" into a real number for the TSD.
3. **The leftover small stuff** — while you're in there anyway: is the kitchen running on the newer or older equipment (ARM vs x86)? How many environments exist against the 100/10 ceiling? Is the login-cookie setting switched on? Quick glances, not tests.

### Two things we're deliberately NOT re-doing
- **A big kitchen-heat test (performance/LCP)** — already scheduled for later once there's real customer traffic to measure against. We just point the TSD at that instead of running our own mini version now.
- **Checking the kitchen doesn't get too big (bundle size)** — a robot already checks this automatically every time anyone changes the code. Nothing new needed.

### One thing we're honestly skipping, and saying so
- **A slow gas leak building up over days (memory leaks)** — genuinely can't be shown in a quick test; it only reveals itself under hours or days of real traffic. Rather than fake a quick version of this, the TSD says plainly: "not provable at this stage, revisit with a real load/soak test once actual integration code exists."

That's the whole hands-on plan — three new tests we write, three quick admin look-arounds, two pointers to work already scheduled, one honest gap. Once we lock in a branch name, Test 1 is the one I'd build first since it's the most complete proof (has both a before and an after).

# V&V Re-Check: SFCC-237 Undici Connection Pool Isolation Claim

I independently re-verified all 11 items against the current state of the repo (branch `develop`, clean except unrelated translation-compile diffs). **Bottom line up front: the original claim holds up on every point I could test. I found no evidence contradicting "7 pools defined, 0 wired up, 0 in-process failure isolation today."** I did find several genuinely new, non-contradicting pieces of context (governance reason for the gap, and which of the 7 pools even have live code behind them yet) that sharpen the finding — flagged clearly below.

---

## 1. `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts` — full read

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding**, with one precision note.

The file (`/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`, 76 lines) defines exactly 7 `Pool` instances from `undici` (line 19: `import { Pool } from 'undici';`):

| Export (code, line) | Origin | connections | connectTimeout | bodyTimeout |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sfccScapiPool` (L22-25) | `` `https://${COMMERCE_API_SHORT_CODE}.api.commercecloud.salesforce.com}` `` | 5 | 5_000 | 8_000 |
| `sfccPaymentsPool` (L33-36) | `SFCC_PAYMENTS_HOST` env, placeholder fallback | 10 | 5_000 | 8_000 |
| `mulesoftPool` (L42-46) | `MULESOFT_BASE_URL` env, placeholder fallback | 20 | 5_000 | 10_000 |
| `marketingCloudAuthPool` (L49-52) | `` `https://${MARKETING_CLOUD_SUBDOMAIN}.auth.marketingcloudapis.com}` `` | 5 | 5_000 | 15_000 |
| `marketingCloudRestPool` (L55-58) | `` `https://${MARKETING_CLOUD_SUBDOMAIN}.rest.marketingcloudapis.com}` `` | 5 | 5_000 | 15_000 |
| `googlePlacesPool` (L61-65) | `'https://places.googleapis.com'` | 5 | 3_000 | 5_000 |
| `booxiPool` (L71-75) | `BOOXI_BASE_URL` env, placeholder fallback | 5 | 3_000 | 5_000 |

This is a 1:1 numeric match with the "7 pools with the same names/caps" description, and with the docs (items 8/9 below). **Precision note:** the *literal string names* `sfcc-scapi`, `sfcc-payments`, etc. do not appear as string values anywhere in this file (`Pool()` takes a positional origin URL, not a name) — those kebab-case identifiers are the docs' table labels, not code tokens. The code's actual export identifiers are `sfccScapiPool`, `sfccPaymentsPool`, `mulesoftPool`, `marketingCloudAuthPool`, `marketingCloudRestPool`, `googlePlacesPool`, `booxiPool`. Conceptually these are unambiguously the same 7 pools — this is a naming-convention difference, not a discrepancy in substance.

Also note the file's own doc-comment (L1-18) explicitly frames this as **not yet wired up**: *"Use the per-call `dispatcher` option on `fetch()` calls inside ssr.js to route requests through the correct pool"* (L5-6) — phrased as an instruction for future work, not a description of existing behavior. Two of the seven (`sfccPaymentsPool`, `booxiPool`) carry explicit `TODO`s (L30-31, L69) saying their real origin hostnames are still unconfirmed placeholders.

## 2. Repo-wide grep for every plausible reference

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding.** Every single hit outside `connectionPools.ts` is either documentation/rules prose or unrelated noise. None wire a pool into a real fetch call.

- **`connectionPools`** (4 hits total): the file's own self-reference in its doc-comment (`connectionPools.ts:9`), plus 3 governance/rules docs describing it as a protected file (`.cursor/rules/tier1FrozenFiles.mdc:55`, `.claude/rules/frozenFiles.md:48`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md:381`) — all read `connectionPools.ts — undici pool isolation (blast-radius mitigation)` in a file-ownership table, not code.
- **`dispatcher`** (case-insensitive, 6 hits): `connectionPools.ts:5,10` (the file's own doc-comment example), `.docs/architecture.md:261,275`, `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md:471,473` (documentation prose), and one false positive — `package-lock.json:36539: "storybook": "dist/bin/dispatcher.js"` — Storybook's own CLI binary path, unrelated to undici.
- **`undici`** (case-insensitive, ~13 hits): `connectionPools.ts:2,8,13,19` (the real usage), `package-lock.json` transitive dependency entries (`undici-types` pulled in by `@formatjs/ts-transformer`; `undici` itself pulled in as `^7.25.0` under some other package's nested `node_modules` — **not a direct dependency of this app**, see item 6), and doc prose in `.docs/architecture.md` / `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` / `.docs/temp/openItems.md:48` / `.docs/integration/01-sfcc.md:141`.
- **Each of the 7 pool export names individually**: every one of `sfccScapiPool`, `sfccPaymentsPool`, `mulesoftPool`, `marketingCloudAuthPool`, `marketingCloudRestPool`, `googlePlacesPool`, `booxiPool` appears **only inside `connectionPools.ts` itself** (its own `export const` line, plus one internal cross-reference comment for `sfccScapiPool` at L29, and the doc-comment's illustrative import at L9 for `sfccPaymentsPool`). **Zero hits in `ssr.js` or any of the four handler files.** No file anywhere imports any of these seven names.
- **`Pool(`** (the undici constructor call): the 7 real calls in `connectionPools.ts` (L22, 33, 42, 49, 55, 61, 71), plus one more hit — `.docs/architecture.md:267: const checkoutPool = new Pool('https://api.checkout-service.com', {` — this is a **fictional, illustrative tutorial snippet** embedded in the doc (fake pool name, fake origin, not a real file or import path in the repo). It's worth flagging precisely because it's literally a worked example of what wiring *would* look like — and the real code doesn't do it.
- **`setGlobalDispatcher`**: exactly 1 hit, in prose only — `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md:473`, a comparative note ("the per-call `dispatcher` option is safer than the `setGlobalDispatcher`..."). **Zero calls to `setGlobalDispatcher` anywhere in actual code.**

## 3. Full content of every `overrides/app/ssr/` file + `ssr.js` — every `fetch()` call

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding.** I read all 6 files in `overrides/app/ssr/` (confirmed exactly these 6 exist, no new file added: `connectionPools.ts`, `contentSecurityPolicy.ts`, `marketingCloud.ts`, `paymentMetadata.ts`, `slasTokens.ts`, `types.ts`) plus `overrides/app/ssr.js`. `contentSecurityPolicy.ts` (CSP directives object) and `types.ts` (TS interfaces) contain **zero** `fetch()` calls. `ssr.js` itself contains **zero** direct `fetch()` calls — it only wires Express routes and delegates to the handler functions imported from `./ssr/*`.

I found exactly **4 fetch calls** total, and quote each in full — **none has a `dispatcher` key**:

1. **`overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts:78`**
   ```js
   const response = await fetch(JWKS_URI);
   ```
   No options object at all — `dispatcher` **absent** (trivially).

2. **`overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts:42-44`**
   ```js
   const response = await fetch(app.sfPayments.metadataUrl, {
     headers: { Accept: 'application/json' },
   });
   ```
   `dispatcher` **absent**.

3. **`overrides/app/ssr/marketingCloud.ts:38-46`**
   ```js
   const tokenResponse = await fetch(tokenUrl, {
     method: 'POST',
     headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
     body: JSON.stringify({
       grant_type: 'client_credentials',
       client_id: clientId,
       client_secret: clientSecret,
     }),
   });
   ```
   `dispatcher` **absent**.

4. **`overrides/app/ssr/marketingCloud.ts:61-75`**
   ```js
   const emailResponse = await fetch(emailUrl, {
     method: 'POST',
     headers: {
       Authorization: `Bearer ${marketingCloudToken}`,
       'Content-Type': 'application/json',
     },
     body: JSON.stringify({
       definitionKey: marketingCloudConfig.templateId,
       recipient: {
         contactKey: emailId,
         to: emailId,
         attributes: { 'magic-link': marketingCloudConfig.magicLink },
       },
     }),
   });
   ```
   `dispatcher` **absent**.

**4 of 4 live fetch calls in the SSR layer lack the dispatcher option** — direct, concrete confirmation of the claim for the code paths that actually run today.

## 4. `overrides/app/request-processor.js` and `worker/main.js`

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding.**

- **`overrides/app/request-processor.js`** (119 lines) is still the **unmodified PWA Kit example/boilerplate**. Its own header says: *"This is an EXAMPLE file. To enable request processing, rename it to 'request-processor.js' and update the `processRequest` function..."* (L8-9) and explicitly warns *"Do not make external requests from this code"* (L20-21). The body only strips query-string parameters (e.g. `usid`/`code` on `/callback`) and has bot-detection logic commented out (L104-112). It contains **zero** network calls, zero isolation/resilience logic. (Corroborated independently by `.claude/rules/frozenFiles.md:60`: *"`overrides/app/request-processor.js` — add here when populated."* — i.e., the project's own governance doc confirms this file is still unpopulated.)
- **`worker/main.js`** is a **7-line stub** — nothing but the BSD-3-Clause license header comment. Zero code, zero logic of any kind.

Neither file contains any isolation/resilience mechanism.

## 5. `git log` for the 7 SSR-related files

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding.** Verified via `git log --oneline --follow` on `develop`, and cross-checked with `git log --all` (every local + remote branch) — identical results, no other branch has additional commits:

| File | Commits (hash / date / subject) |
|---|---|
| `connectionPools.ts` | **`610020e` / 2026-06-19 / "refactor(ssr): split ssr.js into typed helper modules"** — only commit ever |
| `slasTokens.ts` | `2484515` / 2026-06-26 / "chore: ESLint fixes"; `610020e` / 2026-06-19 / same as above |
| `paymentMetadata.ts` | `610020e` / 2026-06-19 / same — only commit |
| `marketingCloud.ts` | `2484515` / 2026-06-26 / "chore: ESLint fixes"; `610020e` / 2026-06-19 / same |
| `ssr.js` | `610020e` / 2026-06-19 / same; `3cfc0d9` / 2026-06-12 / "fix(config): hardcode dev1 proxy hosts, enable SLAS private client, add dev1 env config"; `cd60b7a` / 2026-06-12 / "Initial commit during Detailed Design phase" |
| `request-processor.js` | `cd60b7a` / 2026-06-12 / "Initial commit during Detailed Design phase" — only commit |
| `worker/main.js` | `cd60b7a` / 2026-06-12 / same — only commit |

`connectionPools.ts` has **never been touched since the day it was created** (2026-06-19). Nothing in this set has changed in **~7 weeks** relative to today (2026-08-11). This directly confirms nothing has changed since the claim was last checked.

## 6. `package.json` dependencies/devDependencies — resilience libraries

**CONFIRMED — none exist.** Full contents read at `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/package.json`:

- `"dependencies"` (L114-118): `@contentful/experiences-sdk-react`, `@contentful/live-preview`, `contentful` — only 3 entries, all Contentful-related.
- `"devDependencies"` (L21-41): `@playwright/test`, `@salesforce/retail-react-app`, Storybook packages, `husky`, `jsdom`, `semver`, `ts-morph`, `typescript`, `vitest`, etc. — 18 entries.

No `opossum`, `cockatiel`, `p-retry`, `p-timeout`, or `undici` anywhere in either list. `undici` and `p-timeout` appear **only** in `package-lock.json` as transitive dependencies of other packages (not requested by this app's own `package.json`), so they are not an "other isolation mechanism" available to app code.

## 7. Test files referencing `connectionPools`, `dispatcher`, or the 4 SSR handlers

**CONFIRMED — none exist.** The entire repo (including `e2e/`) contains exactly 3 test files:

## 8. `.docs/architecture.md` — "Blast-Radius Mitigation" section, verbatim

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding, essentially verbatim.** Full section is lines 257-291:

> **## Blast-Radius Mitigation** (L257)
>
> Multiple upstream integrations (SFCC, MuleSoft/Omneo, Global-e, Narvar, Contentful, Didomi, Inside Chat) mean a failure or attack targeting one service must not cascade. A PWA-relevant mitigation can be done in the SSR layer. (L259)
>
> The SSR layer in `overrides/app/ssr.js` uses **Node's native `fetch`**, which is backed by `undici`. Undici's `dispatcher` option (the per-call `dispatcher` option on individual `fetch()` invocations) allows each upstream origin to be given its own connection pool with an independent cap. This prevents a slow or flooded integration (e.g. checkout APIs) from exhausting connections for unrelated origins (e.g. Contentful, JWKS). (L261)

**Via `git blame`**, this exact section was authored by commit `c8157619` (2026-06-17) and last touched by `4be80965` (2026-07-10, table-formatting only). The file's most recent commit overall, `7d9c4af` (2026-07-16), did **not** touch this section (confirmed by blame — no lines in 257-291 attributed to it).

## 9. `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` §12 and §12.1, verbatim

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding**, plus important supporting nuance not previously called out.

**§12 "Graceful Degradation"** (L445-458) — opens: *"Each external system fails independently — one outage does not break a page."* (L447), followed by a per-system failure-mode table (Contentful, Global-e, Didomi, Omneo writes/reads, Google Maps, AP21, Narvar).

**§12.1 "Blast-Radius Containment"** (L460-487), full verbatim text:

> ### 12.1 Blast-Radius Containment (L460)
>
> The failure modes above describe what the PWA does when a single integration is unavailable. This section covers how to limit the *spread* of an attack or outage — ensuring a degraded integration cannot consume shared resources and take down unrelated features. (L462)
>
> #### Edge (outside the PWA — Infrastructure / SI Partner) (L464)

Undici's `dispatcher` option (the per-call `dispatcher` option on individual `fetch()` invocations) allows each upstream origin to be given its own connection pool with an independent cap. This prevents a slow or flooded integration (e.g. checkout APIs) from exhausting connections for unrelated origins (e.g. Contentful, JWKS). (L471)
>
> > **Implementation note:** the per-call `dispatcher` option is safer than the `setGlobalDispatcher` in a managed environment (MRT) since it does not touch the global dispatcher that Salesforce internal libraries may rely on. The `commerce-sdk-react` hooks manage their own HTTP client server-side (Commerce SDK) and are not affected in either approach. (L473)
>
> [same 7-pool table as architecture.md, L477-485, identical names/caps/timeouts]

> **Contentful:** The Contentful SDK (`contentful` v11) does not expose a `dispatcher` hook on its internal fetch calls, so connection isolation for Contentful is not achievable through this pattern. Primary mitigation is the graceful degradation rule in §12 (Render page without editorial content). (L487)

This matches the remembered "7 pools with the same names/caps" exactly. **Two trivial wording diffs vs. architecture.md's copy of the table** (not a substantive disagreement): the `sfcc-payments` row says *"waiting confirmation from Mani"* here (L480) vs. *"confirm with Integration team"* in architecture.md; the `booxi` row says *"TBD"* (L485) here vs. *"TBD — confirm with Integration team"* in architecture.md.

**Genuinely new context worth surfacing (does not contradict the claim, but sharpens it):**
- §12.1 itself draws the exact scoping the original claim uses — it explicitly separates "Edge (outside the PWA)" mitigations (WAF, rate limiting, SFCC Business Manager) from "SSR layer (inside the PWA)" mitigations. So there *is* some blast-radius protection in the overall system — just not inside the Node process, which is precisely what the claim is scoped to. This is corroboration, not contradiction.
- L473 states plainly that `commerce-sdk-react` hooks (i.e., most real SFCC commerce traffic — PDP/PLP/cart/basket) "manage their own HTTP client... and are not affected in either approach" — meaning the 7-pool mechanism was **never designed** to cover the bulk of SFCC traffic, only the four direct-`fetch()` SSR endpoints.
- L487 confirms Contentful — likely the highest-volume SSR-side call — is explicitly **out of scope** for this mechanism by design (SDK limitation), with graceful degradation as the only mitigation.

## 10. `git log` for both docs files

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding**, both have commit history, but the actual blast-radius content is stale relative to "today."

I went further and verified via `git blame` + `git show --stat` on the most recent commit to each file that **the Blast-Radius content specifically was not touched recently**: the last commit to `tsd-architecture.md`, `2224db3` (2026-07-16, "fix: resolve CodeRabbit findings from PR #37 review"), only edited a Stage/UAT topology table plus 4 other unrelated docs (`projectState.md`, `releaseBranchesRules.md`, `openItems.md`, `README.md`) — confirmed by its diffstat (`.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md | 4 ++--`), nowhere near §12/§12.1. The actual §12.1 content was last substantively touched by `4be80965` (2026-07-10, table formatting) — over a month before today's date (2026-08-11) — and no commit, ever, on any branch, has modified the actual code to wire the pools up.

## 11. Broader unbiased sweep for other resilience mechanisms

This is where I actively hunted for something that would contradict the claim. **I found nothing that contradicts it**, but I found three adjacent, genuinely new items worth flagging transparently — none of them provide in-process isolation for the shared Node/MRT SSR runtime:

- **`circuit breaker`**: 0 hits anywhere in the repo.
- **`bulkhead`**: 0 hits anywhere in the repo.
- **`AbortController`**: 2 hits, both in **`overrides/app/hooks/useContentful.ts`** (L31, L94) inside `useContentfulEntry`/`useContentfulEntries`. **NEW FINDING, but does not contradict the claim** — this is client-side React (browser) code (`useState`/`useEffect` hooks fetching directly from `cdn.contentful.com`/`preview.contentful.com`), not server-side SSR code, and it's a standard React "cancel in-flight request on unmount/dependency change" pattern (`return () => controller.abort()`), not a timeout or circuit-breaker — no `setTimeout` is ever wired to the controller. It runs in a different process (the browser) from the shared Node MRT process the claim is about.
- **`AbortSignal.timeout`**: 4 hits, in **`scripts/switchEnv.mjs`** (L690, L733) and **`scripts/sfcc/_shared.mjs`** (L81, L108). **NEW FINDING, but does not contradict the claim** — these are genuine request timeouts, but they live in standalone developer-run CLI tooling (`npm run env`, SFCC site-config sync scripts), executed manually outside the deployed storefront's request-handling process. They don't run in, and have no effect on, the production Node/MRT process serving shopper traffic.
- **`p-timeout`**: 0 direct hits; appears only inside `package-lock.json` as some other package's transitive dependency — not used by any app code.
- **`retry`** (broad sweep, ~50 hits): the overwhelming majority are non-code — UI copy/translation strings (`"account.payments.action.retry": "Retry"`), Playwright CI test-retry config (`playwright.config.js:29,48` — test-runner retries, unrelated to production resilience), and documentation describing **third parties'** own retry behavior (MuleSoft's "Failover-Reversal 2.0", Global-e's own retry mechanism, Adyen Drop-in's own retry, Contentful 429 "exponential backoff and retry" as a documented expectation with no corresponding code found). The one substantive **app-code** hit is **`overrides/app/components/_app-config/index.tsx:222-236`**, which explicitly sets TanStack Query's `retry: false` (queries and mutations) and `retryOnMount: false` (server-side only) — i.e., **retries are deliberately disabled**, the opposite of a resilience mechanism. This doesn't provide isolation either; it just means a failed call fails once and stops, per the comment "Recommended settings for PWA-Kit usages" (L219).

**Additional finding beyond the literal 11-item checklist, surfaced because it materially sharpens the picture:** I checked whether the integrations behind 3 of the 7 pools (`mulesoft`, `google-places`, `booxi`) have *any* implemented call path elsewhere in the repo (components, `config/*.js` `proxyConfigs`, env files) that might bypass `ssr.js` entirely. They do not:
- `config/default.js:209-218`'s `proxyConfigs` array contains only two SFCC entries (`api`, `ocapi`) — no MuleSoft/Google/Booxi proxy config exists.
- `.env.sample:179` shows `MULESOFT_BASE_URL=` blank/unset.
- `.docs/prd/account.md:230,297` and `.docs/integration/06-booxi.md`/`index.md:27` describe Booxi appointment history as still **"scope/timeline TBC"** — not yet built.
- No `places.googleapis.com` fetch exists outside `connectionPools.ts` itself and the CSP allow-list (`contentSecurityPolicy.ts:23,53`, which merely permits the domain, it doesn't call it).

This means **4 of the 7 pools** (`sfcc-scapi`, `sfcc-payments`, `marketing-cloud-auth`, `marketing-cloud-rest`) correspond to integrations with real, currently-shipping `fetch()` calls that concretely bypass their pool today (proven in item 3), while the other **3** (`mulesoft`, `google-places`, `booxi`) correspond to features that have **no implementation at all** in this repo yet — those pools were built speculatively, ahead of the feature code that would eventually need them. Both groups are still accurately described as "100% unused" — this just clarifies *why*, and that the "isolation" story for 3 of the 7 hasn't even reached the stage of having something to isolate.

**Also worth surfacing (governance context, explains *why* nothing has changed, doesn't change the technical fact):** `connectionPools.ts` and the whole `overrides/app/ssr/` directory are listed as **Tier 1 "Frozen Files"** in three separate project rule docs — `.claude/rules/frozenFiles.md:42-58`, `.cursor/rules/tier1FrozenFiles.mdc`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md:381` — owned by "Integration / SI Partner," with the rule: *"These files must not be modified by Claude Code without the developer explicitly naming the file in the prompt AND confirming they have spoken to the listed owner. No exceptions."* This is a plausible institutional reason the gap has persisted (a deliberate change-control gate, not simple oversight) — but it doesn't alter the current-state fact: today, the pools are unused and there is no in-process failure isolation.

---

### Overall verdict

Across all 11 items, **I found nothing that contradicts or changes the original claim**. The claim — 7 undici pools defined in `connectionPools.ts`, zero wiring anywhere else in the codebase (zero imports, zero `dispatcher` usage, zero `Pool(` calls outside the one file, zero test coverage), all 4 live SSR fetch calls confirmed dispatcher-less, no alternative circuit-breaker/bulkhead/resilience library in `package.json`, and no code change to any of the 7 relevant files in ~7 weeks — is **fully substantiated** by direct, current-state inspection. The only things this pass adds are clarifying, non-contradicting context: the governance reason the file is frozen, the split between "pools bypassed by live code" (4) vs. "pools built ahead of unimplemented features" (3), and a few unrelated timeout/cancellation patterns elsewhere (browser-side Contentful hook, dev-tooling scripts) that don't provide in-process isolation for the shared Node/MRT server and thus don't change the "zero failure isolation in the single shared Node process" conclusion.
