## What the three tests together prove

All three trace back to **one single mechanical fact**: today, every integration — built or not yet built — runs inside one shared Node.js process. Each test pressure-tests a different consequence of that one fact, and none of them repeat each other.

**Test 1 — shared process means shared fate for async work.** A rejection in one integration's code can erase an unrelated, already-succeeded result for anything waiting on both. This is the "is this actually real, or just a theoretical risk from the ticket's own description" question — answered against real shipped code, not an invented example, and it surfaced a genuine, fixable bug in the process (`sendMagicLinkEmail`'s missing error handling).

**Test 2 — shared process means shared CPU time, and this one has no fix.** A synchronous, blocking operation anywhere freezes *everything* else on that process, for exactly as long as it runs, with zero relationship to how unrelated the other work is. This is a fundamentally different kind of finding than Test 1 — Test 1's danger goes away once someone adds a try/catch; Test 2's danger is permanent under this architecture. No wiring, no pool, no dispatcher touches it. The only mitigation is a coding rule, not infrastructure.

**Test 3 — the sharing has no boundary where you'd hope one existed.** Same mechanism as Test 1, but it proves the failure doesn't respect the one axis Zimmermann cares about most — region. An AU customer with zero relationship to Marketing Cloud can still lose their result to a US customer's Marketing Cloud failure, purely because of process-sharing and timing. There is no such thing as "AU is safe from a US-only integration's outage" under this model.

### Put together
This isn't three examples of the same thing — it's a complete, non-overlapping case: **(1)** the danger is demonstrated today, not hypothetical; **(2)** even after fixing everything fixable, one category of risk is permanent and unfixable by architecture; **(3)** whatever protection you might assume comes from Zimmermann's own regional structure doesn't actually exist at the process level. Together, that's the real, evidenced cost of Option A — not a paraphrase of the ticket's own description, but three independently reproducible facts backing it.

### What these tests do *not* tell us — and why the Runtime Admin checks still matter
These are all **code-level** findings. They say nothing about how *often* this would actually bite in production, what MRT's platform genuinely allows or costs, or anything about the current live project's configuration. That's a completely different category of question — not "is there a risk" but "what does the platform actually permit, and what's already true about our account" — which is exactly what the Runtime Admin look-arounds are for. They're not redundant with what we just proved; they answer a question no amount of local testing ever could.

content.text:
Good question to press on — and being precise about it matters: **the three tests don't actually demonstrate the specific thing the pools are for.** They demonstrate something adjacent that shares the same root cause but needs a different fix.

**What the pools are specifically for:** resource exhaustion by volume or slowness. If MuleSoft gets flooded or starts responding slowly, and every integration shares one undivided pool of connections, MuleSoft's slow requests can occupy connections that Google Places or SFCC payments needed — so *those* unrelated calls also start failing or timing out, purely because MuleSoft is hogging the shared pool. Giving each origin its own capped pool prevents that specific mechanism: MuleSoft can max out *its own* 20 connections without touching the 5 reserved for Google Places.

**What Tests 1 and 3 actually demonstrated is a different mechanism: a clean, fast HTTP error (503) with no try/catch around it.** Marketing Cloud didn't hang, didn't get flooded, didn't consume any shared connections at all — it just answered quickly with "no." The problem was never about connections; it was that nothing caught the resulting exception. If the dispatcher pools were fully wired right now, `sendMagicLinkEmail` would fail in exactly the same way, at exactly the same speed — a wired pool has no opinion on what your code does after `fetch()` resolves with a bad status. That's a code-level gap, not a network-level one, and it's why I flagged a few turns back that "wire the pools" and "fix this" are two separate pieces of work.

**Test 2 is explicitly unrelated to the pools too** — I said this when we ran it: pools govern sockets, not who holds the CPU. A blocking loop doesn't touch a network connection at all.

**So what actually connects them:** not that the tests prove the pools would help — they don't, directly — but that all four things (the three tests, plus the un-wired pools) are different symptoms of the exact same underlying gap: **there is currently no isolation boundary of any kind between integrations in this shared process** — not at the connection layer, not at the error-handling layer, not at the CPU layer. The pools are the piece of that gap Zimmermann already started building and never finished; the tests found two *other* pieces nobody had started on yet.

**One honest thing worth naming:** none of the three tests we wrote actually exercises the pools' specific scenario — a slow or flooded origin starving a different origin's connections. That's a real, distinct claim that's currently backed only by the design rationale already written in `tsd-architecture.md` §12.1, not by a reproducible test the way the other three findings are. Want me to write that as a fourth test before we move on, or is citing the existing documented rationale enough for the TSD without a dedicated test for it?

I've now exhaustively checked all 15 items. Here's the full report.

## Summary

**No counter-evidence found for any of the three failure modes.** I actively hunted for mitigation, coverage, tests, or documentation across the entire repo (not just the files named in the prompt) and found none that closes any of the three gaps. I did find two things worth flagging prominently: (a) existing "blast-radius" documentation exists but is *provably* about a different problem (network connection pooling, not error propagation), and (b) the one piece of code that implements even that unrelated mitigation is dead code — never imported anywhere.

---

### Failure mode 1 — rejection propagation / missing error handling

**1. Repo-wide search for error-handling wrappers — NO EXISTING COVERAGE FOUND.**
```
grep -rniE "asyncHandler|catchAsync|withErrorHandling|errorBoundary|unhandledRejection|uncaughtException|express-async-errors|safeAsync|wrapAsync" (all .ts/.tsx/.js/.jsx/.json/.md, excl. node_modules)
```
Zero hits, repo-wide. Not a single one of these patterns exists anywhere, in code or comments.

**2. `overrides/app/ssr.js` read in full (191 lines) — FOUND, and it confirms the gap rather than closing it.** Exact route registration for both `sendMagicLinkEmail` call sites:
```js
// lines 150-162
app.post(passwordlessLoginCallback, (req, res) => {
  const slasCallbackToken = req.headers['x-slas-callback-token'];
  const redirectUrl = req.query.redirectUrl;
  validateSlasCallbackToken(slasCallbackToken).then(() => {
    sendMagicLinkEmail(
      req, res,
      config.app.login?.passwordless?.landingPath,
      process.env.MARKETING_CLOUD_PASSWORDLESS_LOGIN_TEMPLATE,
      redirectUrl,
    );
  });
});

// lines 168-178 (reset-password variant — same shape)
app.post(resetPasswordCallback, (req, res) => {
  const slasCallbackToken = req.headers['x-slas-callback-token'];
  validateSlasCallbackToken(slasCallbackToken).then(() => {
    sendMagicLinkEmail(req, res, config.app.login?.resetPassword?.landingPath, process.env.MARKETING_CLOUD_RESET_PASSWORD_TEMPLATE);
  });
});
```
No `try/catch`, no `.catch()` anywhere. Worth noting it's actually **worse** than a simple missing catch: `sendMagicLinkEmail(...)` is called inside the `.then()` callback but its promise is never `return`ed, so it isn't even chained to `validateSlasCallbackToken(...).then(...)`'s own promise — it's a fully orphaned floating promise from the moment it's created. There is no code path, anywhere, by which its rejection could reach anything Express is watching.

**3. Global 4-arg Express error middleware — NO EXISTING COVERAGE FOUND.**
```
grep -rnE "\(err,\s*req,\s*res,\s*next\)|\(error,\s*req,\s*res,\s*next\)" (all .ts/.js)
grep -rnE "app\.use\(\s*\(?\s*\w+\s*,\s*\w+\s*,\s*\w+\s*,\s*\w+\s*\)?\s*=>" (all .ts/.js)
```
Both zero hits, repo-wide. No such middleware is registered anywhere, in `ssr.js` or elsewhere. And even hypothetically: it wouldn't matter here. Because point 2's handler returns synchronously before the async chain settles and `next(err)` is never called, an error middleware would never see this failure — it only catches errors that flow through Express's `next()` mechanism, and this one structurally never does.

**4. `worker/main.js` — FOUND, confirms it's still a stub.** Exactly 6 lines / 224 bytes, pure license header, nothing else:

- Checked all 10 files in `.claude/rules/` (`css.md`, `conventions.md`, `components.md`, `tagging.md`, `testing.md`, `protectedFiles.md`, `squadA.md`, `frozenFiles.md`, `squadB.md`, `typescript.md`) plus `AGENTS.md` for `error.handl|try.catch|catch\(|resilien|fault.toleran|graceful|async.*error|promise.*reject` — the **only** hits are `AGENTS.md:155` "Graceful Degradation" and `AGENTS.md:174` (an unrelated Magento-migration gotcha).

I've now exhaustively checked all 15 items. Here's the full report.

## Summary

**No counter-evidence found for any of the three failure modes.** I actively hunted for mitigation, coverage, tests, or documentation across the entire repo (not just the files named in the prompt) and found none that closes any of the three gaps. I did find two things worth flagging prominently: (a) existing "blast-radius" documentation exists but is *provably* about a different problem (network connection pooling, not error propagation), and (b) the one piece of code that implements even that unrelated mitigation is dead code — never imported anywhere.

---

### Failure mode 1 — rejection propagation / missing error handling

**1. Repo-wide search for error-handling wrappers — NO EXISTING COVERAGE FOUND.**
```
grep -rniE "asyncHandler|catchAsync|withErrorHandling|errorBoundary|unhandledRejection|uncaughtException|express-async-errors|safeAsync|wrapAsync" (all .ts/.tsx/.js/.jsx/.json/.md, excl. node_modules)
```
Zero hits, repo-wide. Not a single one of these patterns exists anywhere, in code or comments.

**2. `overrides/app/ssr.js` read in full (191 lines) — FOUND, and it confirms the gap rather than closing it.** Exact route registration for both `sendMagicLinkEmail` call sites:
```js
// lines 150-162
app.post(passwordlessLoginCallback, (req, res) => {
  const slasCallbackToken = req.headers['x-slas-callback-token'];
  const redirectUrl = req.query.redirectUrl;
  validateSlasCallbackToken(slasCallbackToken).then(() => {
    sendMagicLinkEmail(
      req, res,
      config.app.login?.passwordless?.landingPath,
      process.env.MARKETING_CLOUD_PASSWORDLESS_LOGIN_TEMPLATE,
      redirectUrl,
    );
  });
});

// lines 168-178 (reset-password variant — same shape)
app.post(resetPasswordCallback, (req, res) => {
  const slasCallbackToken = req.headers['x-slas-callback-token'];
  validateSlasCallbackToken(slasCallbackToken).then(() => {
    sendMagicLinkEmail(req, res, config.app.login?.resetPassword?.landingPath, process.env.MARKETING_CLOUD_RESET_PASSWORD_TEMPLATE);
  });
});
```
No `try/catch`, no `.catch()` anywhere. Worth noting it's actually **worse** than a simple missing catch: `sendMagicLinkEmail(...)` is called inside the `.then()` callback but its promise is never `return`ed, so it isn't even chained to `validateSlasCallbackToken(...).then(...)`'s own promise — it's a fully orphaned floating promise from the moment it's created. There is no code path, anywhere, by which its rejection could reach anything Express is watching.

**3. Global 4-arg Express error middleware — NO EXISTING COVERAGE FOUND.**
```
grep -rnE "\(err,\s*req,\s*res,\s*next\)|\(error,\s*req,\s*res,\s*next\)" (all .ts/.js)
grep -rnE "app\.use\(\s*\(?\s*\w+\s*,\s*\w+\s*,\s*\w+\s*,\s*\w+\s*\)?\s*=>" (all .ts/.js)
```
Both zero hits, repo-wide. No such middleware is registered anywhere, in `ssr.js` or elsewhere. And even hypothetically: it wouldn't matter here. Because point 2's handler returns synchronously before the async chain settles and `next(err)` is never called, an error middleware would never see this failure — it only catches errors that flow through Express's `next()` mechanism, and this one structurally never does.

**4. `worker/main.js` — FOUND, confirms it's still a stub.** Exactly 6 lines / 224 bytes, pure license header, nothing else:
```
1  /*
2   * Copyright (c) 2023, Salesforce, Inc.
3   * All rights reserved.
4   * SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
5   * For full license text, see the LICENSE file in the repo root or https://opensource.org/licenses/BSD-3-Clause
6   */
```
`git log --follow --oneline -- worker/main.js` → one commit, ever: `cd60b7a Initial commit during Detailed Design phase`. Never touched since. No `process.on('unhandledRejection', ...)` or `process.on('uncaughtException', ...)` — confirmed both by reading the file and by a repo-wide grep for `unhandledRejection|uncaughtException`, which returns **zero hits anywhere in the entire repo**, not just this file.

**5. Existing tests covering these handlers' error paths — NO EXISTING COVERAGE FOUND.** The only test file anywhere touching `marketingCloud.ts`/`sendMagicLinkEmail`/`emailLink`/`sendMarketingCloudEmail` is `overrides/app/ssr/blastRadius.test.ts` itself — which `git status` shows as **Untracked**, i.e., the file you just wrote. There is no pre-existing test.

**6. `.claude/rules/`, `AGENTS.md`, `.docs/` conventions — FOUND two adjacent-but-non-covering sections; no general "catch your own errors" rule exists anywhere.**
- Checked all 10 files in `.claude/rules/` (`css.md`, `conventions.md`, `components.md`, `tagging.md`, `testing.md`, `protectedFiles.md`, `squadA.md`, `frozenFiles.md`, `squadB.md`, `typescript.md`) plus `AGENTS.md` for `error.handl|try.catch|catch\(|resilien|fault.toleran|graceful|async.*error|promise.*reject` — the **only** hits are `AGENTS.md:155` "Graceful Degradation" and `AGENTS.md:174` (an unrelated Magento-migration gotcha).
- `AGENTS.md:155-157`: *"Each external system must fail independently — one outage must not break the whole page. Two defaults override any per-system behaviour: **fail closed on consent**... and **never silently substitute a different checkout, payment, or commerce flow** when an integration is down — surface an explicit error instead."* This is a **product/UX-level requirement** (what the user should see when an integration is down), not an engineering directive to wrap async handlers in try/catch. It doesn't mention Promise handling, uncaught rejections, or coding patterns at all.
- `.docs/architecture.md:257-291` ("Blast-Radius Mitigation") and `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md:460-487` ("12.1 Blast-Radius Containment") are near-duplicate sections — **both describe only the undici per-origin connection-pool pattern** (isolating socket/connection exhaustion between upstream origins). Neither mentions try/catch, Promise rejection, or `Promise.all`/`allSettled` semantics anywhere.
- Notably, `tsd-architecture.md`'s own "12. Graceful Degradation" table (lines 445-459) lists a specific documented failure mode for Contentful, Global-e, Didomi, Omneo (writes), Omneo (reads), Google Maps, AP21, and Narvar — **Marketing Cloud / magic-link email has no row in this table at all.** Even the one doc that catalogs "what happens when integration X fails" is silent on the exact integration in question.
- No file anywhere states "every integration handler must catch its own errors" or equivalent.

**7. `package.json` — NO EXISTING COVERAGE FOUND.** Full dependency + devDependency list manually reviewed (not just keyword grep) — no `express-async-errors`, `express-async-handler`, or any comparable library.

---

### Failure mode 2 — event-loop / CPU blocking

**8. Repo-wide search for CPU-offload/blocking-detection mechanisms — NO EXISTING COVERAGE FOUND.**
```
grep -rniE "worker_threads|new Worker\(|piscina|workerpool|\bcluster\b|setImmediate|process\.hrtime|toobusy|event-loop-lag|eventloop"
```
Exactly one hit in the whole repo, and it's a false positive: `overrides/app/components/header/index.tsx:348` — `{/* Mobile right: icon cluster */}`, a JSX comment describing a **UI icon grouping** in the header component, unrelated to Node's `cluster` module or any CPU-offload mechanism.

**9. `package.json` — NO EXISTING COVERAGE FOUND.** Same full manual dependency review as item 7 — no `piscina`, `workerpool`, `toobusy`, or similar.

**10. `.docs/architecture.md` / `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` — NO EXISTING COVERAGE FOUND beyond the known undici discussion.** Grepped both for `cpu.bound|worker.thread|event.loop|blocking|blast.radius|per.region|circuit.breaker|bulkhead`. The only substantive hits are the same two Blast-Radius sections already quoted in item 6 (network-layer/connection-pool only). One incidental regex match — `architecture.md:97` / `tsd-architecture.md:531`, the SIT environment-topology row containing "**non-blocking** for Digital releases" — is about release-cadence scheduling, not the event loop; dismissed as irrelevant. There is no mention of CPU-bound work, worker threads, or event-loop protection anywhere in either document.

---

### Failure mode 3 — cross-region / per-region isolation

**11. Per-region isolation/circuit/bulkhead mechanism — NO EXISTING COVERAGE FOUND.** Searched `region` co-occurring with `isolat|circuit|bulkhead|blast` on the same line, across **all** `.ts`/`.tsx`/`.js` files and then again across **all** `.md` files repo-wide. Zero real hits. The one match, `.docs/planning/regionalConfigSyncPlan.md:289` — *"now a wider blast radius than originally scoped — it also touches the e2e fixture"* — uses "blast radius" colloquially to describe the **scope of a config-sync code change** (how many files it touches), not runtime failure isolation between regions. Not relevant.
- `overrides/app/config/countries.ts` (read in full, 100+ lines): purely a URL-slug → SFCC site/locale/currency/`checkoutOwner`/`boutiqueRegion` mapping table. No failure-handling, no isolation, no circuit-breaking concept anywhere in the file.
- `config/sites.js`: grepped for the same terms — no hits; only references are pointers to `regional.md`/`regionalConfigSyncPlan.md` for *routing* rules, not failure isolation.
- No request-scoped context object anywhere scopes error handling by region — the only per-region concept in the codebase is routing/locale/currency/checkout-ownership, exactly as failure mode 3 asserts.

**12. `overrides/app/request-processor.js` — FOUND, confirms it is unchanged.** Re-read in full; still verbatim the Salesforce example stub (`// This is an EXAMPLE file. To enable request processing, rename it to 'request-processor.js'...`). `git log --follow --oneline` shows exactly one commit ever: `cd60b7a Initial commit during Detailed Design phase`. Zero customization, confirmed both by content and by history.

---

### General / recency check

**13. `git log --since="7 days ago"` (and 14 days, for margin) on `overrides/ .docs/ config/ worker/` — FOUND commits, none relevant.**
```
e4c342e feat(config): add US international storefront (ZimmermannUSIntl, /en-ca/)
51c0290 docs(contentful): fix duplicated "only" in the live-preview note
c686912 fix(contentful): noindex preview error paths; 500 on missing config (SFCC-49)
e287ae5 docs(contentful): align preview no-token behaviour (both paths 404 + noindex)
7ed19fa fix(contentful): gate ?preview no-token path with 404 + noindex (SFCC-49)
```
None touch `ssr.js`, any `overrides/app/ssr/*` file, `worker/main.js`, or anything related to error handling, event-loop, or region isolation — all five are either the new US storefront config or Contentful-preview-routing fixes. `git status` on the current branch (`feature/mrt-blast-radius-tests`) shows only translation-compile artifacts modified plus your own two new files (`blastRadius.test.ts`, `.docs/temp/componentStoryReview.md`) untracked. No sign of a concurrent session touching any file relevant to these three failure modes.

**14. `.docs/temp/openItems.md` and `.docs/prd/` — NO EXISTING COVERAGE FOUND.** `openItems.md` read in full: all 41 items across 18 integrations are third-party **credential/contract/documentation** gaps (SFCC MFA scope, Contentful content model, MuleSoft OpenAPI spec, Omneo auth handshake, GiveX/Booxi/Adyen/Google Maps/reCAPTCHA/Narvar/Didomi/GTM/Inside Chat/Optimizely/Crazy Egg/Measmerize/Vimeo credentials and specs) — a completely different category of open item than shared-process architecture risk. Zero mention of rejection propagation, event-loop blocking, or per-region process isolation. Grepped all of `.docs/prd/*.md` for `isolat|circuit|bulkhead|shared.process|single.process` — zero hits.

**15. `overrides/app/ssr/` directory, listed fresh — FOUND, confirms no unexpected file.**
```
blastRadius.test.ts       (7512 bytes, Aug 11 18:55 — untracked, this is your new test)
connectionPools.ts        (3341 bytes, Jul 9)
contentSecurityPolicy.ts  (3370 bytes, Jul 16)
marketingCloud.ts         (5338 bytes, Jul 9)
paymentMetadata.ts        (1860 bytes, Jul 9)
slasTokens.ts             (3335 bytes, Jul 9)
types.ts                  (859 bytes, Jul 9)
```
Exactly the six known files plus your own new test. No other new file exists.

---

### Bonus finding (not one of the 15, but directly relevant — flagging prominently)

While verifying item 6/10, I checked whether the one real mitigation that *does* exist in the codebase — the undici connection pools in `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts` — is actually wired into the code path these failure modes concern. **It is not.**
```
grep -rn "connectionPools" (all .ts/.js)        → only self-referential doc-comment + your test's comment
grep -rn "dispatcher" overrides/                → only inside connectionPools.ts's own doc-comment
grep -n "undici|Pool" ssr.js, marketingCloud.ts, paymentMetadata.ts, slasTokens.ts → zero hits

Genuinely tried to overturn this, not just re-confirm it. Across the whole repo, docs, configs, Confluence, and JIRA:

- **No error-handling safety net exists anywhere.** Zero hits repo-wide for any async-error wrapper (`asyncHandler`, `express-async-errors`, etc.), zero 4-argument Express error middleware, zero `process.on('unhandledRejection', ...)` or `uncaughtException` handler in the entire codebase — not just in `worker/main.js`, which was already known to be an empty stub.

content.text:
## Purpose of Test 1b

Test 1 proves danger that's *conditional*: "if a caller ever aggregates this call with `Promise.all`, it loses an unrelated success." That's real, but someone could reasonably ask "does anything in the code actually do that today?"

Test 1b would close that gap by reproducing the **exact shape of the real call site** — a promise created inside a `.then()` callback and never `return`ed, exactly what `ssr.js` does — instead of the direct, awaited call Test 1 uses. The point isn't a different mechanism; it's proving the danger is **unconditional and already live**, not dependent on some hypothetical future caller writing `Promise.all` badly.

## What it would prove

When a promise is created and nobody holds onto it — no `return`, no `await`, no `.catch()` — and it later rejects, Node.js itself fires a process-level `unhandledRejection` event. Test 1b would register a listener for that exact event, trigger the call the way `ssr.js` actually does, and confirm the event fires with the Marketing Cloud error. That upgrades the finding from "could be a problem depending on how it's used" to "is already an unhandled event in the literal shipped route handler, on the real password-reset and passwordless-login endpoints, every single time Marketing Cloud fails."

## A bigger question this opens up — worth flagging before deciding whether to build it

Here's the part I haven't verified yet, and it matters a lot: in modern Node.js (v15+), an unhandled promise rejection **doesn't just log a warning by default — it crashes the process.** If that default applies here, a single Marketing Cloud hiccup wouldn't just fail one password-reset request — it could kill the entire MRT server instance, taking down every other shopper's in-flight request on that process with it. That would be a dramatically stronger finding than anything we've proven so far.

The catch: testing *that* specifically is riskier to build than what we've done. If I add a listener to check the event fires, that listener itself prevents Node's crash behavior — so it can't also prove the crash happens. Actually proving the crash would need a separate child process (so if it does crash, it's an isolated process dying, not our test runner), which is a bigger, more careful piece of test infrastructure than anything in the suite so far.

So there are really three options here, increasing in weight:
1. **Don't build 1b** — document the orphaned-promise finding as a stated risk in the TSD without a dedicated test.
2. **Build the safe version** — confirm `unhandledRejection` fires for this exact call shape. Proves it's unconditional and live, low complexity.
3. **Build the crash-verification version** — a child-process test confirming whether this actually takes the whole server down. The strongest possible evidence, but real additional build effort and needs care to do safely.

Which of these do you want?

So `catchAndLog` is a straightforward error logging function that captures exceptions and logs them through the logger instance without halting execution, rethrowing, or triggering any other side effects. The key insight is that PWA Kit's runtime in `build-remote-server.js` relies on this behavior for its remote server setup.

Since `catchAndLog` is registered as the listener for unhandled promise rejections, Node's default crash behavior (which would normally trigger in Node 15+) never activates—the presence of any listener prevents that. The error gets logged to whatever aggregation system MRT uses (Sentry, New Relic, CloudWatch, etc.), but the process continues running. This fundamentally changes how severe an unhandled rejection actually is in the deployed environment.

The crash-verification test I was considering would likely just confirm what we've now found in the source code—that no crash occurs—so the urgency around that particular concern drops significantly. However, the underlying problem remains: even though the process survives, the handler only logs the error and doesn't actually resolve the failed request, leaving the shopper hanging.

Since `sendMagicLinkEmail` is called without awaiting it, when it rejects internally, the Express response object never gets a status or message sent back. This means the shopper's password-reset or passwordless-login request just stalls until the 20-second request timeout fires, at which point they get a generic 502 Bad Gateway instead of a meaningful error response—a real UX and reliability problem even if the server doesn't crash.

Beyond the individual shopper experience, if many magic-link requests fail simultaneously (say, during a Marketing Cloud outage), each one hangs for up to 20 seconds while consuming server resources like memory and connection handles, which could strain the system at scale and relates back to the original undici connection pool concerns.

content.text:
## This changes the picture significantly — and resolves the open question

**Found the decisive fact by reading the actual installed framework source, not guessing:** `@salesforce/pwa-kit-runtime`'s own remote-server bootstrap (`build-remote-server.js:1794` — specifically the code that builds the server for *MRT-deployed* environments, not local dev) already does this:

```js
process.on('unhandledRejection', _ssrServer.catchAndLog);
```

And `catchAndLog` itself (`utils/ssr-server/utils.js:64-74`) does exactly what its name says and nothing more:
```js
const catchAndLog = (err, context) => {
  _loggerInstance.default.error(message, { namespace: 'catchAndLog', additionalProperties: { stack: ... } });
};
```
It logs. It doesn't call `process.exit()`, doesn't re-throw, doesn't do anything else.

**This directly answers the crash question: no, the whole MRT process would not crash.** Node's "unhandled rejection kills the process" default (v15+) only applies when *zero* listeners are registered for the event — here, one already is, installed by the framework itself before any of Zimmermann's route code runs. So the scariest version of this finding doesn't hold up. Good news, and worth saying plainly rather than only reporting the alarming version.

**But that doesn't mean the request is fine — it means the failure is quieter and different than "crash."** Since the rejection is only *logged*, nothing ever calls `res.send()`/`res.json()`/`res.status()` on the real Express response for that shopper's password-reset or passwordless-login request. Based on what `mrt-overview.md` already told us (App Server execution time capped at 20s prod / 16s non-prod, then a hard HTTP 502), the actual real-world consequence is almost certainly: **the shopper's request hangs for up to 20 seconds, then gets a generic, unhelpful 502 — while the real cause sits logged somewhere, with no specific error ever surfaced.** That's a genuinely worse experience for the shopper than a fast, clean error, even though the server itself survives.

**This means Test 1b should change shape.** The crash-verification version (child process, higher risk/effort) isn't needed anymore — we already have a definitive, source-level answer. The more valuable version now is much simpler and carries none of the earlier risk: confirm that when this exact orphaned-promise pattern rejects, the mock `res` object never receives *any* response call (`send`/`json`/`status`) — directly evidencing "the shopper gets silence, not an error," which is the real, now-precise finding. No child process required.

One more check for completeness: JIRA and Confluence searches for process crash/auto-restart/supervisor/watchdog/health-check came back empty, same as everything else — nothing anywhere already covers or discusses this.

## Test 1b built and verified — 4/4 passing, lint and type-check clean

**What it proves, in two parts:**

content.text:
## What Test 1b tells us

**It turns Test 1's finding from "could happen" into "does happen."** Test 1 proved a conditional danger — *if* some caller aggregates this function's promise via `Promise.all`, the sibling's success gets lost. Test 1b proves something stronger: the real, already-shipped `ssr.js` route handlers use exactly the dangerous shape today, on production password-reset and passwordless-login routes. No hypothetical caller needed — this is what currently ships.

**It answers the crash question precisely, instead of leaving it as a scary open guess.** Before building this, the honest answer to "would this take down the whole server" was "we don't know, and Node's modern default is to crash on an unhandled rejection." Now we know, from reading `@salesforce/pwa-kit-runtime`'s actual installed code: the framework already registers its own global handler that just logs. **The server survives.** That's a real, meaningful de-escalation, and it's worth stating in the TSD exactly that plainly — this isn't a "the whole site could go down" finding, and saying otherwise would overstate the evidence.

**But surviving isn't the same as fine — it tells us precisely what actually happens instead.** Nothing ever responds to that shopper. Their request sits until MRT's own 20-second (production) or 16-second (non-prod) execution ceiling runs out, then they get a generic 502 with zero indication of what went wrong — while the real cause (a Marketing Cloud failure) gets logged somewhere via the framework, with no path back to the shopper and no guarantee anyone's watching that specific log stream. That's the concrete, bounded, verified consequence — slow, silent, generic failure — not a server crash and not a clean error either.

**It connects to something already flagged elsewhere in this project.** AGENTS.md's accepted-risks section already notes there's no client-side error reporting and detection "relies on support tickets." Test 1b shows exactly where that gap bites in practice: a shopper hits a real failure, gets nothing useful, and the only way anyone finds out is a support ticket or someone happening to check MRT logs.

**What it doesn't change:** the recommendation is untouched — this is still the same root cause (no error handling in `sendMagicLinkEmail`) as Test 1, just precisely characterized instead of assumed. And it's scoped to this one call site — it tells us this exact pattern is possible and unguarded here, not that every integration handler has the same gap (we already separately confirmed the other three handlers *do* catch their own errors properly).

If I had to pick the single most useful piece of evidence in the whole suite for convincing Tim, it's this one — every other test proves something could theoretically go wrong; this one proves something specific already does, on a route real shoppers use, with the exact consequence spelled out rather than guessed at.

## Two findings — one significant

### There are 7 environments, not 6 — there's an undocumented `DEV1`

DEV, **DEV1**, Production, SIT, STG, TEST, UAT. `DEV1` appears in **none** of our sources: no `config/dev1.js`, no push script, no deploy workflow, not in Confluence 05.6's environment table, not in the GitHub Environments list. A repo-wide grep for "dev1" returns **zero hits**.

I traced its history to be sure: `config/dev1.js` was added in commit `3cfc0d9` (June 12 — "hardcode dev1 proxy hosts, enable SLAS private client, add dev1 env config") and later removed in `2c9e49f`. So the repo-side config was deliberately retired — **but the MRT environment itself was never deleted, and something deployed to it yesterday at 9:42 AM.**

**The mechanically interesting part**, which ties straight back to the config-resolution tracing we did earlier: because `getConfig()` falls back to `config/default.js` when there's no `config/{target}.js`, a `pwa-kit-dev push -t dev1` **silently succeeds** — inheriting `default.js`'s config, pointing at the *dev* SCAPI/OCAPI hosts. So DEV1 is a fully deployable environment with no per-tier config, no CI trail, no docs, and no recorded owner.

**To be fair to it, though** — there's a benign reading worth stating alongside: MRT's own docs encourage creating environments freely, and we already know from earlier work that *the shared dev target gets clobbered by other people's branches*. So DEV1 was plausibly created on purpose as someone's isolated dev target — which is itself a small argument *in favour* of environment separation. It's undocumented-and-unwired, not necessarily a mistake.

**Why it matters for the TSD:** it's concrete evidence on two of the ticket's named scoring dimensions — deploy/rollback and ownership. The current one-project model already shows real drift in practice; under Option B that surface multiplies with every additional project.

Also: **Production last deployed Jun 30**, ~6 weeks stale while the other six all deployed Aug 11 — consistent with the earlier finding that the `prod` environment has no vars or secrets configured yet.

**Headroom:** 7 of 100 environments used. Confirms the earlier maths — literal per-integration Option B (18 × 6 = 108) breaches the cap by itself; domain-grouped 3–5 apps (25–37 total) fits fine.

### One caution on the Account Settings screenshot

Those three toggles are **notification preferences, not status indicators**. "x86 Server Architecture End of Life — Enabled" means *email me about x86 EOL* — it does **not** mean any environment is on x86. Worth having on (early warning exists), but **ARM/x86 is still unanswered.** Related, from `config/default.js`: `ssrFunctionNodeVersion: '24.x'`, so the Node EOL alert is unlikely to fire soon.

### Two things left

1. **ARM or x86** — needs a per-environment check: Environments → click any one → Environment Settings → **Advanced**. (The project-level field the docs describe doesn't exist in this UI — that discrepancy is logged.)
2. **How many projects are in the Zimmermann org** — click the **PROJECT** dropdown at the top. Still unchecked, and genuinely useful: it tells us whether Option B would mean adding projects to a near-empty org or a populated one.

The variables include API credentials and configuration details for commerce and content services, starting with things like the Commerce API client ID, host, organization ID, and site information.

What stands out is that all 17 variables exist in a single flat namespace with no grouping or per-integration scoping — anyone with admin or developer access can see and edit every credential. This is a critical observation for the security analysis, as it means the blast radius for a compromised account includes all integrations' secrets at once. I also notice that the Contentful preview token is present on DEV, which aligns with what the TSD mentioned about token provisioning across environments. it for the spike: SFCC/SCAPI, Contentful, Einstein, GTM, Measmerize, Optimizely, and SLAS are all configured here, but there's a notable gap — Mulesoft, Google Cloud, Recaptcha, Adyen, Narvar, Didomi, Global-e, Booxi, CMS webhooks, Marketing Cloud, and Sentry are all missing from this environment setup.

Wait, this is actually significant. Marketing Cloud credentials aren't set on DEV, which means the integration tests that exercise `sendMagicLinkEmail` would hit the credential validation check and throw an error before even attempting the API call — that's a different failure mode than the 503 we're simulating in the tests, but it still results in an uncaught exception from the same function hitting that orphaned promise call site. So this isn't a theoretical problem—it's the actual behavior on DEV right now. Those routes will fail 100% of the time because the credentials aren't set up at all. The question is whether anyone's actually hitting those passwordless login or reset password flows on DEV, since the auth features might still be in progress.

I'm also wondering if those Marketing Cloud environment variables could be configured at the project level instead of per-environment, though from what I saw in the MRT settings, environment variables appear to be scoped to individual environments, not shared across the project.

On the Einstein API side, DEV has the EINSTEIN_API_SITE_ID set, which is expected and fine — the policy is to never enable it on SIT, but DEV is appropriate. The value matches the COMMERCE_API_SITE_ID suffix, which is worth noting for the Einstein investigation.

Looking at the DEV environment settings now, it's correctly marked as non-production, the B2C Commerce instance matches what's documented, and there are eight site IDs configured across the Zimmermann regions — AU, UK, US, EU, EU International, HK, Middle East, and US International.

The access control header isn't configured on DEV, and interestingly the environment is using MRT CDN rather than eCDN, though the documentation notes that Storefront Next stores should be using eCDN.

This raises a question about the distinction between the MRT-level CDN (CloudFront-based, sitting in front of the MRT app) versus the SFCC eCDN/Akamai layer. The architecture docs reference Akamai as the SFCC default, but there's an open item about whether the platform is actually using Cloudflare instead.

Since MRT's DEV environment shows "MRT CDN" as its own setting, that means under Option B each new project environment would need its own CDN configuration, hostname, and certificate — adding to the implementation cost.

The hostname for DEV is zimmermann-dev.sfdc-8tgtt5-ecom1.exp-delivery.com with no custom domain, and it's deployed to Asia Pacific (Sydney) rather than a US region.

But here's the critical finding: the Advanced section in the UI doesn't expose a Server Architecture field at all — I see CDN, Hostname, Region, Log Filtering, and other settings, but no ARM/x86 option anywhere. This confirms the documentation discrepancy I found earlier.

The most likely explanation is that ARM is now the default for all new projects, so the setting only appears in the UI for legacy customers with x86 environments. The API endpoints (`projects_target_*`) would probably reveal this, but I can't query those without credentials. For now, I can only note that the UI doesn't expose this control, which contradicts what the docs claim.

The account-level notification about x86 end-of-life is just a default-on alert, not proof the project actually uses x86. Looking at the environment settings now — the DEV environment is in Sydney with Info-level logging and server-side cookie access enabled.

Source maps are on for DEV, which makes sense for debugging even though the docs warn about performance impacts — I should verify this is disabled on Production. IP restrictions are wide open (no allowed IPs means all are permitted), and the proxy configs are the critical piece: there are exactly two routes set up, one pointing to the SCAPI endpoint and another to OCAPI, which matches what I'd expect from the default config file.

What's important to flag is that the MRT environment has its own proxy settings separate from what's bundled in the code — they currently align, but they're independent and could drift apart over time, which is an operational risk worth monitoring.

Looking at the DEV environment specifically, I'm noticing it has no access controls, no IP allowlist, a public hostname, and source maps are enabled. That means the full client bundle source is exposed to anyone who finds the URL, and it's pointing at a real SFCC sandbox with actual data behind it.

But I need to be careful about scope here — this is really an environment-hardening issue, not a topology one. The TSD is about the MRT app structure, so I should flag this as a separate finding rather than weave it into the main analysis. That said, it does touch on the security blast radius angle: Option B would multiply the number of environments needing hardening, even though splitting apps wouldn't directly solve the access control problem.

Now looking at the environment variables more carefully — there are 17 on DEV today, and under Option A with all integrations built out, that could balloon to 40-50 in a single flat namespace visible to all admins across seven environments. Option B would scope secrets per project, which is genuinely better for isolation, but that advantage is moot since Option B isn't viable for the platform anyway. So the honest framing for the TSD is that Option A accepts a flat secrets model per environment as a trade-off, mitigated by access discipline and role-based controls.

I need to update memory with a DEV environment deep-dive: the 17 current env vars in that flat namespace, the absence of MARKETING_CLOUD_* credentials confirming Test 1b will definitely fail on DEV, all 8 site IDs including ZimmermannUSIntl showing US-INTL is live, the B2C instance matching Confluence, and the ap-southeast-2 Sydney region being intentional rather than defaulting to us-east-1.

Now looking at the proxy and environment configuration details: there are exactly 2 proxy configs (SCAPI and OCAPI) which validates what I found in the codebase, but there's a critical gotcha—MRT proxy settings are completely separate from the bundle's proxy settings, so they could drift independently. The ARM/x86 field is missing from this UI too, confirming the doc discrepancy is unresolvable through the interface; I can infer it's likely ARM but can't verify it. Production Environment is disabled on DEV, and the collateral shows no access control headers, no IP allowlist, source maps exposed, and the default public hostname—all pointing to an environment that needs hardening.…

## DEV environment deep-dive 2026-08-12 (Environment Variables + Environment Settings, full scroll)

**Proxy Configs — FIRSTHAND CONFIRMATION of the codebase finding.** DEV's MRT-side proxy list is
**exactly two entries**, matching `config/default.js`'s `ssrParameters.proxyConfigs` precisely:
`/mobify/proxy/api/*` → `https://qmyt7hks.api.commercecloud.salesforce.com/*` (SCAPI) and
`/mobify/proxy/ocapi/*` → `https://bkzk-002.dx.commercecloud.salesforce.com/*` (OCAPI). No
MuleSoft, Google, or Booxi proxy exists on the live platform either — the code and the platform
agree.

**NEW OPERATIONAL GOTCHA (from the UI's own help text):** *"Proxy settings on the Managed Runtime
are separate from proxy settings in the bundle."* So proxies have **two independent sources of
truth** — the MRT environment settings *and* the deployed bundle's `config/*.js`. They currently
agree, but nothing enforces that; they can silently drift. Relevant to the TSD's deploy/ownership
dimensions, and it multiplies under Option B (N projects × M environments × 2 places to keep in
sync). Worth an explicit note in §5/§7.

**Environment Variables: 17 on DEV, one flat namespace, zero per-integration scoping.**
`COMMERCE_API_{CLIENT_ID,OCAPI_HOST,ORGANIZATION_ID,SHORT_CODE,SITE_ID}`, `CONTENTFUL_{DELIVERY_TOKEN,
ENVIRONMENT_ID,HOST,PREVIEW_TOKEN,SPACE_ID}`, `EINSTEIN_API_SITE_ID`, `GTM_CONTAINER_ID`,
`MEASMERIZE_BRAND_CODE`, `OPTIMIZELY_PROJECT_ID`, `PUBLIC__app__features__shopperContext__enabled`,
`PWA_KIT_SLAS_CLIENT_SECRET`, `STOREFRONT_PREVIEW_DEBUG`. All values masked in the UI. **Concrete
§4.3 Trade-offs evidence:** the platform offers no sub-scoping *within* a project — every
integration's credentials share one flat per-environment list, readable/editable by all 4 project
Admins. With ~18 integrations built this becomes ~40-50 vars in one list × 7 environments. Option B
*would* have scoped this per project — but since Option B isn't platform-viable, the honest framing
is "accepted trade-off, mitigated by access discipline and rotation, not by architecture."
(Note: `PWA_KIT_SLAS_CLIENT_SECRET` living here as an MRT env var is *correct* — the earlier
security smell in [[project_release_branch_status]] was about it being a plaintext **GitHub**
Environment *Variable*, a different store. No issue on the MRT side.)

**SIGNIFICANT — `MARKETING_CLOUD_*` is NOT set on DEV.** No `MARKETING_CLOUD_CLIENT_ID`,
`_CLIENT_SECRET`, or `_SUBDOMAIN` in the list, and MRT has no project-level env-var store to inherit
from (Project Settings has only Name/ID, Environment Defaults, Delete). So at runtime on DEV,
`marketingCloud.ts`'s `sendMarketingCloudEmail` hits its own guard —
`if (!clientId || !clientSecret || !subdomain) throw new Error('Marketing Cloud credentials are
missing...')` — and throws. **This means Test 1b's failure mode is not a hypothetical outage
scenario on DEV; it is the guaranteed, 100%-of-the-time behaviour of the passwordless-login and
reset-password callback routes on that tier today**: throw → orphaned promise at the `ssr.js` call
site → framework logs it → shopper gets no response → 20s/16s ceiling → generic 502. A *different*
trigger than the 503 the test simulates, but the identical uncaught path from the same function.
Strongest available evidence for the TSD's §1.3 Impact section. Caveat to state honestly: whether
those routes are actually exercised on DEV yet is unverified (auth flows are later-sprint work) —
the route registration exists unconditionally in `ssr.js`, so the behaviour is certain *if* hit.

**Also confirmed on DEV:** Environment ID `dev`; **Production Environment = Disabled**; B2C Commerce
Instance `bkzk_002` (matches Confluence 05.6's `f_ecom_bkzk_002`); **Site IDs = all 8 storefronts
including `ZimmermannUSIntl`** (firsthand corroboration of [[project_usintl_status]]'s "live on
dev"); **Region = Asia Pacific (Sydney)** — deliberately chosen, not MRT's `us-east-1` default
(backup region per docs = Singapore); Log Filtering `Info`; Server-Side Cookie Access **Enabled** at
the environment level too (not just the project default); CDN = **"MRT CDN"** (a third data point
against the Akamai-vs-Cloudflare open item tracked in [[project_env_topology_doc_conflicts]] — note
MRT's own CDN sits in front of the app, likely distinct from SFCC's eCDN; don't conflate); Hostname
= default `zimmermann-dev.sfdc-8tgtt5-ecom1.exp-delivery.com`, no custom domain.

**ARM/x86 — NOW DOUBLY UNRESOLVED, and unresolvable via this UI.** The Advanced section on the
*environment* exposes CDN, Hostname, Region, Log Filtering, Server-Side Cookie Access, Source Maps,
Allowed IP Addresses, Proxy Configs, Proxy User Agent — and **no Server Architecture field**, just
as Project Settings had none. So mrt-administration.md's instructions describe a control that
doesn't exist in this tenant's UI at either level. Plausible reasons (all unverified): docs ahead of
the deployed UI, the field is hidden when nothing is on x86, or it's API-only
(`projects_target_partial_update`). **Reasonable inference, explicitly NOT a verified fact:** ARM is
"the default for all new projects", the project's repo history starts 2026-06-12, and no x86 toggle
is surfaced — so it's *probably* ARM. Do not assert this in the TSD as confirmed; either mark it an
open item or have someone check via the MRT API. The account-level "x86 EOL" notification toggle
being Enabled is a default-on *notification preference*, not evidence of x86 usage.

**COLLATERAL (environment hardening — separate concern, do NOT fold into this TSD):** DEV has **no
Access Control Header configured** ("You haven't configured access control"), **no IP allowlist**
("No Allowed IP Addresses" = all IPs permitted), a **default public hostname**, and **Source Maps
Enabled**. Net effect: DEV is publicly reachable by anyone with the URL, serving readable source
maps, against a real SFCC sandbox (`bkzk_002`). Defensible for a dev tier, but worth a deliberate
decision rather than a default — and per the MRT docs, access control headers exist precisely to
stop bots bypassing CDN perimeter security and search crawlers indexing the wrong environment.
Also worth confirming Source Maps is **Disabled** on Production (not checked). This is orthogonal to
app topology — splitting into more apps wouldn't fix it, it would multiply the hardening surface —
so it belongs in its own ticket, not §5 of this TSD.

**Still open after this pass:** (a) **how many projects exist in the Zimmermann org** — the PROJECT
dropdown, still unchecked, directly relevant to Option B headroom; (b) **ARM vs x86** — not
answerable through the UI (see above); needs the MRT API or Support, or gets recorded as an open
item; (c) the commercial cost of an additional project (account team, not Runtime Admin).

## PRODUCTION + SIT inspected 2026-08-12 — two high-consequence findings

### ⚠️ FINDING A (highest consequence of the whole pass): PROD runs in a DIFFERENT AWS REGION to every other environment

**Production Region = `US East (Ohio)`. DEV, DEV1, SIT (and by inference the rest) = `Asia Pacific
(Sydney)`.** Meanwhile Production's own OCAPI proxy destination is
`https://production-ap01-zimmermann.demandware.net/*` — **`ap01` = an Asia-Pacific SFCC realm.** So
as currently configured, production would run its Node/SSR layer in Ohio while its SFCC backend sits
in Asia-Pacific, and its primary audience (AU — the `/` root storefront and x-default hreflang
target) is also in Asia-Pacific. Every SSR render on a cache miss would cross the Pacific to reach
SFCC, then serve back to AU shoppers from Ohio.

**Why this is material, tied to signed commitments:**
- `architecture.md` §9 / TSD §9: **LCP ≤ 2s at p75 mobile is client-mandated and contractual.**
  Origin region is one of the largest single determinants of that number for uncached/SSR traffic.
- `architecture.md` §9.3 / TSD §9.3 claims **Stage "mirrors production infrastructure (same MRT
  bundle size class, same CDN/edge configuration, same SFCC realm tier)"** and is therefore the
  environment where the contractual LCP figure is validated. **STG is Sydney; PROD is Ohio** — so
  Stage demonstrably does *not* mirror production on the biggest latency variable, and any LCP
  sign-off measured on Stage would not be representative of production. This invalidates a stated
  premise of the performance-measurement approach, not just a config nit.
- **Honest nuance to include, don't overstate:** MRT's CDN caches at global edge locations, so
  *cache-hit* traffic is largely insulated from origin region. The exposure is on SSR/cache-miss
  renders (PWA Kit server-renders every page), personalised routes, and the MRT→SFCC OCAPI hop.
  Real and worth fixing; not "every request is slow".
- **Fixable now, cheaply:** Region is editable in Environment Settings → Advanced, and prod is not
  live yet (see Finding B) — no traffic, no data, nothing to migrate. This is a catch-it-before-
  go-live finding, not an incident. MRT's docs note `ap-southeast-2` (Sydney) fails over to
  `ap-southeast-1` (Singapore); `us-east-2` (Ohio) fails over to `us-east-1` (N. Virginia).

### ⚠️ FINDING B: the `Production Environment` flag is **Disabled** on Production

Per mrt-overview.md, marking an environment production is what buys **prioritised monitoring by
Salesforce Support** and **Log Center debugging access** (and is what counts against the org's
10-production cap). Production currently has it **Disabled**, so it has neither. Also unconfigured
on Production: **B2C Commerce Instance = `None`**, **Site IDs = empty**, and (user-confirmed) **no
environment variables at all**. Consistent with [[project_release_branch_status]]'s finding that the
`prod` GitHub Environment is empty — prod is genuinely not stood up, and the Jun 30 bundle is
provisioning-only. All of the above belong on a go-live checklist.

**Correcting my own earlier framing on access control:** I flagged "no Access Control Header" as a
general gap. On **Production** that is arguably *correct* — prod must be publicly reachable; the
relevant prod use is requiring the header so traffic can't bypass the customer CDN (Akamai) and hit
the MRT origin directly, which matters only once a custom domain + CDN are in front (neither exists
yet). The genuine gap is on the **non-production** tiers (dev/dev1/sit — and presumably test/uat/stg),
which are publicly reachable with no header and no IP allowlist. Likewise **Source Maps**: correctly
**Disabled** on Production, Enabled on dev/dev1/sit — so someone *did* think about prod hardening
there. My earlier collateral note over-generalised; the accurate version is "source maps on the
non-prod tiers", which is defensible.

### SIT — internally consistent, and the Einstein policy is genuinely being honoured

## Runtime Admin pass complete — all 7 environments inspected

**UAT: Sydney**, internally consistent, matches Confluence exactly (`bkzk_dev` / `development-ap01`). CPA preview token present, so the "dev/test/sit/uat only, never staging/prod" boundary holds across all seven. Nice corroborating detail — UAT's OCAPI host ends `.net` (a `demandware.net` realm) while DEV/TEST/SIT end `.com` (sandbox hosts), exactly the split Confluence's table implies.

### The region finding, now in its sharpest form
**Sydney (5): DEV, DEV1, SIT, UAT, STG. Ohio (2): TEST, PROD.**

The promotion path is DEV → TEST → SIT → UAT → STG → PROD. So **every business-and-performance validation tier — SIT, UAT, and STG — sits in Sydney while Production sits in Ohio.** The entire validation chain is region-unrepresentative of the thing it validates for. That specifically breaks `architecture.md` §9.3, which designates STG as the tier where the contractual LCP ≤ 2s p75-mobile number gets signed off *because* it "mirrors production infrastructure." It demonstrably doesn't, on the single biggest latency variable. Prod's own SFCC backend is `production-ap01` (Asia-Pacific) too, so as configured prod would cross the Pacific for every SSR-side OCAPI call.

  `bkzk-002`.)

content.text:
## All 7 environments verified in text form — zero discrepancies

Cross-checked SIT, STG, TEST, UAT (plus DEV and DEV1 earlier) line by line against everything I'd recorded from the screenshots. **Every variable name, every masked suffix, every setting matches exactly.** No corrections needed anywhere.

Two things the text format genuinely added:

**1. The ARM/x86 finding is now airtight.** The complete Advanced field list is CDN, Hostname, Region, Log Filtering, Server-Side Cookie Access, Source Maps, Allowed IP Addresses, Proxy Configs, Proxy User Agent, Delete Environment. No Server Architecture field — confirmed from a full text enumeration rather than my reading of screenshots.

**2. I spotted `CONTENTFUL_HOST` exists only on DEV, not on SIT/TEST/UAT — and then found it doesn't matter.** My first thought was that this could break Contentful preview on the three tiers that have a preview *token* but no host var. I checked the code before saying so, and that instinct was wrong: `CONTENTFUL_HOST` appears in exactly two places repo-wide (`.env.sample` as an empty declaration, and the TSD as a doc reference) and is **read by no code at all**. [contentful.ts](overrides/app/config/contentful.ts) hardcodes both hosts as constants and its config type has no host field. So it's a vestigial variable — DEV having it is harmless dead config, the others lacking it is functionally irrelevant. Worth one line in an `.env.sample` cleanup, nothing more.

Glad I checked rather than reporting it — it would have been a false alarm, and it's a small addition to the recurring "documented config has drifted from actual config" theme alongside `mobify.config.js` and the MRT-vs-bundle proxy duplication.

### Where the Runtime Admin work stands
Complete for all seven environments. The four out-of-scope findings (region split, prod flag + unconfigured prod/STG, DEV1's orphaned mixed config, no access control on non-prod tiers) are logged as a separate task to raise as their own ticket(s).

**Two items remain genuinely open**, both non-blocking since Option B fails on platform grounds regardless:
1. **PROJECT dropdown** — how many projects in the Zimmermann org (one click; last thing bearing on Option B headroom)
2. **ARM vs x86** — conclusively not in the UI; needs the MRT API or Support, or goes in the TSD as a stated open item

Want to grab that project count, or shall we call the Runtime Admin checks done and move to the TSD?

Now I'm thinking through where to save the TSD file locally. The repo has a `.docs/temp/` directory with some older pre-template documents, but I need to figure out the right location for this new template-based version.

Looking at the directory structure, `.docs/temp/` seems like the right staging area for working documents before they go to Confluence. I'll name it following the template convention: `TSD-SFCC-681-mrt-application-topology.md`. Before I proceed, I should verify I'm on the correct branch where the test file lives.

I'm on `feature/mrt-blast-radius-tests` which is fine for a local draft — the user said to hold off on building and just write locally. Since this is destined for Confluence anyway, I won't commit it unless they ask. Now I need to write the actual TSD with solid content across all sections, starting with the document metadata and author information.

The problem statement needs to be tight and focused — no solutions or tech choices yet, just what's broken. The storefront's server-side integration layer on Managed Runtime currently handles only a handful of systems, but we need to support roughly 18 external integrations that don't have code yet.

The real issue is that we've never made a deliberate choice about how many Managed Runtime applications to run or how to distribute integration code across them — we're just using whatever the PWA Kit scaffold gave us by default. Since deployment topology locks in how code gets packaged and rolled back, changing this later becomes expensive once integrations are live. Plus, there's zero isolation between integrations in that shared layer right now, so a bug in one integration can break unrelated requests. So 1.3 is really about the consequences of inaction: if we don't decide the topology now, it'll crystallize by accident once we have eighteen integrations depending on it, making retrofit prohibitively expensive. The isolation gap we found in one integration becomes a recurring risk across all of them, and every deployment becomes a full-stack operation with no clear ownership of the decision.

For success, I need four concrete criteria: a signed-off topology document from the Technical Lead, verification of the current state against the live system with corrections to any stale docs, reproducible tests that prove the isolation behavior rather than just claiming it works, and a recorded decision that lets the integration work proceed without reopening this question. There's also the risk that without a clear position, the FED and SFCC squads will build against divergent assumptions.

Now I'm looking at the constraints that shape the options. The platform is SFCC B2C Commerce with PWA Kit on Managed Runtime, which only hosts PWA Kit applications—not general-purpose containers. Each project deploys as a single immutable bundle per environment, and the org has limits of 100 total environments and 10 production ones, with 7 currently in use. The execution model runs on a single Node.js instance... LCP must stay under 2 seconds at the 75th percentile on mobile per the contract. Each external system needs to fail independently so one outage doesn't cascade across the page. The core configuration files and worker logic are locked down as Tier 1 changes with no exceptions, and any topology shift will touch at least one of them. The integration scope covers roughly 18 systems documented in the integration folder, though if more systems get added later, it would expand the environment variables and module count but wouldn't fundamentally change the topology approach.

I'm also accounting for a few key assumptions: the Zimmermann license allows additional projects without extra cost, though that only affects Option B's pricing which is already ruled out architecturally. The Zimmermann infrastructure runs on ARM processors, which matters if there's ever a migration deadline. And I'm assuming no integration will need process-level isolation beyond what in-process module boundaries can provide—if one does, it would need to live outside MRT entirely as a separate infrastructure decision.

Now I'm moving into the options analysis and laying out the summary table comparing Option A against the alternatives.

For Option A specifically, I'm identifying the key advantages: it's the only model the platform currently supports with zero migration overhead, it has a simple single-bundle deployment pipeline that's already built and proven, it allows a single server-side render to pull data from multiple integrations in one request without network hops between apps, it maintains the unified session and cookie context that the eight-storefront model depends on, and it achieves isolation through in-process module boundaries per integration.

But there are real tradeoffs: all integrations run in the same Node process, so a CPU-intensive operation or unhandled error in one can cascade to unrelated requests, a single immutable bundle means rolling back one integration reverts everything shipped together, the environment-variable namespace is flat and shared across all integrations with no sub-scoping, and isolation relies entirely on convention rather than platform enforcement.

Option B would provide genuine process-level isolation with separate memory and event-loop contexts for each integration. every SSR render hits that 2-second LCP target, and the single-domain session model rules out splitting by hostname. Option B is disqualified because the platform only supports PWA Kit applications, not arbitrary Node services.

Now I'm moving into the recommendation section — Option A as a single modular MRT application, with rationale tied back to the constraints and success criteria, plus the trade-offs we're accepting.

Then I'll lay out the technical implementation path: the request flow, where module isolation happens, the component and API changes with actual file paths, the pool and dispatcher pattern for the module contract, error handling, and configuration notes. I need to flag that §5 is scoped for a later ticket since the user ruled implementation out of scope for this spike.

After that comes testing and validation mapped back to the acceptance criteria, a regression risk assessment, then risks and mitigations, and finally the decision record with sign-off.

I should also add a References section following the SFCC-249 precedent, and consider appendices for the environment inventory table and any out-of-scope findings that don't fit cleanly into the main sections.

I need to be careful not to bloat the document though — recording out-of-scope findings as "raised separately" shows they were found and routed properly, which is the honest approach. I'll keep it tight with just one appendix listing those findings and noting they're being handled elsewhere.

Now I'm ready to write the actual file, keeping it professional and thorough without unnecessary padding. I'll use the date format 12 Aug 2026 and start drafting.…

# TSD: MRT Application Topology — Single vs Per-Integration ## Document Information | Field | Value | | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Document ID** | TSD-SFCC-681 | | **Author(s)** | Marcel Angelo Navarro — Squad A / Frontend Development Lead | | **Reviewer(s)** | Tim Lavelle — Technical Lead · Gideon R. Linsangan — SFCC Squad (collaborator per ticket) | | **Created** | 12 Aug 2026 | | **Version** | v0.1 — Draft | | **Status** | Draft | | **Related Jira** | SFCC-681 (clones SFCC-237, which was closed at Sprint 2 rollover) | --- ## Version History | Version | Date | Summary of Change | Author | | ------- | ----------- | ----------------- | --------------------- | | v0.1 | 12 Aug 2026 | Initial draft | Marcel Angelo Navarro | --- ## 1. Problem Statement ### 1.1 Context The storefront runs on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT), where a Node/Express layer performs all server-side work: the SSR render, proxying to upstream APIs, token exchange, and server-side calls to integrated systems. Today that layer serves a small number of integrations. Approximately 18 external systems are in scope for the programme (`.docs/integration/`), and nearly all of them have no code written yet. Integration build-out begins in the coming sprints. ### 1.2 Problem How many MRT applications the storefront deploys — and how integration code is divided across them — has never been decided. The current arrangement is a default inherited from the PWA Kit scaffold, not a deliberate choice, and it has never been documented or signed off. Because deployment topology determines how code is packaged, deployed, and rolled back, it becomes progressively more expensive to change once integration code exists across many systems. Compounding this, the server-side layer currently provides **no failure isolation of any kind** between integrations. Seven per-origin connection pools were written for this purpose (`overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`) but are imported nowhere and attached to no request, so every integration shares one undivided execution and connection context. This is present-state fact, verified in code and by test (§6), not a projection. ### 1.3 Impact if Not Solved - Topology is set by accretion rather than decision. Each integration that lands without an agreed position makes the arrangement harder to change, and the decision is effectively made by whoever writes the first proxy. - The isolation gap persists and compounds. It was found by chance in the only integration that currently has real code, and nothing in the codebase, review process, or CI prevents the same pattern recurring in the ~17 integrations still to be built. - Deploy and rollback blast radius stays coupled: a bad change to one integration forces a rollback that also reverts every other integration shipped in the same bundle. - Squad A (FED) and the SFCC squad have no shared written position to build against, risking divergent assumptions about where integration code belongs. ### 1.4 Success Criteria 1. A single documented position on how many MRT applications the storefront deploys and how integration code is divided across them, signed off by the Technical Lead (§8). 2. The as-is baseline is verified against the live platform and the codebase rather than assumed, with any inaccuracies in existing documentation corrected. 3. The chosen topology's failure-isolation behaviour is demonstrated by reproducible automated tests rather than asserted. 4. The position is recorded specifically enough that integration build-out can proceed without re-opening the question. --- ## 2. Constraints & Assumptions ### 2.1 Constraints | Constraint | Detail | | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Platform | SFCC B2C Commerce + PWA Kit on Managed Runtime. MRT hosts **only applications created from a PWA Kit template** — it is not general-purpose Node or container hosting. | | MRT application model | One project has many bundles, but **each environment has exactly one bundle designated as deployed**. A bundle is the entire built application and is immutable once created. | | MRT organisation limits | Maximum **100 total environments** and **10 production environments** per organisation, raisable only by Salesforce Support. Currently 7 environments in use. | | Execution model | A single Node.js/Express process per environment ("App Server"), serverless and auto-scaling. Hard request-execution ceiling of **20s production / 16s non-production**, after which MRT returns HTTP 502. **Unhandled promise rejections break app rendering.** | | Storefront scope | Must work across all **8 storefronts in 6 regions** (AU, UK, US Domestic, US International, EU Domestic, EU International, HK, ME). The decisive factor is not a trade-off between the two but a platform constraint: MRT hosts only PWA Kit storefront bundles, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application at all. Once that is established, Option A is the only option that satisfies the §2 constraints, and it satisfies them without migration cost because it is the current state. The recommendation is qualified in one important respect. Endorsing Option A is not an endorsement of the status quo, because the status quo includes an isolation gap that is real and demonstrated: today's arrangement has no isolation between integrations at any level, despite documentation describing per-origin connection pooling as though it were in place. A rollback triggered by one integration reverts every integration in that bundle. Accepted; mitigated only by release discipline and small changes. - **Coarse credential and access scoping.** All integrations' credentials share one flat environment-variable namespace per environment, and MRT project roles are all-or-nothing — everyone who needs deploy or variable access for any integration has it for all of them. Currently four people, all Admin. Accepted for now; revisit if the team grows materially. - **Isolation depends on convention.** Nothing in the platform or the current CI setup enforces the module boundaries in §5. Accepted, with the mitigation in §7. --- ## 5. Technical Implementation > Scope note: this section specifies the implementation of the chosen option. A shopper request arrives at the MRT environment and is handled by the single Express app in `overrides/app/ssr.js`. 2. The route handler for the relevant surface delegates to an integration module under `overrides/app/ssr/` (one module per integration, as today). 3. The module issues its upstream call via `fetch`, passing the `dispatcher` option bound to **its own** connection pool from `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`, so its connection usage is capped independently of every other integration. 4. The pool applies that integration's own `connectTimeout` and `bodyTimeout`, bounding how long a slow upstream can hold a connection — and keeping the request inside MRT's 20s/16s execution ceiling rather than being terminated by it. 5. On success, the module returns typed data to the handler, which renders or responds. 6. **Error path:** if the upstream fails, times out, or returns a non-OK status, the module catches it at its own boundary and converts it to an explicit outcome — an HTTP error response for a dedicated endpoint, or a degraded-but-rendered result for a page surface per the graceful degradation constraint. The rejection **must not** propagate out of the module. 7. **Error path:** the route registration awaits (or explicitly `.catch()`es) the module call, so no integration failure can become an unobserved floating promise. Problem Statement ### 1.1 Context The storefront runs on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT), where a Node/Express layer performs all server-side work: the SSR render, proxying to upstream APIs, token exchange, and server-side calls to integrated systems. Today that layer serves a small number of integrations. Approximately 18 external systems are in scope for the programme (`.docs/integration/`), and nearly all of them have no code written yet. Integration build-out begins in the coming sprints. ### 1.2 Problem How many MRT applications the storefront deploys — and how integration code is divided across them — has never been decided. The current arrangement is a default inherited from the PWA Kit scaffold, not a deliberate choice, and it has never been documented or signed off. Because deployment topology determines how code is packaged, deployed, and rolled back, it becomes progressively more expensive to change once integration code exists across many systems. Compounding this, the server-side layer currently provides **no failure isolation of any kind** between integrations. Seven per-origin connection pools were written for this purpose (`overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`) but are imported nowhere and attached to no request, so every integration shares one undivided execution and connection context. This is present-state fact, verified in code and by test (§6), not a projection. ### 1.3 Impact if Not Solved - Topology is set by accretion rather than decision. Each integration that lands without an agreed position makes the arrangement harder to change, and the decision is effectively made by whoever writes the first proxy. - The isolation gap persists and compounds. It was found by chance in the only integration that currently has real code, and nothing in the codebase, review process, or CI prevents the same pattern recurring in the ~17 integrations still to be built. - Deploy and rollback blast radius stays coupled: a bad change to one integration forces a rollback that also reverts every other integration shipped in the same bundle. - Squad A (FED) and the SFCC squad have no shared written position to build against, risking divergent assumptions about where integration code belongs. ### 1.4 Success Criteria 1. A single documented position on how many MRT applications the storefront deploys and how integration code is divided across them, signed off by the Technical Lead (§8). 2. The as-is baseline is verified against the live platform and the codebase rather than assumed, with any inaccuracies in existing documentation corrected. 3. The chosen topology's failure-isolation behaviour is demonstrated by reproducible automated tests rather than asserted. 4. The position is recorded specifically enough that integration build-out can proceed without re-opening the question. --- ## 2. Constraints & Assumptions ### 2.1 Constraints | Constraint | Detail | | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Platform | SFCC B2C Commerce + PWA Kit on Managed Runtime. MRT hosts **only applications created from a PWA Kit template** — it is not general-purpose Node or container hosting. | | MRT application model | One project has many bundles, but **each environment has exactly one bundle designated as deployed**. A bundle is the entire built application and is immutable once created. | | MRT organisation limits | Maximum **100 total environments** and **10 production environments** per organisation, raisable only by Salesforce Support. Currently 7 environments in use. | | Execution model | A single Node.js/Express process per environment ("App Server"), serverless and auto-scaling. Hard request-execution ceiling of **20s production / 16s non-production**, after which MRT returns HTTP 502. **Unhandled promise rejections break app rendering.** | | Storefront scope | Must work across all **8 storefronts in 6 regions** (AU, UK, US Domestic, US International, EU Domestic, EU International, HK, ME). No single-market workarounds. | | Session and domain model | All 8 storefronts are path-prefixed on a **single first-party domain**; the `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie depends on this. An MRT environment binds to exactly **one** External Hostname, and a hostname can serve only one environment at a time. | | Performance | **LCP ≤ 2s at p75 mobile** is client-mandated and contractual (`architecture.md` §9).
