That is a separate infrastructure decision, not a change to MRT application topology. See §7. | --- ## 3. Options Analysis ### 3.1 Options Summary | Option | Pros | Cons | Viable? | | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | | **Option A** — Single MRT application, all integrations in one bundle | + The only model the platform supports, so zero migration cost — it is the current state.
+ One bundle per environment: the existing 6-workflow deploy pipeline, version guard and tag promotion already work against it.
+ A single SSR render composes many integrations with no cross-app network hop, protecting LCP.
+ One shared session, cookie and CSP context, which the single-domain 8-storefront session model requires.
+ Isolation is achievable in-process per integration (connection pools, timeouts, error boundaries). | − All integrations share one Node process: no process, memory or event-loop isolation. A CPU-bound or unhandled-rejection failure in one integration can affect unrelated concurrent requests (demonstrated, §6).
− One immutable bundle per environment: rolling back one integration reverts every integration shipped in that bundle.
− One flat environment-variable namespace per environment shared by all integrations; MRT offers no sub-scoping within a project, and project roles are all-or-nothing.
− Isolation must be actively implemented and maintained by convention; nothing in the platform enforces it. | **Yes** | | **Option B** — Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain | + Would provide true process-level isolation (memory, event loop, crash domain) per integration.
+ Would provide independent bundle lineage, so one integration could be deployed or rolled back without touching others.
+ Would scope environment variables and project role assignments per integration domain. | − **Not supported by the platform.** MRT hosts only PWA Kit template applications; every project must be a full storefront bundle, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application.
− Salesforce's own ISV integration guidance offers no such pattern.
− A literal per-integration reading (~18 systems × 6 tiers = 108 environments) exceeds the 100-environment organisation cap on its own.
− Cross-application calls would add a network hop to the SSR path, working directly against LCP ≤ 2s.
− Hostname-per-environment binding conflicts with the single first-party domain session model. | **No** | ### 3.2 Option Detail #### Option A — Single MRT application One PWA Kit project (`zimmermann`) produces one bundle, deployed to one environment per tier. All integration code — proxy routes, token exchange, server-side API calls — lives inside that single Express application, organised as separate modules. It satisfies every constraint in §2 by construction, because it is the model the platform is built around: one bundle per environment, one hostname per environment, one shared session context across all 8 path-prefixed storefronts. Its weakness is that isolation between integrations is a matter of code discipline rather than infrastructure, and must be built deliberately (§5). #### Option B — Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain *(Not viable)* The proposal was that each integration, or each domain grouping of integrations, would be deployed as its own Managed Runtime application, giving each one an independent process, deploy lineage, and credential scope. This was explored in full rather than dismissed, because on paper it addresses precisely the weaknesses of Option A identified above, and because the question was raised specifically to be settled with evidence rather than assumption. It is not viable, for a reason that is architectural rather than a matter of configuration or budget: **MRT will not host it.** Managed Runtime is documented as supporting only applications created from a PWA Kit template — a full React + Express + PWA Kit storefront bundle — and is not a general-purpose Node or microservice hosting platform. An integration's backend cannot be packaged as an MRT application because it is not a storefront. This was confirmed from three independent directions: the platform documentation's own constraint statement; the former Integration Lead's direct assessment that multiple independent Node processes cannot be run inside an MRT environment; and Salesforce's own B2C Commerce Headless Integration guidance for partners, which states that every Composable Storefront must have a project created in Runtime Admin and offers exactly three delivery shapes for backend integration logic — an SFCC cartridge, a Node module extending the same PWA Kit server, or an externally-hosted API — with no fourth pattern of a sibling MRT application. It was finally confirmed firsthand in Runtime Admin: the Create-a-New-Project flow asks only for a name, a project ID, and two environment defaults. There is no application-type field, because the platform assumes every project is a storefront. MRT's genuine multi-project support exists for a different purpose — separating distinct brands or domains, each of which is itself a full storefront — not for decomposing one storefront's backend. Even setting the hosting constraint aside, three of Option B's consequences would independently count against it: the literal per-integration form breaches the organisation environment cap; every cross-application call would add a network hop to the SSR path that the LCP budget cannot absorb; and the hostname-per-environment binding is incompatible with the single-domain session model the eight storefronts depend on. The isolation goals behind Option B remain legitimate. They are addressed within Option A in §5, and the one case Option A genuinely cannot serve is recorded as a risk in §7. --- ## 4. Recommended Option & Rationale ### 4.1 Recommended Option **Option A — Single MRT application, implemented as a modular single application.** ### 4.2 Rationale Option A is recommended because Option B is not available. The decisive factor is not a trade-off between the two but a platform constraint: MRT hosts only PWA Kit storefront bundles, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application at all. Once that is established, Option A is the only option that satisfies the §2 constraints, and it satisfies them without migration cost because it is the current state. The recommendation is qualified in one important respect. Endorsing Option A is not an endorsement of the status quo, because the status quo includes an isolation gap that is real and demonstrated: today's arrangement has no isolation between integrations at any level, despite documentation describing per-origin connection pooling as though it were in place. The recommendation is therefore Option A **implemented as a modular single application** — one bundle, with integration code in clearly separated modules, each with its own connection pool, timeout budget, and error boundary. This is the "middle option" the originating ticket asked to be considered; it is not a third topology but the correct implementation shape of Option A, and it is specified in §5. Adopting Option A without that work would leave success criterion 1.4.3 unmet. ### 4.3 Trade-offs Accepted - **Shared-process failure modes remain.** Even fully implemented, in-process module boundaries do not give memory, event-loop, or crash isolation. A synchronous CPU-bound operation in any integration will block every other concurrent request on that process, and no connection pool or configuration prevents it (demonstrated, §6). This is mitigated by a coding rule, not by infrastructure, and is accepted as a permanent property of the chosen topology. - **Coupled deploy and rollback granularity.** One immutable bundle per environment means the unit of deploy and rollback is the whole application. A rollback triggered by one integration reverts every integration in that bundle. Accepted; mitigated only by release discipline and small changes. - **Coarse credential and access scoping.** All integrations' credentials share one flat environment-variable namespace per environment, and MRT project roles are all-or-nothing — everyone who needs deploy or variable access for any integration has it for all of them. Currently four people, all Admin. Accepted for now; revisit if the team grows materially. - **Isolation depends on convention.** Nothing in the platform or the current CI setup enforces the module boundaries in §5. Accepted, with the mitigation in §7. --- ## 5. Technical Implementation > Scope note: this section specifies the implementation of the chosen option. The work itself is > deliberately **not** part of this spike — it is specified here so it can be picked up as its own > ticket once §8 is signed off, and because §1.4 cannot be met by a recommendation that leaves the > isolation gap undefined. Three of the files below are absolute Tier 1 (§2.1), so the implementing > ticket must secure owner approval before starting. ### 5.1 High-Level Sequence 1. A shopper request arrives at the MRT environment and is handled by the single Express app in `overrides/app/ssr.js`. 2. The route handler for the relevant surface delegates to an integration module under `overrides/app/ssr/` (one module per integration, as today). 3. The module issues its upstream call via `fetch`, passing the `dispatcher` option bound to **its own** connection pool from `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`, so its connection usage is capped independently of every other integration. 4. The pool applies that integration's own `connectTimeout` and `bodyTimeout`, bounding how long a slow upstream can hold a connection — and keeping the request inside MRT's 20s/16s execution ceiling rather than being terminated by it. 5. On success, the module returns typed data to the handler, which renders or responds. 6. **Error path:** if the upstream fails, times out, or returns a non-OK status, the module catches it at its own boundary and converts it to an explicit outcome — an HTTP error response for a dedicated endpoint, or a degraded-but-rendered result for a page surface per the graceful degradation constraint. The rejection **must not** propagate out of the module. 7. **Error path:** the route registration awaits (or explicitly `.catch()`es) the module call, so no integration failure can become an unobserved floating promise. Today two routes do not do this (§5.2), which is why a Marketing Cloud failure currently produces no response at all rather than an error response. ### 5.2 Component / API Changes | File / Endpoint | Change Required | Type | | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | | `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts` | Confirm pool definitions against real hostnames; resolve the two placeholder origins (`sfcc-payments`, `booxi`). Currently defines 7 pools but is imported nowhere. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccScapiPool` on the JWKS `fetch` (line ~78, currently a bare global-dispatcher call). | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccPaymentsPool` on the metadata `fetch` (line ~42). | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/marketingCloud.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: marketingCloudAuthPool` / `marketingCloudRestPool` on the two `fetch` calls (lines ~38, ~61). **Add a try/catch boundary** — this module currently has none. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr.js` **(Tier 1)** | Await or `.catch()` the `sendMagicLinkEmail` calls in the passwordless-login and reset-password routes (lines ~150 and ~168). Both currently create an unobserved floating promise. | Modified | | `config/default.js` **(Tier 1)** | Add a `proxyConfigs` entry per new MRT-mediated integration as each is built (MuleSoft, Google Places, Booxi). Only SCAPI and OCAPI exist today. | Modified | | Runtime Admin → Environment Settings | Matching MRT-side proxy entry per environment. **MRT proxy config is a separate source of truth from the bundle's** — both must be updated together. | Modified | | `.claude/rules/` (new or existing rule file) | Document the integration-module contract in §5.3 so it is enforced at review time. | New | ### 5.3 Data Structures / Interfaces The contract every integration module must satisfy: ```ts // Each integration owns exactly one pool, and every outbound call uses it. import { mulesoftPool } from './connectionPools'; // 1. All outbound calls pass their own dispatcher. const response = await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { /* ... */ }, body: JSON.stringify(payload), dispatcher: mulesoftPool, // ← per-integration connection cap + timeouts }); // 2. Every module resolves to an explicit outcome. It never throws past its own boundary. type IntegrationResult = | { kind: 'ok'; data: T } | { kind: 'error'; reason: string; status?: number }; // 3. Every route registration observes the promise. app.post(path, (req, res) => { void handler(req, res).catch((err) => { // log, then always respond — never leave the request unanswered }); }); ``` Pool boundaries and caps are per `tsd-architecture.md` §12.1 (7 pools: `sfcc-scapi`, `sfcc-payments`, `mulesoft`, `marketing-cloud-auth`, `marketing-cloud-rest`, `google-places`, `booxi`). Caps there are derived from expected rather than observed concurrency and should be validated by the Stage load-test pass described in §9.3 of that document. ### 5.4 Error Handling & Edge Cases | Scenario | Expected Behaviour | Type | | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | | An integration's upstream returns a non-OK status | The owning module catches it and returns an explicit error outcome. The request receives a response describing the failure — never silence. | Error | | An integration's upstream is slow or unresponsive | Its pool's `bodyTimeout` aborts the call before MRT's 20s/16s ceiling, releasing the connection. Other integrations' pools are unaffected. | Error | | An integration floods its own connection pool | Only that integration's calls queue. Other integrations retain their own capped connections. | Edge case | | A page surface needs an integration that is unavailable | The page renders without that integration's contribution, per the graceful degradation constraint — except where an explicit error is mandated (checkout). | Edge case | | An integration performs a synchronous CPU-bound operation | **Not preventable by this design.** Every concurrent request on the process blocks for the duration. Prevented only by the coding rule; see §7. | Error | | Contentful (SDK does not expose a `dispatcher` hook) | Connection isolation is not achievable via this pattern; graceful degradation is the mitigation. See §7 for a correction to the existing documented claim. | Edge case | ### 5.5 Configuration & Environment Notes No new environment variables are introduced by the topology decision itself. Each future integration adds its own credentials to the per-environment variable set, and a matching proxy entry in **both** `config/default.js` and the MRT environment's own proxy configuration. One finding relevant to the LCP constraint in §2.1 is recorded here because it materially affects any performance measurement of the chosen topology, though it is not itself a topology issue: the seven MRT environments are split across two AWS regions — DEV, DEV1, SIT, UAT and STG in Asia Pacific (Sydney), TEST and Production in US East (Ohio). Because STG is the tier designated for contractual LCP sign-off and Production sits in a different region, Stage-measured performance figures are not currently representative of Production. This is being raised separately (Appendix A) and should be resolved before any LCP sign-off, under either topology. --- ## 6. Testing & Validation ### 6.1 Test Coverage Mapping to §1.4: criterion 3 requires the isolation behaviour to be demonstrated rather than asserted. The suite below exists and passes (`overrides/app/ssr/blastRadius.test.ts`, 4 tests). | Test Type | What is Being Tested | Pass Criteria | | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Unit / Integration | Rejection propagation between integrations, using the real `paymentMetadataHandler` and `sendMagicLinkEmail`. One integration fails; an unrelated one succeeds. | Currently: an aggregating caller loses the successful result entirely. After §5: the successful result survives its sibling's failure. | | Unit / Integration | The real `ssr.js` call shape — an unobserved floating promise inside a `.then()` — when its integration fails. | Currently: becomes a process-level unhandled rejection and the response object is never written to, so the shopper receives nothing until MRT's ceiling returns a 502. After §5: an explicit response. | | Unit / Integration | Cross-region blast radius: an AU-scoped call and an unrelated US-scoped call in flight together, the US one failing. | Currently: the AU result is lost despite AU not using the failing integration. After §5: the AU result is unaffected. | | Unit | Event-loop blocking: a synchronous CPU-bound operation alongside an unrelated fast operation. | The fast operation is delayed by the full duration of the blocking work. **This test documents an accepted limitation and is expected to keep passing after §5** — it is not fixed by that work. | | Integration | Per-pool isolation under load once §5 is implemented: a saturated or slow origin must not starve a different origin's pool. | An unrelated integration's call completes within its own timeout while another integration's pool is saturated. **Not yet written** — depends on §5. | | E2E / Playwright | Not applicable. | This TSD decides deployment topology and ships no user-facing surface, so there is no user journey to assert. Recorded explicitly rather than omitted. | Performance validation is not duplicated here: per-pool queue-depth and connection-wait metrics are already scheduled for the Stage load-test pass in `tsd-architecture.md` §9.3, and bundle size is already gated in CI. See §5.5 regarding the region caveat on Stage measurements. ### 6.2 Regression Risk The topology decision itself changes no code and therefore carries no regression risk. The §5 implementation does, and it is concentrated in two places. First, attaching a `dispatcher` to existing `fetch` calls changes connection behaviour for SLAS token validation, payment metadata, and Marketing Cloud email — all on authentication and checkout paths, so a mis-set cap or timeout would surface as intermittent failures there rather than as an obvious break. The four tests above cover the failure-isolation behaviour but not cap tuning, which is why the load-test row is listed as required. Second, `overrides/app/ssr.js` is the entry point for every request, so the route-handler change must be verified across all 8 storefronts rather than one. Note also that the `commerce-sdk-react` hooks manage their own HTTP client and are unaffected by pool changes, which usefully bounds the risk: the bulk of SFCC commerce traffic does not traverse these pools at all. --- ## 7. The gap was originally introduced this way. | **High** | Document the contract as a rule in `.claude/rules/`, add it to the PR checklist, and consider an ast-grep or lint rule matching a `fetch(` in `overrides/app/ssr/` with no `dispatcher` key. | Squad A | | A future integration proves genuinely CPU-bound or requires process isolation, which Option A cannot provide at any level of implementation quality. | Low | Host that integration's layer **outside** MRT (general-purpose cloud compute, or a vendor-hosted API per Salesforce's Connected App pattern) and call it from the single app over HTTP via its own pool. Moot in practice while Contentful is browser-direct, but should not be inherited as fact. Already flagged independently in SFCC-249's risk register. | PWA TSD owner | | ARM vs x86 server architecture is unverified (not exposed in Runtime Admin at either level); x86 loses deployability after 31 Jan 2027. | Low | Confirm via the MRT Admin API or Salesforce Support. Independent of topology, but worth closing while attention is on the platform. | Integration / Platform | --- ## 8. Decision Record | Date | Decision Maker | Decision | Outcome / Rationale | | ------ | ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 12 Aug | Marcel Angelo Navarro (author) | Scope this TSD to two options rather than three. | The originating ticket's "middle option (single modular app)" is not a distinct topology — it is Option A correctly implemented, so it is specified in §5 instead of §3. | | 12 Aug | Manikandan Ramachandran (former Integration Lead) | Multiple independent Node processes cannot be run inside a single MRT environment. | Corroborated by MRT platform documentation, by Salesforce's ISV integration guidance, and firsthand in Runtime Admin. Basis for Option B being marked not viable. | | 12 Aug | Marcel Angelo Navarro (author) | Record the as-is isolation state as "none", not "network-level". | The ticket text described per-origin pooling as in place. Corrected in §1.2. | | 12 Aug | Marcel Angelo Navarro (author) | Keep environment-configuration findings out of this TSD. | They exist identically under either topology, so they are not topology decisions. Routed separately — Appendix A. Per the "one TSD = one problem" rule. | | _TBC_ | Tim Lavelle (Technical Lead) | TSD approved for implementation | _Pending review._ | ### Sign-off | Role | Name | Date | Status | | --------------------------- | --------------------- | ----------- | ----------------------------- | | Author | Marcel Angelo Navarro | 12 Aug 2026 | Submitted | | Technical Lead / Reviewer | Tim Lavelle | _TBC_ | _Approved / Changes Required_ | --- ## Appendix A — Findings raised separately (not part of this TSD) Surfaced while verifying the as-is baseline in Runtime Admin. [TSD-SFCC-681-mrt-application-topology.md](.docs/temp/TSD-SFCC-681-mrt-application-topology.md) — v0.1, Draft. Not committed, not published anywhere.

**How I handled the judgement calls:**

**Option B gets a genuinely substantial §3.2 entry**, not the template's one-sentence minimum — you asked for it explored then invalidated, so it walks through the proposal, states why it fails architecturally (MRT hosts only PWA Kit bundles), and names all four confirmation sources including the firsthand Runtime Admin evidence. It closes by acknowledging the isolation goals behind it were legitimate and pointing to where they're addressed. `Viable? = No` in the summary table.

**§4.2 is deliberately qualified.** Recommending Option A could read as rubber-stamping the status quo, which would be wrong — the status quo contains a demonstrated isolation gap that documentation describes as already solved. So the recommendation is explicitly Option A *implemented as a modular single application*, with a line stating that adopting it without the §5 work leaves success criterion 1.4.3 unmet.

**§2.1 constraints are fully rewritten** — none of the template's boilerplate survived. 8 storefronts, not 7-or-6; no "everything routes through MuleSoft" claim.

**§6 lists the event-loop test as expected to keep passing after the fix.** It documents an accepted permanent limitation rather than a defect, and pretending otherwise would misrepresent it. The Playwright row says "not applicable" with the reason, rather than being silently dropped.

**§7 puts "§5 never gets implemented" as the top risk at High likelihood** — honestly, that's the real risk here, and the second (the contract not being followed) is rated High too since that's precisely how the original gap appeared.

**Two things I'd flag for your review:**

1. **§8's Decision Record attributes a decision to Mani.** He's recorded as the source of the platform constraint, which is accurate and load-bearing — but he's the *former* Integration Lead, so you may want Tim or Gideon to countersign that line rather than resting the central finding on a departed colleague's assessment. The three corroborating sources are cited alongside it, so it doesn't stand alone.

2. **The region finding appears twice** — one paragraph in §5.5 (because it materially affects LCP measurement of the chosen topology) and fully in Appendix A. That's deliberate, but if you think it's scope creep into a topology TSD, the §5.5 paragraph is the one to cut.

1 # TSD: MRT Application Topology — Single vs Per-Integration 2 3 ## Document Information 4 5 | Field | Value | 6 | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 7 | **Document ID** | TSD-SFCC-681 | 8 | **Author(s)** | Marcel Angelo Navarro — Squad A / Frontend Development Lead | 9 | **Reviewer(s)** | Tim Lavelle — Technical Lead · Gideon R. Linsangan — SFCC Squad (collaborator per ticket) | 10 | **Created** | 12 Aug 2026 | 11 | **Version** | v0.1 — Draft | 12 | **Status** | Draft | 13 | **Related Jira** | SFCC-681 (clones SFCC-237, which was closed at Sprint 2 rollover) | 14 15 --- 16 17 ## Version History 18 19 | Version | Date | Summary of Change | Author | 20 | ------- | ----------- | ----------------- | --------------------- | 21 | v0.1 | 12 Aug 2026 | Initial draft | Marcel Angelo Navarro | 22 23 --- 24 25 ## 1. Problem Statement 26 27 ### 1.1 Context 28 29 The storefront runs on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT), where a Node/Express layer performs all 30 server-side work: the SSR render, proxying to upstream APIs, token exchange, and server-side calls to 31 integrated systems. Today that layer serves a small number of integrations. Approximately 18 external 32 systems are in scope for the programme (`.docs/integration/`), and nearly all of them have no code 33 written yet. Integration build-out begins in the coming sprints. 34 35 ### 1.2 Problem 36 37 How many MRT applications the storefront deploys — and how integration code is divided across them — 38 has never been decided. The current arrangement is a default inherited from the PWA Kit scaffold, not 39 a deliberate choice, and it has never been documented or signed off. Because deployment topology 40 determines how code is packaged, deployed, and rolled back, it becomes progressively more expensive 41 to change once integration code exists across many systems. 42 43 Compounding this, the server-side layer currently provides **no failure isolation of any kind** 44 between integrations. Seven per-origin connection pools were written for this purpose 45 (`overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`) but are imported nowhere and attached to no request, so 46 every integration shares one undivided execution and connection context. This is present-state 47 fact, verified in code and by test (§6), not a projection. 48 49 ### 1.3 Impact if Not Solved 50 51 - Topology is set by accretion rather than decision. Each integration that lands without an agreed 52 position makes the arrangement harder to change, and the decision is effectively made by whoever 53 writes the first proxy. 54 - The isolation gap persists and compounds. It was found by chance in the only integration that 55 currently has real code, and nothing in the codebase, review process, or CI prevents the same 56 pattern recurring in the ~17 integrations still to be built. 57 - Deploy and rollback blast radius stays coupled: a bad change to one integration forces a rollback 58 that also reverts every other integration shipped in the same bundle. 59 - Squad A (FED) and the SFCC squad have no shared written position to build against, risking 60 divergent assumptions about where integration code belongs. 61 62 ### 1.4 Success Criteria 63 64 1. A single documented position on how many MRT applications the storefront deploys and how 65 integration code is divided across them, signed off by the Technical Lead (§8). 66 2. The as-is baseline is verified against the live platform and the codebase rather than assumed, 67 with any inaccuracies in existing documentation corrected. 68 3. The chosen topology's failure-isolation behaviour is demonstrated by reproducible automated tests 69 rather than asserted. 70 4. The position is recorded specifically enough that integration build-out can proceed without 71 re-opening the question. 72 73 --- 74 75 ## 2. Constraints & Assumptions 76 77 ### 2.1 Constraints 78 79 | Constraint | Detail | 80 | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 81 | Platform | SFCC B2C Commerce + PWA Kit on Managed Runtime. MRT hosts **only applications created from a PWA Kit template** — it is not general-purpose Node or container hosting. | 82 | MRT application model | One project has many bundles, but **each environment has exactly one bundle designated as deployed**. A bundle is the entire built application and is immutable once created. | 83 | MRT organisation limits | Maximum **100 total environments** and **10 production environments** per organisation, raisable only by Salesforce Support. Currently 7 environments in use. | 84 | Execution model | A single Node.js/Express process per environment ("App Server"), serverless and auto-scaling. Hard request-execution ceiling of **20s production / 16s non-production**, after which MRT returns HTTP 502. **Unhandled promise rejections break app rendering.** | 85 | Storefront scope | Must work across all **8 storefronts in 6 regions** (AU, UK, US Domestic, US International, EU Domestic, EU International, HK, ME). No single-market workarounds. | 86 | Session and domain model | All 8 storefronts are path-prefixed on a **single first-party domain**; the `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie depends on this. An MRT environment binds to exactly **one** External Hostname, and a hostname can serve only one environment at a time. | 87 | Performance | **LCP ≤ 2s at p75 mobile** is client-mandated and contractual (`architecture.md` §9). Any added network hop on the SSR path counts against it. | 88 | Graceful degradation | Each external system must fail independently — one outage must not break a whole page (AGENTS.md > Graceful Degradation). | 89 | Tier 1 change control | `config/default.js`, `config/sites.js`, `overrides/app/ssr.js` and `worker/main.js` are **absolute** Tier 1 under AGENTS.md Hard Rule #4 — the verified-session exception does not apply. Any topology or isolation change touches at least one of these. | 90 91 ### 2.2 Assumptions 92 93 | Assumption | Risk if Wrong | 94 | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 95 | The ~18 systems in `.docs/integration/` remain the integration scope for this decision. | Materially more systems would grow the per-environment variable surface and module count, but would not change the topology conclusion — Option B stays unsupported regardless of integration count. | 96 | Zimmermann's MRT agreement permits additional projects at no additional licence cost. | Affects only Option B's cost line. Option B is already non-viable on architectural grounds, so the recommendation does not change either way. Unconfirmed with the account team. | 97 | The `zimmermann` project runs on ARM rather than x86 server architecture. | If x86, environments must be migrated before **31 Jan 2027** or lose the ability to deploy. Not exposed in Runtime Admin at project or environment level, so unverified. Independent of the topology decision. | 98 | No in-scope integration requires process-level isolation that in-process module boundaries cannot provide. | If one does — for example a genuinely CPU-bound workload — it must be hosted outside MRT entirely. That is a separate infrastructure decision, not a change to MRT application topology. See §7. | 99 100 --- 101 102 ## 3. Options Analysis 103 104 ### 3.1 Options Summary 105 106 | Option | Pros | Cons | Viable? | 107 | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | 108 | **Option A** — Single MRT application, all integrations in one bundle | + The only model the platform supports, so zero migration cost — it is the current state.
+ One bundle per environment: the existing 6-workflow deploy pipeline, version guard and tag promotion already work against it.
+ A single SSR render composes many integrations with no cross-app network hop, protecting LCP.
+ One shared session, cookie and CSP context, which the single-domain 8-storefront session model requires.
+ Isolation is achievable in-process per integration (connection pools, timeouts, error boundaries). | − All integrations share one Node process: no process, memory or event-loop isolation. A CPU-bound or unhandled-rejection failure in one integration can affect unrelated concurrent requests (demonstrated, §6).
− One immutable bundle per environment: rolling back one integration reverts every integration shipped in that bundle.
− One flat environment-variable namespace per environment shared by all integrations; MRT offers no sub-scoping within a project, and project roles are all-or-nothing.
− Isolation must be actively implemented and maintained by convention; nothing in the platform enforces it. | **Yes** | 109 | **Option B** — Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain | + Would provide true process-level isolation (memory, event loop, crash domain) per integration.
+ Would provide independent bundle lineage, so one integration could be deployed or rolled back without touching others.
+ Would scope environment variables and project role assignments per integration domain. | − **Not supported by the platform.** MRT hosts only PWA Kit template applications; every project must be a full storefront bundle, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application.
− Salesforce's own ISV integration guidance offers no such pattern.
− A literal per-integration reading (~18 systems × 6 tiers = 108 environments) exceeds the 100-environment organisation cap on its own.
− Cross-application calls would add a network hop to the SSR path, working directly against LCP ≤ 2s.
− Hostname-per-environment binding conflicts with the single first-party domain session model. | **No** | 110 111 ### 3.2 Option Detail 112 113 #### Option A — Single MRT application 114 115 One PWA Kit project (`zimmermann`) produces one bundle, deployed to one environment per tier. All 116 integration code — proxy routes, token exchange, server-side API calls — lives inside that single 117 Express application, organised as separate modules. It satisfies every constraint in §2 by 118 construction, because it is the model the platform is built around: one bundle per environment, one 119 hostname per environment, one shared session context across all 8 path-prefixed storefronts. Its 120 weakness is that isolation between integrations is a matter of code discipline rather than 121 infrastructure, and must be built deliberately (§5). 122 123 #### Option B — Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain *(Not viable)* 124 125 The proposal was that each integration, or each domain grouping of integrations, would be deployed as 126 its own Managed Runtime application, giving each one an independent process, deploy lineage, and 127 credential scope. This was explored in full rather than dismissed, because on paper it addresses 128 precisely the weaknesses of Option A identified above, and because the question was raised 129 specifically to be settled with evidence rather than assumption. 130 131 It is not viable, for a reason that is architectural rather than a matter of configuration or 132 budget: **MRT will not host it.** Managed Runtime is documented as supporting only applications 133 created from a PWA Kit template — a full React + Express + PWA Kit storefront bundle — and is not a 134 general-purpose Node or microservice hosting platform. An integration's backend cannot be packaged as 135 an MRT application because it is not a storefront. This was confirmed from three independent 136 directions: the platform documentation's own constraint statement; the former Integration Lead's 137 direct assessment that multiple independent Node processes cannot be run inside an MRT environment; 138 and Salesforce's own B2C Commerce Headless Integration guidance for partners, which states that every 139 Composable Storefront must have a project created in Runtime Admin and offers exactly three delivery 140 shapes for backend integration logic — an SFCC cartridge, a Node module extending the same PWA Kit 141 server, or an externally-hosted API — with no fourth pattern of a sibling MRT application. It was 142 finally confirmed firsthand in Runtime Admin: the Create-a-New-Project flow asks only for a name, a 143 project ID, and two environment defaults. There is no application-type field, because the platform 144 assumes every project is a storefront. 145 146 MRT's genuine multi-project support exists for a different purpose — separating distinct brands or 147 domains, each of which is itself a full storefront — not for decomposing one storefront's backend. 148 Even setting the hosting constraint aside, three of Option B's consequences would independently 149 count against it: the literal per-integration form breaches the organisation environment cap; every 150 cross-application call would add a network hop to the SSR path that the LCP budget cannot absorb; and 151 the hostname-per-environment binding is incompatible with the single-domain session model the eight 152 storefronts depend on. 153 154 The isolation goals behind Option B remain legitimate. They are addressed within Option A in §5, and 155 the one case Option A genuinely cannot serve is recorded as a risk in §7. 156 157 --- 158 159 ## 4. Recommended Option & Rationale 160 161 ### 4.1 Recommended Option 162 163 **Option A — Single MRT application, implemented as a modular single application.** 164 165 ### 4.2 Rationale 166 167 Option A is recommended because Option B is not available. The decisive factor is not a trade-off 168 between the two but a platform constraint: MRT hosts only PWA Kit storefront bundles, so an 169 integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application at all. Once that is established, Option A 170 is the only option that satisfies the §2 constraints, and it satisfies them without migration cost 171 because it is the current state. 172 173 The recommendation is qualified in one important respect. Endorsing Option A is not an endorsement of 174 the status quo, because the status quo includes an isolation gap that is real and demonstrated: 175 today's arrangement has no isolation between integrations at any level, despite documentation 176 describing per-origin connection pooling as though it were in place. The recommendation is therefore 177 Option A **implemented as a modular single application** — one bundle, with integration code in 178 clearly separated modules, each with its own connection pool, timeout budget, and error boundary. 179 This is the "middle option" the originating ticket asked to be considered; it is not a third topology 180 but the correct implementation shape of Option A, and it is specified in §5. Adopting Option A 181 without that work would leave success criterion 1.4.3 unmet. 182 183 ### 4.3 Trade-offs Accepted 184 185 - **Shared-process failure modes remain.** Even fully implemented, in-process module boundaries do 186 not give memory, event-loop, or crash isolation. A synchronous CPU-bound operation in any 187 integration will block every other concurrent request on that process, and no connection pool or 188 configuration prevents it (demonstrated, §6). This is mitigated by a coding rule, not by 189 infrastructure, and is accepted as a permanent property of the chosen topology. 190 - **Coupled deploy and rollback granularity.** One immutable bundle per environment means the unit of 191 deploy and rollback is the whole application. A rollback triggered by one integration reverts every 192 integration in that bundle. Accepted; mitigated only by release discipline and small changes. 193 - **Coarse credential and access scoping.** All integrations' credentials share one flat 194 environment-variable namespace per environment, and MRT project roles are all-or-nothing — everyone 195 who needs deploy or variable access for any integration has it for all of them. Currently four 196 people, all Admin. Accepted for now; revisit if the team grows materially. 197 - **Isolation depends on convention.** Nothing in the platform or the current CI setup enforces the 198 module boundaries in §5. Accepted, with the mitigation in §7. 199 200 --- 201 202 ## 5. Technical Implementation 203 204 > Scope note: this section specifies the implementation of the chosen option. The work itself is 205 > deliberately **not** part of this spike — it is specified here so it can be picked up as its own 206 > ticket once §8 is signed off, and because §1.4 cannot be met by a recommendation that leaves the 207 > isolation gap undefined. Three of the files below are absolute Tier 1 (§2.1), so the implementing 208 > ticket must secure owner approval before starting. 209 210 ### 5.1 High-Level Sequence 211 212 1. A shopper request arrives at the MRT environment and is handled by the single Express app in 213 `overrides/app/ssr.js`. 214 2. The route handler for the relevant surface delegates to an integration module under 215 `overrides/app/ssr/` (one module per integration, as today). 216 3. The module issues its upstream call via `fetch`, passing the `dispatcher` option bound to **its 217 own** connection pool from `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`, so its connection usage is 218 capped independently of every other integration. 219 4. The pool applies that integration's own `connectTimeout` and `bodyTimeout`, bounding how long a 220 slow upstream can hold a connection — and keeping the request inside MRT's 20s/16s execution 221 ceiling rather than being terminated by it. 222 5. On success, the module returns typed data to the handler, which renders or responds. 223 6. **Error path:** if the upstream fails, times out, or returns a non-OK status, the module catches it 224 at its own boundary and converts it to an explicit outcome — an HTTP error response for a 225 dedicated endpoint, or a degraded-but-rendered result for a page surface per the graceful 226 degradation constraint. The rejection **must not** propagate out of the module. 227 7. **Error path:** the route registration awaits (or explicitly `.catch()`es) the module call, so no 228 integration failure can become an unobserved floating promise. Today two routes do not do this 229 (§5.2), which is why a Marketing Cloud failure currently produces no response at all rather than 230 an error response. 231 232 ### 5.2 Component / API Changes 233 234 | File / Endpoint | Change Required | Type | 235 | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | 236 | `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts` | Confirm pool definitions against real hostnames; resolve the two placeholder origins (`sfcc-payments`, `booxi`). Currently defines 7 pools but is imported nowhere. | Modified | 237 | `overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccScapiPool` on the JWKS `fetch` (line ~78, currently a bare global-dispatcher call). | Modified | 238 | `overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccPaymentsPool` on the metadata `fetch` (line ~42). | Modified | 239 | `overrides/app/ssr/marketingCloud.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: marketingCloudAuthPool` / `marketingCloudRestPool` on the two `fetch` calls (lines ~38, ~61). **Add a try/catch boundary** — this module currently has none. | Modified | 240 | `overrides/app/ssr.js` **(Tier 1)** | Await or `.catch()` the `sendMagicLinkEmail` calls in the passwordless-login and reset-password routes (lines ~150 and ~168). Each future integration 293 adds its own credentials to the per-environment variable set, and a matching proxy entry in **both** 294 `config/default.js` and the MRT environment's own proxy configuration. 295 296 One finding relevant to the LCP constraint in §2.1 is recorded here because it materially affects any 297 performance measurement of the chosen topology, though it is not itself a topology issue: the seven 298 MRT environments are split across two AWS regions — DEV, DEV1, SIT, UAT and STG in Asia Pacific 299 (Sydney), TEST and Production in US East (Ohio). This is being raised separately (Appendix A) and should be 302 resolved before any LCP sign-off, under either topology. 303 304 --- 305 306 ## 6. After §5: an explicit response. | 317 | Unit / Integration | Cross-region blast radius: an AU-scoped call and an unrelated US-scoped call in flight together, the US one failing. | Currently: the AU result is lost despite AU not using the failing integration. See §5.5 regarding the region caveat on Stage measurements. 325 326 ### 6.2 Regression Risk 327 328 The topology decision itself changes no code and therefore carries no regression risk. The §5 329 implementation does, and it is concentrated in two places. First, attaching a `dispatcher` to 330 existing `fetch` calls changes connection behaviour for SLAS token validation, payment metadata, and 331 Marketing Cloud email — all on authentication and checkout paths, so a mis-set cap or timeout would 332 surface as intermittent failures there rather than as an obvious break. # TSD: MRT Application Topology — Single vs Per-Integration ## Document Information | Field | Value | | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Document ID** | TSD-SFCC-681 | | **Author(s)** | Marcel Angelo Navarro — Squad A / Frontend Development Lead | | **Reviewer(s)** | Tim Lavelle — Technical Lead · Gideon R. Linsangan — SFCC Squad (collaborator per ticket) | | **Created** | 12 Aug 2026 | | **Version** | v0.1 — Draft | | **Status** | Draft | | **Related Jira** | SFCC-681 (clones SFCC-237, which was closed at Sprint 2 rollover) | --- ## Version History | Version | Date | Summary of Change | Author | | ------- | ----------- | ----------------- | --------------------- | | v0.1 | 12 Aug 2026 | Initial draft | Marcel Angelo Navarro | --- ## 1. Problem Statement ### 1.1 Context The storefront runs on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT), where a Node/Express layer performs all server-side work: the SSR render, proxying to upstream APIs, token exchange, and server-side calls to integrated systems. Today that layer serves a small number of integrations. Approximately 18 external systems are in scope for the programme (`.docs/integration/`), and nearly all of them have no code written yet. Integration build-out begins in the coming sprints. ### 1.2 Problem How many MRT applications the storefront deploys — and how integration code is divided across them — has never been decided. The current arrangement is a default inherited from the PWA Kit scaffold, not a deliberate choice, and it has never been documented or signed off. Because deployment topology determines how code is packaged, deployed, and rolled back, it becomes progressively more expensive to change once integration code exists across many systems. Compounding this, the server-side layer currently provides **no failure isolation of any kind** between integrations. Seven per-origin connection pools were written for this purpose (`overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`) but are imported nowhere and attached to no request, so every integration shares one undivided execution and connection context. This is present-state fact, verified in code and by test (§6), not a projection. ### 1.3 Impact if Not Solved - Topology is set by accretion rather than decision. Each integration that lands without an agreed position makes the arrangement harder to change, and the decision is effectively made by whoever writes the first proxy. - The isolation gap persists and compounds. It was found by chance in the only integration that currently has real code, and nothing in the codebase, review process, or CI prevents the same pattern recurring in the ~17 integrations still to be built. - Deploy and rollback blast radius stays coupled: a bad change to one integration forces a rollback that also reverts every other integration shipped in the same bundle. - Squad A (FED) and the SFCC squad have no shared written position to build against, risking divergent assumptions about where integration code belongs. ### 1.4 Success Criteria 1. A single documented position on how many MRT applications the storefront deploys and how integration code is divided across them, signed off by the Technical Lead (§8). 2. The as-is baseline is verified against the live platform and the codebase rather than assumed, with any inaccuracies in existing documentation corrected. 3. The chosen topology's failure-isolation behaviour is demonstrated by reproducible automated tests rather than asserted. 4. The position is recorded specifically enough that integration build-out can proceed without re-opening the question. --- ## 2. Constraints & Assumptions ### 2.1 Constraints | Constraint | Detail | | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Platform | SFCC B2C Commerce + PWA Kit on Managed Runtime. MRT hosts **only applications created from a PWA Kit template** — it is not general-purpose Node or container hosting. | | MRT application model | One project has many bundles, but **each environment has exactly one bundle designated as deployed**. A bundle is the entire built application and is immutable once created. | | MRT organisation limits | Maximum **100 total environments** and **10 production environments** per organisation, raisable only by Salesforce Support. Currently 7 environments in use. | | Execution model | A single Node.js/Express process per environment ("App Server"), serverless and auto-scaling. Hard request-execution ceiling of **20s production / 16s non-production**, after which MRT returns HTTP 502. **Unhandled promise rejections break app rendering.** | | Storefront scope | Must work across all **8 storefronts in 6 regions** (AU, UK, US Domestic, US International, EU Domestic, EU International, HK, ME). No single-market workarounds. | | Session and domain model | All 8 storefronts are path-prefixed on a **single first-party domain**; the `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie depends on this. An MRT environment binds to exactly **one** External Hostname, and a hostname can serve only one environment at a time. | | Performance | **LCP ≤ 2s at p75 mobile** is client-mandated and contractual (`architecture.md` §9). Any added network hop on the SSR path counts against it. | | Graceful degradation | Each external system must fail independently — one outage must not break a whole page (AGENTS.md > Graceful Degradation). | | Tier 1 change control | `config/default.js`, `config/sites.js`, `overrides/app/ssr.js` and `worker/main.js` are **absolute** Tier 1 under AGENTS.md Hard Rule #4 — the verified-session exception does not apply. Any topology or isolation change touches at least one of these. | ### 2.2 Assumptions | Assumption | Risk if Wrong | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | The ~18 systems in `.docs/integration/` remain the integration scope for this decision. | Materially more systems would grow the per-environment variable surface and module count, but would not change the topology conclusion — Option B stays unsupported regardless of integration count. | | Zimmermann's MRT agreement permits additional projects at no additional licence cost. | Affects only Option B's cost line. Option B is already non-viable on architectural grounds, so the recommendation does not change either way. Unconfirmed with the account team. | | The `zimmermann` project runs on ARM rather than x86 server architecture. | If x86, environments must be migrated before **31 Jan 2027** or lose the ability to deploy. Not exposed in Runtime Admin at project or environment level, so unverified. Independent of the topology decision. | | No in-scope integration requires process-level isolation that in-process module boundaries cannot provide. | If one does — for example a genuinely CPU-bound workload — it must be hosted outside MRT entirely. That is a separate infrastructure decision, not a change to MRT application topology. See §7. | --- ## 3. Options Analysis ### 3.1 Options Summary | Option | Pros | Cons | Viable? | | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | | **Option A** — Single MRT application, all integrations in one bundle | + The only model the platform supports, so zero migration cost — it is the current state.
+ One bundle per environment: the existing 6-workflow deploy pipeline, version guard and tag promotion already work against it.
+ A single SSR render composes many integrations with no cross-app network hop, protecting LCP.
+ One shared session, cookie and CSP context, which the single-domain 8-storefront session model requires.
+ Isolation is achievable in-process per integration (connection pools, timeouts, error boundaries). | − All integrations share one Node process: no process, memory or event-loop isolation. A CPU-bound or unhandled-rejection failure in one integration can affect unrelated concurrent requests (demonstrated, §6).
− One immutable bundle per environment: rolling back one integration reverts every integration shipped in that bundle.
− One flat environment-variable namespace per environment shared by all integrations; MRT offers no sub-scoping within a project, and project roles are all-or-nothing.
− Isolation must be actively implemented and maintained by convention; nothing in the platform enforces it. | **Yes** | | **Option B** — Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain | + Would provide true process-level isolation (memory, event loop, crash domain) per integration.
+ Would provide independent bundle lineage, so one integration could be deployed or rolled back without touching others.
+ Would scope environment variables and project role assignments per integration domain. | − **Not supported by the platform.** MRT hosts only PWA Kit template applications; every project must be a full storefront bundle, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application.
− Salesforce's own ISV integration guidance offers no such pattern.
− A literal per-integration reading (~18 systems × 6 tiers = 108 environments) exceeds the 100-environment organisation cap on its own.
− Cross-application calls would add a network hop to the SSR path, working directly against LCP ≤ 2s.
− Hostname-per-environment binding conflicts with the single first-party domain session model. | **No** | ### 3.2 Option Detail #### Option A — Single MRT application One PWA Kit project (`zimmermann`) produces one bundle, deployed to one environment per tier. All integration code — proxy routes, token exchange, server-side API calls — lives inside that single Express application, organised as separate modules. It satisfies every constraint in §2 by construction, because it is the model the platform is built around: one bundle per environment, one hostname per environment, one shared session context across all 8 path-prefixed storefronts. Its weakness is that isolation between integrations is a matter of code discipline rather than infrastructure, and must be built deliberately (§5). #### Option B — Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain *(Not viable)* The proposal was that each integration, or each domain grouping of integrations, would be deployed as its own Managed Runtime application, giving each one an independent process, deploy lineage, and credential scope. This was explored in full rather than dismissed, because on paper it addresses precisely the weaknesses of Option A identified above, and because the question was raised specifically to be settled with evidence rather than assumption. It is not viable, for a reason that is architectural rather than a matter of configuration or budget: **MRT will not host it.** Managed Runtime is documented as supporting only applications created from a PWA Kit template — a full React + Express + PWA Kit storefront bundle — and is not a general-purpose Node or microservice hosting platform. An integration's backend cannot be packaged as an MRT application because it is not a storefront. This was confirmed from three independent directions: the platform documentation's own constraint statement; the former Integration Lead's direct assessment that multiple independent Node processes cannot be run inside an MRT environment; and Salesforce's own B2C Commerce Headless Integration guidance for partners, which states that every Composable Storefront must have a project created in Runtime Admin and offers exactly three delivery shapes for backend integration logic — an SFCC cartridge, a Node module extending the same PWA Kit server, or an externally-hosted API — with no fourth pattern of a sibling MRT application. It was finally confirmed firsthand in Runtime Admin: the Create-a-New-Project flow asks only for a name, a project ID, and two environment defaults. There is no application-type field, because the platform assumes every project is a storefront. MRT's genuine multi-project support exists for a different purpose — separating distinct brands or domains, each of which is itself a full storefront — not for decomposing one storefront's backend. Even setting the hosting constraint aside, three of Option B's consequences would independently count against it: the literal per-integration form breaches the organisation environment cap; every cross-application call would add a network hop to the SSR path that the LCP budget cannot absorb; and the hostname-per-environment binding is incompatible with the single-domain session model the eight storefronts depend on. The isolation goals behind Option B remain legitimate. They are addressed within Option A in §5, and the one case Option A genuinely cannot serve is recorded as a risk in §7. --- ## 4. Recommended Option & Rationale ### 4.1 Recommended Option **Option A — Single MRT application, implemented as a modular single application.** ### 4.2 Rationale Option A is recommended because Option B is not available. The decisive factor is not a trade-off between the two but a platform constraint: MRT hosts only PWA Kit storefront bundles, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application at all. Once that is established, Option A is the only option that satisfies the §2 constraints, and it satisfies them without migration cost because it is the current state. The recommendation is qualified in one important respect. Endorsing Option A is not an endorsement of the status quo, because the status quo includes an isolation gap that is real and demonstrated: today's arrangement has no isolation between integrations at any level, despite documentation describing per-origin connection pooling as though it were in place. The recommendation is therefore Option A **implemented as a modular single application** — one bundle, with integration code in clearly separated modules, each with its own connection pool, timeout budget, and error boundary. This is the "middle option" the originating ticket asked to be considered; it is not a third topology but the correct implementation shape of Option A, and it is specified in §5. Adopting Option A without that work would leave success criterion 1.4.3 unmet. ### 4.3 Trade-offs Accepted - **Shared-process failure modes remain.** Even fully implemented, in-process module boundaries do not give memory, event-loop, or crash isolation. A synchronous CPU-bound operation in any integration will block every other concurrent request on that process, and no connection pool or configuration prevents it (demonstrated, §6). This is mitigated by a coding rule, not by infrastructure, and is accepted as a permanent property of the chosen topology. - **Coupled deploy and rollback granularity.** One immutable bundle per environment means the unit of deploy and rollback is the whole application. A rollback triggered by one integration reverts every integration in that bundle. Accepted; mitigated only by release discipline and small changes. - **Coarse credential and access scoping.** All integrations' credentials share one flat environment-variable namespace per environment, and MRT project roles are all-or-nothing — everyone who needs deploy or variable access for any integration has it for all of them. Currently four people, all Admin. Accepted for now; revisit if the team grows materially. - **Isolation depends on convention.** Nothing in the platform or the current CI setup enforces the module boundaries in §5. Accepted, with the mitigation in §7. --- ## 5. Technical Implementation > Scope note: this section specifies the implementation of the chosen option. The work itself is > deliberately **not** part of this spike — it is specified here so it can be picked up as its own > ticket once §8 is signed off, and because §1.4 cannot be met by a recommendation that leaves the > isolation gap undefined. Three of the files below are absolute Tier 1 (§2.1), so the implementing > ticket must secure owner approval before starting. ### 5.1 High-Level Sequence 1. A shopper request arrives at the MRT environment and is handled by the single Express app in `overrides/app/ssr.js`. 2. The route handler for the relevant surface delegates to an integration module under `overrides/app/ssr/` (one module per integration, as today). 3. The module issues its upstream call via `fetch`, passing the `dispatcher` option bound to **its own** connection pool from `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`, so its connection usage is capped independently of every other integration. 4. The pool applies that integration's own `connectTimeout` and `bodyTimeout`, bounding how long a slow upstream can hold a connection — and keeping the request inside MRT's 20s/16s execution ceiling rather than being terminated by it. 5. On success, the module returns typed data to the handler, which renders or responds. 6. **Error path:** if the upstream fails, times out, or returns a non-OK status, the module catches it at its own boundary and converts it to an explicit outcome — an HTTP error response for a dedicated endpoint, or a degraded-but-rendered result for a page surface per the graceful degradation constraint. The rejection **must not** propagate out of the module. 7. **Error path:** the route registration awaits (or explicitly `.catch()`es) the module call, so no integration failure can become an unobserved floating promise. Today two routes do not do this (§5.2), which is why a Marketing Cloud failure currently produces no response at all rather than an error response. ### 5.2 Component / API Changes | File / Endpoint | Change Required | Type | | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | | `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts` | Confirm pool definitions against real hostnames; resolve the two placeholder origins (`sfcc-payments`, `booxi`). Currently defines 7 pools but is imported nowhere. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccScapiPool` on the JWKS `fetch` (line ~78, currently a bare global-dispatcher call). | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccPaymentsPool` on the metadata `fetch` (line ~42). | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/marketingCloud.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: marketingCloudAuthPool` / `marketingCloudRestPool` on the two `fetch` calls (lines ~38, ~61). **Add a try/catch boundary** — this module currently has none. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr.js` **(Tier 1)** | Await or `.catch()` the `sendMagicLinkEmail` calls in the passwordless-login and reset-password routes (lines ~150 and ~168). Both currently create an unobserved floating promise. | Modified | | `config/default.js` **(Tier 1)** | Add a `proxyConfigs` entry per new MRT-mediated integration as each is built (MuleSoft, Google Places, Booxi). Only SCAPI and OCAPI exist today. | Modified | | Runtime Admin → Environment Settings | Matching MRT-side proxy entry per environment. **MRT proxy config is a separate source of truth from the bundle's** — both must be updated together. | Modified | | `.claude/rules/` (new or existing rule file) | Document the integration-module contract in §5.3 so it is enforced at review time. | New | ### 5.3 Data Structures / Interfaces The contract every integration module must satisfy: ```ts // Each integration owns exactly one pool, and every outbound call uses it. import { mulesoftPool } from './connectionPools'; // 1. All outbound calls pass their own dispatcher. const response = await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { /* ... */ }, body: JSON.stringify(payload), dispatcher: mulesoftPool, // ← per-integration connection cap + timeouts }); // 2. Every module resolves to an explicit outcome. It never throws past its own boundary. type IntegrationResult = | { kind: 'ok'; data: T } | { kind: 'error'; reason: string; status?: number }; // 3. Every route registration observes the promise. app.post(path, (req, res) => { void handler(req, res).catch((err) => { // log, then always respond — never leave the request unanswered }); }); ``` Pool boundaries and caps are per `tsd-architecture.md` §12.1 (7 pools: `sfcc-scapi`, `sfcc-payments`, `mulesoft`, `marketing-cloud-auth`, `marketing-cloud-rest`, `google-places`, `booxi`). Caps there are derived from expected rather than observed concurrency and should be validated by the Stage load-test pass described in §9.3 of that document. ### 5.4 Error Handling & Edge Cases | Scenario | Expected Behaviour | Type | | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | | An integration's upstream returns a non-OK status | The owning module catches it and returns an explicit error outcome. The request receives a response describing the failure — never silence. | Error | | An integration's upstream is slow or unresponsive | Its pool's `bodyTimeout` aborts the call before MRT's 20s/16s ceiling, releasing the connection. Other integrations' pools are unaffected. | Error | | An integration floods its own connection pool | Only that integration's calls queue. Other integrations retain their own capped connections. | Edge case | | A page surface needs an integration that is unavailable | The page renders without that integration's contribution, per the graceful degradation constraint — except where an explicit error is mandated (checkout). | Edge case | | An integration performs a synchronous CPU-bound operation | **Not preventable by this design.** Every concurrent request on the process blocks for the duration. Prevented only by the coding rule; see §7. | Error | | Contentful (SDK does not expose a `dispatcher` hook) | Connection isolation is not achievable via this pattern; graceful degradation is the mitigation. See §7 for a correction to the existing documented claim. | Edge case | ### 5.5 Configuration & Environment Notes No new environment variables are introduced by the topology decision itself. Each future integration adds its own credentials to the per-environment variable set, and a matching proxy entry in **both** `config/default.js` and the MRT environment's own proxy configuration. One finding relevant to the LCP constraint in §2.1 is recorded here because it materially affects any performance measurement of the chosen topology, though it is not itself a topology issue: the seven MRT environments are split across two AWS regions — DEV, DEV1, SIT, UAT and STG in Asia Pacific (Sydney), TEST and Production in US East (Ohio). Because STG is the tier designated for contractual LCP sign-off and Production sits in a different region, Stage-measured performance figures are not currently representative of Production. This is being raised separately (Appendix A) and should be resolved before any LCP sign-off, under either topology. --- ## 6. Testing & Validation ### 6.1 Test Coverage Mapping to §1.4: criterion 3 requires the isolation behaviour to be demonstrated rather than asserted. The suite below exists and passes (`overrides/app/ssr/blastRadius.test.ts`, 4 tests). | Test Type | What is Being Tested | Pass Criteria | | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Unit / Integration | Rejection propagation between integrations, using the real `paymentMetadataHandler` and `sendMagicLinkEmail`. One integration fails; an unrelated one succeeds. | Currently: an aggregating caller loses the successful result entirely. After §5: the successful result survives its sibling's failure. | | Unit / Integration | The real `ssr.js` call shape — an unobserved floating promise inside a `.then()` — when its integration fails. | Currently: becomes a process-level unhandled rejection and the response object is never written to, so the shopper receives nothing until MRT's ceiling returns a 502. After §5: an explicit response. | | Unit / Integration | Cross-region blast radius: an AU-scoped call and an unrelated US-scoped call in flight together, the US one failing. | Currently: the AU result is lost despite AU not using the failing integration. After §5: the AU result is unaffected. | | Unit | Event-loop blocking: a synchronous CPU-bound operation alongside an unrelated fast operation. | The fast operation is delayed by the full duration of the blocking work. **This test documents an accepted limitation and is expected to keep passing after §5** — it is not fixed by that work. | | Integration | Per-pool isolation under load once §5 is implemented: a saturated or slow origin must not starve a different origin's pool. | An unrelated integration's call completes within its own timeout while another integration's pool is saturated. **Not yet written** — depends on §5. | | E2E / Playwright | Not applicable. | This TSD decides deployment topology and ships no user-facing surface, so there is no user journey to assert. Recorded explicitly rather than omitted. | Performance validation is not duplicated here: per-pool queue-depth and connection-wait metrics are already scheduled for the Stage load-test pass in `tsd-architecture.md` §9.3, and bundle size is already gated in CI. See §5.5 regarding the region caveat on Stage measurements. ### 6.2 Regression Risk The topology decision itself changes no code and therefore carries no regression risk. The §5 implementation does, and it is concentrated in two places. First, attaching a `dispatcher` to existing `fetch` calls changes connection behaviour for SLAS token validation, payment metadata, and Marketing Cloud email — all on authentication and checkout paths, so a mis-set cap or timeout would surface as intermittent failures there rather than as an obvious break. The four tests above cover the failure-isolation behaviour but not cap tuning, which is why the load-test row is listed as required. Second, `overrides/app/ssr.js` is the entry point for every request, so the route-handler change must be verified across all 8 storefronts rather than one. Note also that the `commerce-sdk-react` hooks manage their own HTTP client and are unaffected by pool changes, which usefully bounds the risk: the bulk of SFCC commerce traffic does not traverse these pools at all. --- ## 7. Risks & Mitigations | Risk | Likelihood | Mitigation | Owner | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | | §5 is never implemented, leaving Option A endorsed but its isolation gap open — the state this TSD exists to correct. | **High** | Raise the §5 work as its own ticket at sign-off and sequence it **before** the bulk of integration build-out. It is cheap now and grows more expensive per integration added. | Technical Lead / Squad A | | The module contract in §5.3 is not followed by future integrations, since nothing enforces it. The gap was originally introduced this way. | **High** | Document the contract as a rule in `.claude/rules/`, add it to the PR checklist, and consider an ast-grep or lint rule matching a `fetch(` in `overrides/app/ssr/` with no `dispatcher` key. | Squad A | | A future integration proves genuinely CPU-bound or requires process isolation, which Option A cannot provide at any level of implementation quality. | Low | Host that integration's layer **outside** MRT (general-purpose cloud compute, or a vendor-hosted API per Salesforce's Connected App pattern) and call it from the single app over HTTP via its own pool. Reassess if it arises. | Technical Lead | | Connection-pool caps in `tsd-architecture.md` §12.1 are derived from expected, not observed, concurrency and may be wrong under real traffic. | Med | Validate against per-pool queue-depth and connection-wait metrics in the Stage load-test pass (§9.3 of that document) and revise before go-live.
