# TSD: MRT Application Topology (Single vs Per-Integration) ## Document Information | Field | Value | | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Document ID** | TSD-SFCC-681 | | **Author(s)** | Marcel Angelo Navarro, Squad A / Frontend Development Lead | | **Reviewer(s)** | Tim Lavelle, Technical Lead | | **Created** | 12 Aug 2026 | | **Version** | v0.1 (Draft) | | **Status** | Draft | | **Related Jira** | SFCC-681 (clones SFCC-237, which was closed at Sprint 2 rollover) | --- ## Version History | Version | Date | Summary of Change | Author | | ------- | ----------- | ----------------- | --------------------- | | v0.1 | 12 Aug 2026 | Initial draft | Marcel Angelo Navarro | --- ## 1. Problem Statement ### 1.1 Context The storefront runs on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT), where a Node/Express layer performs all server-side work: the SSR render, proxying to upstream APIs, token exchange, and server-side calls to integrated systems. Today that layer serves just three integration touchpoints: SLAS token validation, payment method metadata, and Marketing Cloud email. Only two proxy origins are configured, SCAPI and OCAPI. Approximately 18 external systems are in scope for the programme (`.docs/integration/`), and nearly all of them have no code written yet. Integration build-out begins in the coming sprints. ### 1.2 Problem How many MRT applications the storefront deploys, and how integration code is divided across them, has never been decided. The current arrangement is a default inherited from the PWA Kit scaffold, not a deliberate choice, and it has never been documented or signed off. Because deployment topology determines how code is packaged, deployed, and rolled back, it becomes progressively more expensive to change once integration code exists across many systems. Compounding this, the server-side layer currently provides **no failure isolation of any kind** between integrations. Seven per-origin connection pools were written for this purpose (`overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`) but are imported nowhere and attached to no request, so every integration shares one undivided execution and connection context. This is present-state fact, verified in code and by test (§6), not a projection. ### 1.3 Impact if Not Solved - Topology is set by accretion rather than decision. Each integration that lands without an agreed position makes the arrangement harder to change, and the decision is effectively made by whoever writes the first proxy. - The isolation gap persists and compounds. It was found by chance in the only integration that currently has real code, and nothing in the codebase, review process, or CI prevents the same pattern recurring in the ~17 integrations still to be built. - Deploy and rollback blast radius stays coupled: a bad change to one integration forces a rollback that also reverts every other integration shipped in the same bundle. - Squad A (FED) and the SFCC squad have no shared written position to build against, risking divergent assumptions about where integration code belongs. ### 1.4 Success Criteria 1. A single documented position on how many MRT applications the storefront deploys and how integration code is divided across them, signed off by the Technical Lead (§8). 2. The as-is baseline is verified against the live platform and the codebase rather than assumed, with any inaccuracies in existing documentation corrected. 3. The chosen topology's failure-isolation behaviour is demonstrated by reproducible automated tests rather than asserted. 4. The position is recorded specifically enough that integration build-out can proceed without re-opening the question. --- ## 2. Constraints & Assumptions ### 2.1 Constraints | Constraint | Detail | | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Platform | SFCC B2C Commerce + PWA Kit on Managed Runtime. MRT hosts **only applications created from a PWA Kit template**. It is not general-purpose Node or container hosting. | | MRT application model | One project has many bundles, but **each environment has exactly one bundle designated as deployed**. A bundle is the entire built application and is immutable once created. | | MRT organisation limits | Maximum **100 total environments** and **10 production environments** per organisation, raisable only by Salesforce Support. Currently 7 environments in use. | | Execution model | A single Node.js/Express process per environment ("App Server"), serverless and auto-scaling. Hard request-execution ceiling of **20s production / 16s non-production**, after which MRT returns HTTP 502. **Unhandled promise rejections break app rendering.** | | Storefront scope | Must work across all **8 storefronts in 6 regions** (AU, UK, US Domestic, US International, EU Domestic, EU International, HK, ME). No single-market workarounds. | | Session and domain model | All 8 storefronts are path-prefixed on a **single first-party domain**; the `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie depends on this. An MRT environment binds to exactly **one** External Hostname, and a hostname can serve only one environment at a time. | | Performance | **LCP ≤ 2s at p75 mobile** is client-mandated and contractual (`architecture.md` §9). Any added network hop on the SSR path counts against it. | | Graceful degradation | Each external system must fail independently: one outage must not break a whole page (AGENTS.md > Graceful Degradation). | | Tier 1 change control | `config/default.js`, `config/sites.js`, `overrides/app/ssr.js` and `worker/main.js` are **absolute** Tier 1 under AGENTS.md Hard Rule #4. The verified-session exception does not apply. Any topology or isolation change touches at least one of these. | ### 2.2 Assumptions | Assumption | Risk if Wrong | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | The ~18 systems in `.docs/integration/` remain the integration scope for this decision. | Materially more systems would grow the per-environment variable surface and module count, but would not change the topology conclusion. Option B stays unsupported regardless of integration count. | | Zimmermann's MRT agreement permits additional projects at no additional licence cost. | Affects only Option B's cost line. Option B is already non-viable on architectural grounds, so the recommendation does not change either way. Unconfirmed with the account team. | | The `zimmermann` project runs on ARM rather than x86 server architecture. | If x86, environments must be migrated before **31 Jan 2027** or lose the ability to deploy. Not exposed in Runtime Admin at project or environment level, so unverified. Independent of the topology decision. | | No in-scope integration requires process-level isolation that in-process module boundaries cannot provide. | If one does, for example a genuinely CPU-bound workload, it must be hosted outside MRT entirely. That is a separate infrastructure decision, not a change to MRT application topology. See §7. | --- ## 3. Options Analysis ### 3.1 Options Summary | Option | Pros | Cons | Viable? | | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | | **Option A**: Single MRT application, all integrations in one bundle | + The only model the platform supports, so zero migration cost, since it is the current state.
+ One bundle per environment: the existing 6-workflow deploy pipeline, version guard and tag promotion already work against it.
+ A single SSR render composes many integrations with no cross-app network hop, protecting LCP.
+ One shared session, cookie and CSP context, which the single-domain 8-storefront session model requires.
+ Isolation is achievable in-process per integration (connection pools, timeouts, error boundaries). | - All integrations share one Node process: no process, memory or event-loop isolation. A CPU-bound or unhandled-rejection failure in one integration can affect unrelated concurrent requests (demonstrated, §6).
- One immutable bundle per environment: rolling back one integration reverts every integration shipped in that bundle.
- One flat environment-variable namespace per environment shared by all integrations; MRT offers no sub-scoping within a project, and project roles are all-or-nothing.
- Isolation must be actively implemented and maintained by convention; nothing in the platform enforces it. | **Yes** | | **Option B**: Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain | + Would provide true process-level isolation (memory, event loop, crash domain) per integration.
+ Would provide independent bundle lineage, so one integration could be deployed or rolled back without touching others.
+ Would scope environment variables and project role assignments per integration domain. | - **Not supported by the platform.** MRT hosts only PWA Kit template applications; every project must be a full storefront bundle, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application.
- Salesforce's own ISV integration guidance offers no such pattern.
- A literal per-integration reading (~18 systems × 6 tiers = 108 environments) exceeds the 100-environment organisation cap on its own.
- Cross-application calls would add a network hop to the SSR path, working directly against LCP ≤ 2s.
- Hostname-per-environment binding conflicts with the single first-party domain session model. | **No** | ### 3.2 Option Detail #### Option A: Single MRT application One PWA Kit project (`zimmermann`) produces one bundle, deployed to one environment per tier. All integration code (proxy routes, token exchange, server-side API calls) lives inside that single Express application, organised as separate modules. It satisfies every constraint in §2 by construction, because it is the model the platform is built around: one bundle per environment, one hostname per environment, one shared session context across all 8 path-prefixed storefronts. Its weakness is that isolation between integrations is a matter of code discipline rather than infrastructure, and must be built deliberately (§5). #### Option B: Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain *(Not viable)* The proposal was that each integration, or each domain grouping of integrations, would be deployed as its own Managed Runtime application, giving each one an independent process, deploy lineage, and credential scope. This was explored in full rather than dismissed, because on paper it addresses precisely the weaknesses of Option A identified above, and because the question was raised specifically to be settled with evidence rather than assumption. It is not viable, for a reason that is architectural rather than a matter of configuration or budget: **MRT will not host it.** Managed Runtime is documented as supporting only applications created from a PWA Kit template, a full React + Express + PWA Kit storefront bundle, and is not a general-purpose Node or microservice hosting platform. An integration's backend cannot be packaged as an MRT application because it is not a storefront. This was confirmed from three independent directions: the platform documentation's own constraint statement; the former Integration Lead's direct assessment that multiple independent Node processes cannot be run inside an MRT environment; and Salesforce's own B2C Commerce Headless Integration guidance for partners, which states that every Composable Storefront must have a project created in Runtime Admin and offers exactly three delivery shapes for backend integration logic (an SFCC cartridge, a Node module extending the same PWA Kit server, or an externally-hosted API) with no fourth pattern of a sibling MRT application. It was finally confirmed firsthand in Runtime Admin: the Create-a-New-Project flow asks only for a name, a project ID, and two environment defaults. There is no application-type field, because the platform assumes every project is a storefront. MRT's genuine multi-project support exists for a different purpose: separating distinct brands or domains, each of which is itself a full storefront, not decomposing one storefront's backend. Even setting the hosting constraint aside, three of Option B's consequences would independently count against it: the literal per-integration form breaches the organisation environment cap; every cross-application call would add a network hop to the SSR path that the LCP budget cannot absorb; and the hostname-per-environment binding is incompatible with the single-domain session model the eight storefronts depend on. The isolation goals behind Option B remain legitimate. They are addressed within Option A in §5, and the one case Option A genuinely cannot serve is recorded as a risk in §7. --- ## 4. Recommended Option & Rationale ### 4.1 Recommended Option **Option A: Single MRT application, implemented as a modular single application.** ### 4.2 Rationale Option A is recommended because Option B is not available. The decisive factor is not a trade-off between the two but a platform constraint: MRT hosts only PWA Kit storefront bundles, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application at all. Once that is established, Option A is the only option that satisfies the §2 constraints, and it satisfies them without migration cost because it is the current state. The recommendation is qualified in one important respect. Endorsing Option A is not an endorsement of the status quo, because the status quo includes an isolation gap that is real and demonstrated: today's arrangement has no isolation between integrations at any level, despite documentation describing per-origin connection pooling as though it were in place. The recommendation is therefore Option A **implemented as a modular single application**: one bundle, with integration code in clearly separated modules, each with its own connection pool, timeout budget, and error boundary. This is the "middle option" the originating ticket asked to be considered; it is not a third topology but the correct implementation shape of Option A, and it is specified in §5. Adopting Option A without that work would leave success criterion 1.4.3 unmet. ### 4.3 Trade-offs Accepted - **Shared-process failure modes remain.** Even fully implemented, in-process module boundaries do not give memory, event-loop, or crash isolation. A synchronous CPU-bound operation in any integration will block every other concurrent request on that process, and no connection pool or configuration prevents it (demonstrated, §6). This is mitigated by a coding rule, not by infrastructure, and is accepted as a permanent property of the chosen topology. - **Coupled deploy and rollback granularity.** One immutable bundle per environment means the unit of deploy and rollback is the whole application. A rollback triggered by one integration reverts every integration in that bundle. Accepted; mitigated only by release discipline and small changes. - **Coarse credential and access scoping.** All integrations' credentials share one flat environment-variable namespace per environment, and MRT project roles are all-or-nothing: everyone who needs deploy or variable access for any integration has it for all of them. Currently four people, all Admin. Accepted for now; revisit if the team grows materially. - **Isolation depends on convention.** Nothing in the platform or the current CI setup enforces the module boundaries in §5. Accepted, with the mitigation in §7. --- ## 5. Technical Implementation > Scope note: this section specifies the implementation of the chosen option. The work itself is > deliberately **not** part of this spike. It is specified here so it can be picked up as its own > ticket once §8 is signed off, and because §1.4 cannot be met by a recommendation that leaves the > isolation gap undefined. Three of the files below are absolute Tier 1 (§2.1), so the implementing > ticket must secure owner approval before starting. ### 5.1 High-Level Sequence 1. A shopper request arrives at the MRT environment and is handled by the single Express app in `overrides/app/ssr.js`. 2. The route handler for the relevant surface delegates to an integration module under `overrides/app/ssr/` (one module per integration, as today). 3. The module issues its upstream call via `fetch`, passing the `dispatcher` option bound to **its own** connection pool from `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`, so its connection usage is capped independently of every other integration. 4. The pool applies that integration's own `connectTimeout` and `bodyTimeout`, bounding how long a slow upstream can hold a connection, and keeping the request inside MRT's 20s/16s execution ceiling rather than being terminated by it. 5. On success, the module returns typed data to the handler, which renders or responds. 6. **Error path:** if the upstream fails, times out, or returns a non-OK status, the module catches it at its own boundary and converts it to an explicit outcome: an HTTP error response for a dedicated endpoint, or a degraded-but-rendered result for a page surface per the graceful degradation constraint. The rejection **must not** propagate out of the module. 7. **Error path:** the route registration awaits (or explicitly `.catch()`es) the module call, so no integration failure can become an unobserved floating promise. Today two routes do not do this (§5.2), which is why a Marketing Cloud failure currently produces no response at all rather than an error response. ### 5.2 Component / API Changes | File / Endpoint | Change Required | Type | | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | | `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts` | Confirm pool definitions against real hostnames; resolve the two placeholder origins (`sfcc-payments`, `booxi`). Currently defines 7 pools but is imported nowhere. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccScapiPool` on the JWKS `fetch` (line ~78, currently a bare global-dispatcher call). | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccPaymentsPool` on the metadata `fetch` (line ~42). | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/marketingCloud.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: marketingCloudAuthPool` / `marketingCloudRestPool` on the two `fetch` calls (lines ~38, ~61). **Add a try/catch boundary**; this module currently has none. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr.js` **(Tier 1)** | Await or `.catch()` the `sendMagicLinkEmail` calls in the passwordless-login and reset-password routes (lines ~150 and ~168). Both currently create an unobserved floating promise. | Modified | | `config/default.js` **(Tier 1)** | Add a `proxyConfigs` entry per new MRT-mediated integration as each is built (MuleSoft, Google Places, Booxi). Only SCAPI and OCAPI exist today. | Modified | | Runtime Admin, Environment Settings | Matching MRT-side proxy entry per environment. **MRT proxy config is a separate source of truth from the bundle's**; both must be updated together. | Modified | | `.claude/rules/` (new or existing rule file) | Document the integration-module contract in §5.3 so it is enforced at review time. | New | ### 5.3 Data Structures / Interfaces The contract every integration module must satisfy: ```ts // Each integration owns exactly one pool, and every outbound call uses it. import { mulesoftPool } from './connectionPools'; // 1. All outbound calls pass their own dispatcher. const response = await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { /* ... */ }, body: JSON.stringify(payload), dispatcher: mulesoftPool, // per-integration connection cap + timeouts }); // 2. Every module resolves to an explicit outcome. It never throws past its own boundary. type IntegrationResult = | { kind: 'ok'; data: T } | { kind: 'error'; reason: string; status?: number }; // 3. Every route registration observes the promise. app.post(path, (req, res) => { void handler(req, res).catch((err) => { // log, then always respond; never leave the request unanswered }); }); ``` Pool boundaries and caps are per `tsd-architecture.md` §12.1 (7 pools: `sfcc-scapi`, `sfcc-payments`, `mulesoft`, `marketing-cloud-auth`, `marketing-cloud-rest`, `google-places`, `booxi`). Caps there are derived from expected rather than observed concurrency and should be validated by the Stage load-test pass described in §9.3 of that document. ### 5.4 Error Handling & Edge Cases | Scenario | Expected Behaviour | Type | | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | | An integration's upstream returns a non-OK status | The owning module catches it and returns an explicit error outcome. The request receives a response describing the failure, never silence. | Error | | An integration's upstream is slow or unresponsive | Its pool's `bodyTimeout` aborts the call before MRT's 20s/16s ceiling, releasing the connection. Other integrations' pools are unaffected. | Error | | An integration floods its own connection pool | Only that integration's calls queue. Other integrations retain their own capped connections. | Edge case | | A page surface needs an integration that is unavailable | The page renders without that integration's contribution, per the graceful degradation constraint, except where an explicit error is mandated (checkout). | Edge case | | An integration performs a synchronous CPU-bound operation | **Not preventable by this design.** Every concurrent request on the process blocks for the duration. Prevented only by the coding rule; see §7. | Error | | Contentful (SDK does not expose a `dispatcher` hook) | Connection isolation is not achievable via this pattern; graceful degradation is the mitigation. See §7 for a correction to the existing documented claim. | Edge case | ### 5.5 Configuration & Environment Notes No new environment variables are introduced by the topology decision itself. Each future integration adds its own credentials to the per-environment variable set, and a matching proxy entry in **both** `config/default.js` and the MRT environment's own proxy configuration. One finding relevant to the LCP constraint in §2.1 is recorded here because it materially affects any performance measurement of the chosen topology, though it is not itself a topology issue: the seven MRT environments are split across two AWS regions. DEV, DEV1, SIT, UAT and STG sit in Asia Pacific (Sydney); TEST and Production sit in US East (Ohio). Because STG is the tier designated for contractual LCP sign-off and Production sits in a different region, Stage-measured performance figures are not currently representative of Production. This is being raised separately and should be resolved before any LCP sign-off, under either topology. --- ## 6. Testing & Validation ### 6.1 Test Coverage Mapping to §1.4: criterion 3 requires the isolation behaviour to be demonstrated rather than asserted. The suite below exists and passes (`overrides/app/ssr/blastRadius.test.ts`, 4 tests). | Test Type | What is Being Tested | Pass Criteria | | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Unit / Integration | Rejection propagation between integrations, using the real `paymentMetadataHandler` and `sendMagicLinkEmail`. One integration fails; an unrelated one succeeds. | Currently: an aggregating caller loses the successful result entirely. After §5: the successful result survives its sibling's failure. | | Unit / Integration | The real `ssr.js` call shape (an unobserved floating promise inside a `.then()`) when its integration fails. | Currently: becomes a process-level unhandled rejection and the response object is never written to, so the shopper receives nothing until MRT's ceiling returns a 502. After §5: an explicit response. | | Unit / Integration | Cross-region blast radius: an AU-scoped call and an unrelated US-scoped call in flight together, the US one failing. | Currently: the AU result is lost despite AU not using the failing integration. After §5: the AU result is unaffected. | | Unit | Event-loop blocking: a synchronous CPU-bound operation alongside an unrelated fast operation. | The fast operation is delayed by the full duration of the blocking work. **This test documents an accepted limitation and is expected to keep passing after §5**; it is not fixed by that work. | | Integration | Per-pool isolation under load once §5 is implemented: a saturated or slow origin must not starve a different origin's pool. | An unrelated integration's call completes within its own timeout while another integration's pool is saturated. **Not yet written**; depends on §5. | | E2E / Playwright | Not applicable. | This TSD decides deployment topology and ships no user-facing surface, so there is no user journey to assert. # TSD: MRT Application Topology (Single vs Per-Integration) ## Document Information | Field | Value | | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Document ID** | TSD-SFCC-681 | | **Author(s)** | Marcel Angelo Navarro, Squad A / Frontend Development Lead | | **Reviewer(s)** | Tim Lavelle, Technical Lead | | **Created** | 12 Aug 2026 | | **Version** | v0.1 (Draft) | | **Status** | Draft | | **Related Jira** | SFCC-681 (clones SFCC-237, which was closed at Sprint 2 rollover) | --- ## Version History | Version | Date | Summary of Change | Author | | ------- | ----------- | ----------------- | --------------------- | | v0.1 | 12 Aug 2026 | Initial draft | Marcel Angelo Navarro | --- ## 1. Problem Statement ### 1.1 Context The storefront runs on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT), where a Node/Express layer performs all server-side work: the SSR render, proxying to upstream APIs, token exchange, and server-side calls to integrated systems. Today that layer serves just three integration touchpoints: SLAS token validation, payment method metadata, and Marketing Cloud email. Only two proxy origins are configured, SCAPI and OCAPI. Approximately 18 external systems are in scope for the programme (`.docs/integration/`), and nearly all of them have no code written yet. Integration build-out begins in the coming sprints. ### 1.2 Problem How many MRT applications the storefront deploys, and how integration code is divided across them, has never been decided. The current arrangement is a default inherited from the PWA Kit scaffold, not a deliberate choice, and it has never been documented or signed off. Because deployment topology determines how code is packaged, deployed, and rolled back, it becomes progressively more expensive to change once integration code exists across many systems. Compounding this, the server-side layer currently provides **no failure isolation of any kind** between integrations. Seven per-origin connection pools were written for this purpose (`overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`) but are imported nowhere and attached to no request, so every integration shares one undivided execution and connection context. This is present-state fact, verified in code and by test (§6), not a projection. ### 1.3 Impact if Not Solved - Topology is set by accretion rather than decision. Each integration that lands without an agreed position makes the arrangement harder to change, and the decision is effectively made by whoever writes the first proxy. - The isolation gap persists and compounds. It was found by chance in the only integration that currently has real code, and nothing in the codebase, review process, or CI prevents the same pattern recurring in the ~17 integrations still to be built. - Deploy and rollback blast radius stays coupled: a bad change to one integration forces a rollback that also reverts every other integration shipped in the same bundle. - Squad A (FED) and the SFCC squad have no shared written position to build against, risking divergent assumptions about where integration code belongs. ### 1.4 Success Criteria 1. A single documented position on how many MRT applications the storefront deploys and how integration code is divided across them, signed off by the Technical Lead (§8). 2. The as-is baseline is verified against the live platform and the codebase rather than assumed, with any inaccuracies in existing documentation corrected. 3. The chosen topology's failure-isolation behaviour is demonstrated by reproducible automated tests rather than asserted. 4. The position is recorded specifically enough that integration build-out can proceed without re-opening the question. --- ## 2. Constraints & Assumptions ### 2.1 Constraints | Constraint | Detail | | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Platform | SFCC B2C Commerce + PWA Kit on Managed Runtime. MRT hosts **only applications created from a PWA Kit template**. It is not general-purpose Node or container hosting. | | MRT application model | One project has many bundles, but **each environment has exactly one bundle designated as deployed**. A bundle is the entire built application and is immutable once created. | | MRT organisation limits | Maximum **100 total environments** and **10 production environments** per organisation, raisable only by Salesforce Support. Currently 7 environments in use. | | Execution model | A single Node.js/Express process per environment ("App Server"), serverless and auto-scaling. Hard request-execution ceiling of **20s production / 16s non-production**, after which MRT returns HTTP 502. **Unhandled promise rejections break app rendering.** | | Storefront scope | Must work across all **8 storefronts in 6 regions** (AU, UK, US Domestic, US International, EU Domestic, EU International, HK, ME). No single-market workarounds. | | Session and domain model | All 8 storefronts are path-prefixed on a **single first-party domain**; the `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie depends on this. An MRT environment binds to exactly **one** External Hostname, and a hostname can serve only one environment at a time. | | Performance | **LCP ≤ 2s at p75 mobile** is client-mandated and contractual (`architecture.md` §9). Any added network hop on the SSR path counts against it. | | Graceful degradation | Each external system must fail independently: one outage must not break a whole page (AGENTS.md > Graceful Degradation). | | Tier 1 change control | `config/default.js`, `config/sites.js`, `overrides/app/ssr.js` and `worker/main.js` are **absolute** Tier 1 under AGENTS.md Hard Rule #4. The verified-session exception does not apply. Any topology or isolation change touches at least one of these. | ### 2.2 Assumptions | Assumption | Risk if Wrong | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | The ~18 systems in `.docs/integration/` remain the integration scope for this decision. | Materially more systems would grow the per-environment variable surface and module count, but would not change the topology conclusion. Option B stays unsupported regardless of integration count. | | Zimmermann's MRT agreement permits additional projects at no additional licence cost. | Affects only Option B's cost line. Option B is already non-viable on architectural grounds, so the recommendation does not change either way. Unconfirmed with the account team. | | The `zimmermann` project runs on ARM rather than x86 server architecture. | If x86, environments must be migrated before **31 Jan 2027** or lose the ability to deploy. Not exposed in Runtime Admin at project or environment level, so unverified. Independent of the topology decision. | | No in-scope integration requires process-level isolation that in-process module boundaries cannot provide. | If one does, for example a genuinely CPU-bound workload, it must be hosted outside MRT entirely. That is a separate infrastructure decision, not a change to MRT application topology. See §7. | --- ## 3. Options Analysis ### 3.1 Options Summary | Option | Pros | Cons | Viable? | | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | | **Option A**: Single MRT application, all integrations in one bundle | + The only model the platform supports, so zero migration cost, since it is the current state.
+ One bundle per environment: the existing 6-workflow deploy pipeline, version guard and tag promotion already work against it.
+ A single SSR render composes many integrations with no cross-app network hop, protecting LCP.
+ One shared session, cookie and CSP context, which the single-domain 8-storefront session model requires.
+ Isolation is achievable in-process per integration (connection pools, timeouts, error boundaries). | - All integrations share one Node process: no process, memory or event-loop isolation. A CPU-bound or unhandled-rejection failure in one integration can affect unrelated concurrent requests (demonstrated, §6).
- One immutable bundle per environment: rolling back one integration reverts every integration shipped in that bundle.
- One flat environment-variable namespace per environment shared by all integrations; MRT offers no sub-scoping within a project, and project roles are all-or-nothing.
- Isolation must be actively implemented and maintained by convention; nothing in the platform enforces it. | **Yes** | | **Option B**: Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain | + Would provide true process-level isolation (memory, event loop, crash domain) per integration.
+ Would provide independent bundle lineage, so one integration could be deployed or rolled back without touching others.
+ Would scope environment variables and project role assignments per integration domain. | - **Not supported by the platform.** MRT hosts only PWA Kit template applications; every project must be a full storefront bundle, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application.
- Salesforce's own ISV integration guidance offers no such pattern.
- A literal per-integration reading (~18 systems × 6 tiers = 108 environments) exceeds the 100-environment organisation cap on its own.
- Cross-application calls would add a network hop to the SSR path, working directly against LCP ≤ 2s.
- Hostname-per-environment binding conflicts with the single first-party domain session model. | **No** | ### 3.2 Option Detail #### Option A: Single MRT application One PWA Kit project (`zimmermann`) produces one bundle, deployed to one environment per tier. All integration code (proxy routes, token exchange, server-side API calls) lives inside that single Express application, organised as separate modules. It satisfies every constraint in §2 by construction, because it is the model the platform is built around: one bundle per environment, one hostname per environment, one shared session context across all 8 path-prefixed storefronts. Its weakness is that isolation between integrations is a matter of code discipline rather than infrastructure, and must be built deliberately (§5). #### Option B: Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain *(Not viable)* The proposal was that each integration, or each domain grouping of integrations, would be deployed as its own Managed Runtime application, giving each one an independent process, deploy lineage, and credential scope. This was explored in full rather than dismissed, because on paper it addresses precisely the weaknesses of Option A identified above, and because the question was raised specifically to be settled with evidence rather than assumption. It is not viable, for a reason that is architectural rather than a matter of configuration or budget: **MRT will not host it.** Managed Runtime is documented as supporting only applications created from a PWA Kit template, a full React + Express + PWA Kit storefront bundle, and is not a general-purpose Node or microservice hosting platform. An integration's backend cannot be packaged as an MRT application because it is not a storefront. This was confirmed from three independent directions: the platform documentation's own constraint statement; the former Integration Lead's direct assessment that multiple independent Node processes cannot be run inside an MRT environment; and Salesforce's own B2C Commerce Headless Integration guidance for partners, which states that every Composable Storefront must have a project created in Runtime Admin and offers exactly three delivery shapes for backend integration logic (an SFCC cartridge, a Node module extending the same PWA Kit server, or an externally-hosted API) with no fourth pattern of a sibling MRT application. It was finally confirmed firsthand in Runtime Admin: the Create-a-New-Project flow asks only for a name, a project ID, and two environment defaults. There is no application-type field, because the platform assumes every project is a storefront. MRT's genuine multi-project support exists for a different purpose: separating distinct brands or domains, each of which is itself a full storefront, not decomposing one storefront's backend. Even setting the hosting constraint aside, three of Option B's consequences would independently count against it: the literal per-integration form breaches the organisation environment cap; every cross-application call would add a network hop to the SSR path that the LCP budget cannot absorb; and the hostname-per-environment binding is incompatible with the single-domain session model the eight storefronts depend on. The isolation goals behind Option B remain legitimate. They are addressed within Option A in §5, and the one case Option A genuinely cannot serve is recorded as a risk in §7. --- ## 4. Recommended Option & Rationale ### 4.1 Recommended Option **Option A: Single MRT application, implemented as a modular single application.** ### 4.2 Rationale Option A is recommended because Option B is not available. The decisive factor is not a trade-off between the two but a platform constraint: MRT hosts only PWA Kit storefront bundles, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application at all. Once that is established, Option A is the only option that satisfies the §2 constraints, and it satisfies them without migration cost because it is the current state. The recommendation is qualified in one important respect. Endorsing Option A is not an endorsement of the status quo, because the status quo includes an isolation gap that is real and demonstrated: today's arrangement has no isolation between integrations at any level, despite documentation describing per-origin connection pooling as though it were in place. The recommendation is therefore Option A **implemented as a modular single application**: one bundle, with integration code in clearly separated modules, each with its own connection pool, timeout budget, and error boundary. This is the "middle option" the originating ticket asked to be considered; it is not a third topology but the correct implementation shape of Option A, and it is specified in §5. Adopting Option A without that work would leave success criterion 1.4.3 unmet. ### 4.3 Trade-offs Accepted - **Shared-process failure modes remain.** Even fully implemented, in-process module boundaries do not give memory, event-loop, or crash isolation. A synchronous CPU-bound operation in any integration will block every other concurrent request on that process, and no connection pool or configuration prevents it (demonstrated, §6). This is mitigated by a coding rule, not by infrastructure, and is accepted as a permanent property of the chosen topology. - **Coupled deploy and rollback granularity.** One immutable bundle per environment means the unit of deploy and rollback is the whole application. A rollback triggered by one integration reverts every integration in that bundle. Accepted; mitigated only by release discipline and small changes. - **Coarse credential and access scoping.** All integrations' credentials share one flat environment-variable namespace per environment, and MRT project roles are all-or-nothing: everyone who needs deploy or variable access for any integration has it for all of them. Currently four people, all Admin. Accepted for now; revisit if the team grows materially. - **Isolation depends on convention.** Nothing in the platform or the current CI setup enforces the module boundaries in §5. Accepted, with the mitigation in §7. --- ## 5. Technical Implementation > Scope note: this section specifies the implementation of the chosen option. The work itself is > deliberately **not** part of this spike. It is specified here so it can be picked up as its own > ticket once §8 is signed off, and because §1.4 cannot be met by a recommendation that leaves the > isolation gap undefined. Three of the files below are absolute Tier 1 (§2.1), so the implementing > ticket must secure owner approval before starting. ### 5.1 High-Level Sequence 1. A shopper request arrives at the MRT environment and is handled by the single Express app in `overrides/app/ssr.js`. 2. The route handler for the relevant surface delegates to an integration module under `overrides/app/ssr/` (one module per integration, as today). 3. The module issues its upstream call via `fetch`, passing the `dispatcher` option bound to **its own** connection pool from `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`, so its connection usage is capped independently of every other integration. 4. The pool applies that integration's own `connectTimeout` and `bodyTimeout`, bounding how long a slow upstream can hold a connection, and keeping the request inside MRT's 20s/16s execution ceiling rather than being terminated by it. 5. On success, the module returns typed data to the handler, which renders or responds. 6. **Error path:** if the upstream fails, times out, or returns a non-OK status, the module catches it at its own boundary and converts it to an explicit outcome: an HTTP error response for a dedicated endpoint, or a degraded-but-rendered result for a page surface per the graceful degradation constraint. The rejection **must not** propagate out of the module. 7. **Error path:** the route registration awaits (or explicitly `.catch()`es) the module call, so no integration failure can become an unobserved floating promise. Today two routes do not do this (§5.2), which is why a Marketing Cloud failure currently produces no response at all rather than an error response. ### 5.2 Component / API Changes | File / Endpoint | Change Required | Type | | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | | `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts` | Confirm pool definitions against real hostnames; resolve the two placeholder origins (`sfcc-payments`, `booxi`). Currently defines 7 pools but is imported nowhere. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccScapiPool` on the JWKS `fetch` (line ~78, currently a bare global-dispatcher call). | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccPaymentsPool` on the metadata `fetch` (line ~42). | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/marketingCloud.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: marketingCloudAuthPool` / `marketingCloudRestPool` on the two `fetch` calls (lines ~38, ~61). **Add a try/catch boundary**; this module currently has none. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr.js` **(Tier 1)** | Await or `.catch()` the `sendMagicLinkEmail` calls in the passwordless-login and reset-password routes (lines ~150 and ~168). Both currently create an unobserved floating promise. | Modified | | `config/default.js` **(Tier 1)** | Add a `proxyConfigs` entry per new MRT-mediated integration as each is built (MuleSoft, Google Places, Booxi). Only SCAPI and OCAPI exist today. | Modified | | Runtime Admin, Environment Settings | Matching MRT-side proxy entry per environment. **MRT proxy config is a separate source of truth from the bundle's**; both must be updated together. | Modified | | `.claude/rules/` (new or existing rule file) | Document the integration-module contract in §5.3 so it is enforced at review time. | New | ### 5.3 Data Structures / Interfaces The contract every integration module must satisfy: ```ts // Each integration owns exactly one pool, and every outbound call uses it. import { mulesoftPool } from './connectionPools'; // 1. All outbound calls pass their own dispatcher. const response = await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { /* ... */ }, body: JSON.stringify(payload), dispatcher: mulesoftPool, // per-integration connection cap + timeouts }); // 2. Every module resolves to an explicit outcome. It never throws past its own boundary. type IntegrationResult = | { kind: 'ok'; data: T } | { kind: 'error'; reason: string; status?: number }; // 3. Every route registration observes the promise. app.post(path, (req, res) => { void handler(req, res).catch((err) => { // log, then always respond; never leave the request unanswered }); }); ``` Pool boundaries and caps are per `tsd-architecture.md` §12.1 (7 pools: `sfcc-scapi`, `sfcc-payments`, `mulesoft`, `marketing-cloud-auth`, `marketing-cloud-rest`, `google-places`, `booxi`). Caps there are derived from expected rather than observed concurrency and should be validated by the Stage load-test pass described in §9.3 of that document. ### 5.4 Error Handling & Edge Cases | Scenario | Expected Behaviour | Type | | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | | An integration's upstream returns a non-OK status | The owning module catches it and returns an explicit error outcome. The request receives a response describing the failure, never silence. | Error | | An integration's upstream is slow or unresponsive | Its pool's `bodyTimeout` aborts the call before MRT's 20s/16s ceiling, releasing the connection. Other integrations' pools are unaffected. | Error | | An integration floods its own connection pool | Only that integration's calls queue. Other integrations retain their own capped connections. | Edge case | | A page surface needs an integration that is unavailable | The page renders without that integration's contribution, per the graceful degradation constraint, except where an explicit error is mandated (checkout). | Edge case | | An integration performs a synchronous CPU-bound operation | **Not preventable by this design.** Every concurrent request on the process blocks for the duration. Prevented only by the coding rule; see §7. | Error | | Contentful (SDK does not expose a `dispatcher` hook) | Connection isolation is not achievable via this pattern; graceful degradation is the mitigation. See §7 for a correction to the existing documented claim. | Edge case | ### 5.5 Configuration & Environment Notes No new environment variables are introduced by the topology decision itself. Each future integration adds its own credentials to the per-environment variable set, and a matching proxy entry in **both** `config/default.js` and the MRT environment's own proxy configuration. One finding relevant to the LCP constraint in §2.1 is recorded here because it materially affects any performance measurement of the chosen topology, though it is not itself a topology issue: the seven MRT environments are split across two AWS regions. DEV, DEV1, SIT, UAT and STG sit in Asia Pacific (Sydney); TEST and Production sit in US East (Ohio). Because STG is the tier designated for contractual LCP sign-off and Production sits in a different region, Stage-measured performance figures are not currently representative of Production. This is being raised separately and should be resolved before any LCP sign-off, under either topology. --- ## 6. Testing & Validation ### 6.1 Test Coverage Mapping to §1.4: criterion 3 requires the isolation behaviour to be demonstrated rather than asserted. One integration fails; an unrelated one succeeds. | Currently: an aggregating caller loses the successful result entirely. After §5: the successful result survives its sibling's failure. | | Unit / Integration | The real `ssr.js` call shape (an unobserved floating promise inside a `.then()`) when its integration fails. | Currently: becomes a process-level unhandled rejection and the response object is never written to, so the shopper receives nothing until MRT's ceiling returns a 502. After §5: an explicit response. | | Unit / Integration | Cross-region blast radius: an AU-scoped call and an unrelated US-scoped call in flight together, the US one failing. | Currently: the AU result is lost despite AU not using the failing integration. After §5: the AU result is unaffected. | | Unit | Event-loop blocking: a synchronous CPU-bound operation alongside an unrelated fast operation. | The fast operation is delayed by the full duration of the blocking work. **This test documents an accepted limitation and is expected to keep passing after §5**; it is not fixed by that work. | | Integration | Per-pool isolation under load once §5 is implemented: a saturated or slow origin must not starve a different origin's pool. | An unrelated integration's call completes within its own timeout while another integration's pool is saturated. **Not yet written**; depends on §5. | | E2E / Playwright | Not applicable. | This TSD decides deployment topology and ships no user-facing surface, so there is no user journey to assert. Recorded explicitly rather than omitted. | Performance validation is not duplicated here: per-pool queue-depth and connection-wait metrics are already scheduled for the Stage load-test pass in `tsd-architecture.md` §9.3, and bundle size is already gated in CI. See §5.5 regarding the region caveat on Stage measurements. ### 6.2 Regression Risk The topology decision itself changes no code and therefore carries no regression risk. The §5 implementation does, and it is concentrated in two places. First, attaching a `dispatcher` to existing `fetch` calls changes connection behaviour for SLAS token validation, payment metadata, and Marketing Cloud email, all on authentication and checkout paths, so a mis-set cap or timeout would surface as intermittent failures there rather than as an obvious break. The four tests above cover the failure-isolation behaviour but not cap tuning, which is why the load-test row is listed as required. Second, `overrides/app/ssr.js` is the entry point for every request, so the route-handler change must be verified across all 8 storefronts rather than one. Note also that the `commerce-sdk-react` hooks manage their own HTTP client and are unaffected by pool changes, which usefully bounds the risk: the bulk of SFCC commerce traffic does not traverse these pools at all. --- ## 7. Removed. §3.2 now cites three sources that all stand on their own: the platform documentation, Salesforce's ISV guidance, and the firsthand Runtime Admin check. The argument is no weaker — arguably cleaner, since every source is now something a reviewer can independently verify.

## The four findings

All surfaced while verifying the as-is baseline in Runtime Admin. None is a topology question — they'd be identical under either option — which is why they came out of the TSD.

**1. Region split across environments.** Sydney: DEV, DEV1, SIT, UAT, STG. Ohio: TEST, Production. So the entire validation chain sits in a different AWS region from Production. This directly contradicts `architecture.md` §9.3, which designates STG as the tier where contractual LCP sign-off happens *because* it "mirrors production infrastructure" — it doesn't, on the biggest latency variable. Production's SFCC backend is also `production-ap01` (Asia-Pacific), so as configured prod would cross the Pacific for every SSR-side OCAPI call. Fixable cheaply right now: Region is an editable field and neither Production nor STG is configured yet. *(This is the one finding that survives in the TSD, as the §5.5 paragraph you kept.)*

**2. Production and STG aren't stood up.** Production's `Production Environment` flag is **Disabled**, so it has neither Salesforce priority monitoring nor Log Center access. It also has no environment variables, no B2C Commerce instance association, and no site IDs. STG likewise has zero environment variables — notable because STG is the designated contractual performance-test tier.

**3. DEV1 is an orphaned environment.** Mani's test environment. It appears in no repo config, no CI workflow, and no Confluence environment table, yet remains live and deployable — something deployed to it on 11 Aug. It points at SFCC instance `bkzk_001`, which appears in no documentation, while its own `COMMERCE_API_ORGANIZATION_ID` reads `_002`. Its SCAPI credentials appear copied from DEV (five masked suffixes identical), suggesting the vars were cloned from DEV but the platform bindings were pointed at a different sandbox. Worth noting the owner has moved off the project.

**4. No access hardening on any non-production tier.** No access-control header and no IP allowlist on DEV, DEV1, SIT, TEST, UAT or STG — all reachable by anyone with the URL, on default public hostnames, with source maps enabled. (Production correctly has source maps disabled; and for Production, "no access-control header" is arguably right until a custom domain and CDN are in front.)

Holding off on raising these, as you said. They're recorded in memory and in the task list, so they won't get lost while you decide what to do with them.

Problem Statement 26 27 ### 1.1 Context 28 29 The storefront runs on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT), where a Node/Express layer performs all 30 server-side work: the SSR render, proxying to upstream APIs, token exchange, and server-side calls to 31 integrated systems. Today that layer serves just three integration touchpoints: SLAS token 32 validation, payment method metadata, and Marketing Cloud email. Only two proxy origins are 33 configured, SCAPI and OCAPI. Approximately 18 external systems are in scope for the programme 34 (`.docs/integration/`), and nearly all of them have no code written yet. Integration build-out 35 begins in the coming sprints. 36 37 ### 1.2 Problem 38 39 How many MRT applications the storefront deploys, and how integration code is divided across them, 40 has never been decided. The current arrangement is a default inherited from the PWA Kit scaffold, not 41 a deliberate choice, and it has never been documented or signed off. Because deployment topology 42 determines how code is packaged, deployed, and rolled back, it becomes progressively more expensive 43 to change once integration code exists across many systems. 44 45 Compounding this, the server-side layer currently provides **no failure isolation of any kind** 46 between integrations. Seven per-origin connection pools were written for this purpose 47 (`overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`) but are imported nowhere and attached to no request, so 48 every integration shares one undivided execution and connection context. This is present-state 49 fact, verified in code and by test (§6), not a projection. 50 51 ### 1.3 Impact if Not Solved 52 53 - Topology is set by accretion rather than decision. Each integration that lands without an agreed 54 position makes the arrangement harder to change, and the decision is effectively made by whoever 55 writes the first proxy. 56 - The isolation gap persists and compounds. It was found by chance in the only integration that 57 currently has real code, and nothing in the codebase, review process, or CI prevents the same 58 pattern recurring in the ~17 integrations still to be built. 59 - Deploy and rollback blast radius stays coupled: a bad change to one integration forces a rollback 60 that also reverts every other integration shipped in the same bundle. 61 - Squad A (FED) and the SFCC squad have no shared written position to build against, risking 62 divergent assumptions about where integration code belongs. 63 64 ### 1.4 Success Criteria 65 66 1. A single documented position on how many MRT applications the storefront deploys and how 67 integration code is divided across them, signed off by the Technical Lead (§8). 68 2. The as-is baseline is verified against the live platform and the codebase rather than assumed, 69 with any inaccuracies in existing documentation corrected. 70 3. The chosen topology's failure-isolation behaviour is demonstrated by reproducible automated tests 71 rather than asserted. 72 4. The position is recorded specifically enough that integration build-out can proceed without 73 re-opening the question. 74 75 --- 76 77 ## 2. Constraints & Assumptions 78 79 ### 2.1 Constraints 80 81 | Constraint | Detail | 82 | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 83 | Platform | SFCC B2C Commerce + PWA Kit on Managed Runtime. MRT hosts **only applications created from a PWA Kit template**. It is not general-purpose Node or container hosting. | 84 | MRT application model | One project has many bundles, but **each environment has exactly one bundle designated as deployed**. A bundle is the entire built application and is immutable once created. | 85 | MRT organisation limits | Maximum **100 total environments** and **10 production environments** per organisation, raisable only by Salesforce Support. Currently 7 environments in use. | 86 | Execution model | A single Node.js/Express process per environment ("App Server"), serverless and auto-scaling. Hard request-execution ceiling of **20s production / 16s non-production**, after which MRT returns HTTP 502. **Unhandled promise rejections break app rendering.** | 87 | Storefront scope | Must work across all **8 storefronts in 6 regions** (AU, UK, US Domestic, US International, EU Domestic, EU International, HK, ME). No single-market workarounds. | 88 | Session and domain model | All 8 storefronts are path-prefixed on a **single first-party domain**; the `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie depends on this. An MRT environment binds to exactly **one** External Hostname, and a hostname can serve only one environment at a time. | 89 | Performance | **LCP ≤ 2s at p75 mobile** is client-mandated and contractual (`architecture.md` §9). Any added network hop on the SSR path counts against it. | 90 | Graceful degradation | Each external system must fail independently: one outage must not break a whole page (AGENTS.md > Graceful Degradation). | 91 | Tier 1 change control | `config/default.js`, `config/sites.js`, `overrides/app/ssr.js` and `worker/main.js` are **absolute** Tier 1 under AGENTS.md Hard Rule #4. The verified-session exception does not apply. Any topology or isolation change touches at least one of these. | 92 93 ### 2.2 Assumptions 94 95 | Assumption | Risk if Wrong | 96 | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 97 | The ~18 systems in `.docs/integration/` remain the integration scope for this decision. | Materially more systems would grow the per-environment variable surface and module count, but would not change the topology conclusion. Option B stays unsupported regardless of integration count. | 98 | Zimmermann's MRT agreement permits additional projects at no additional licence cost. | Affects only Option B's cost line. Option B is already non-viable on architectural grounds, so the recommendation does not change either way. Unconfirmed with the account team. | 99 | The `zimmermann` project runs on ARM rather than x86 server architecture. | If x86, environments must be migrated before **31 Jan 2027** or lose the ability to deploy. Not exposed in Runtime Admin at project or environment level, so unverified. Independent of the topology decision. | 100 | No in-scope integration requires process-level isolation that in-process module boundaries cannot provide. | If one does, for example a genuinely CPU-bound workload, it must be hosted outside MRT entirely. That is a separate infrastructure decision, not a change to MRT application topology. See §7. | 101 102 --- 103 104 ## 3. Options Analysis 105 106 ### 3.1 Options Summary 107 108 | Option | Pros | Cons | Viable? | 109 | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | 110 | **Option A**: Single MRT application, all integrations in one bundle | + The only model the platform supports, so zero migration cost, since it is the current state.
+ One bundle per environment: the existing 6-workflow deploy pipeline, version guard and tag promotion already work against it.
+ A single SSR render composes many integrations with no cross-app network hop, protecting LCP.
+ One shared session, cookie and CSP context, which the single-domain 8-storefront session model requires.
+ Isolation is achievable in-process per integration (connection pools, timeouts, error boundaries). | - All integrations share one Node process: no process, memory or event-loop isolation. A CPU-bound or unhandled-rejection failure in one integration can affect unrelated concurrent requests (demonstrated, §6).
- One immutable bundle per environment: rolling back one integration reverts every integration shipped in that bundle.
- One flat environment-variable namespace per environment shared by all integrations; MRT offers no sub-scoping within a project, and project roles are all-or-nothing.
- Isolation must be actively implemented and maintained by convention; nothing in the platform enforces it. | **Yes** | 111 | **Option B**: Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain | + Would provide true process-level isolation (memory, event loop, crash domain) per integration.
+ Would provide independent bundle lineage, so one integration could be deployed or rolled back without touching others.
+ Would scope environment variables and project role assignments per integration domain. | - **Not supported by the platform.** MRT hosts only PWA Kit template applications; every project must be a full storefront bundle, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application.
- Salesforce's own ISV integration guidance offers no such pattern.
- A literal per-integration reading (~18 systems × 6 tiers = 108 environments) exceeds the 100-environment organisation cap on its own.
- Cross-application calls would add a network hop to the SSR path, working directly against LCP ≤ 2s.
- Hostname-per-environment binding conflicts with the single first-party domain session model. | **No** | 112 113 ### 3.2 Option Detail 114 115 #### Option A: Single MRT application 116 117 One PWA Kit project (`zimmermann`) produces one bundle, deployed to one environment per tier. All 118 integration code (proxy routes, token exchange, server-side API calls) lives inside that single 119 Express application, organised as separate modules. It satisfies every constraint in §2 by 120 construction, because it is the model the platform is built around: one bundle per environment, one 121 hostname per environment, one shared session context across all 8 path-prefixed storefronts. Its 122 weakness is that isolation between integrations is a matter of code discipline rather than 123 infrastructure, and must be built deliberately (§5). 124 125 #### Option B: Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain *(Not viable)* 126 127 The proposal was that each integration, or each domain grouping of integrations, would be deployed as 128 its own Managed Runtime application, giving each one an independent process, deploy lineage, and 129 credential scope. This was explored in full rather than dismissed, because on paper it addresses 130 precisely the weaknesses of Option A identified above, and because the question was raised 131 specifically to be settled with evidence rather than assumption. 132 133 It is not viable, for a reason that is architectural rather than a matter of configuration or 134 budget: **MRT will not host it.** Managed Runtime is documented as supporting only applications 135 created from a PWA Kit template, a full React + Express + PWA Kit storefront bundle, and is not a 136 general-purpose Node or microservice hosting platform. An integration's backend cannot be packaged as 137 an MRT application because it is not a storefront. This was confirmed from three independent 138 directions. First, the platform documentation's own constraint statement. Second, Salesforce's own 139 B2C Commerce Headless Integration guidance for partners, which states that every Composable 140 Storefront must have a project created in Runtime Admin and offers exactly three delivery shapes for 141 backend integration logic (an SFCC cartridge, a Node module extending the same PWA Kit server, or an 142 externally-hosted API) with no fourth pattern of a sibling MRT application. Third, firsthand in 143 Runtime Admin: the Create-a-New-Project flow asks only for a name, a project ID, and two environment 144 defaults. There is no application-type field, because the platform assumes every project is a 145 storefront. 146 147 MRT's genuine multi-project support exists for a different purpose: separating distinct brands or 148 domains, each of which is itself a full storefront, not decomposing one storefront's backend. 149 Even setting the hosting constraint aside, three of Option B's consequences would independently 150 count against it: the literal per-integration form breaches the organisation environment cap; every 151 cross-application call would add a network hop to the SSR path that the LCP budget cannot absorb; and 152 the hostname-per-environment binding is incompatible with the single-domain session model the eight 153 storefronts depend on. 154 155 The isolation goals behind Option B remain legitimate. They are addressed within Option A in §5, and 156 the one case Option A genuinely cannot serve is recorded as a risk in §7. 157 158 --- 159 160 ## 4. Recommended Option & Rationale 161 162 ### 4.1 Recommended Option 163 164 **Option A: Single MRT application, implemented as a modular single application.** 165 166 ### 4.2 Rationale 167 168 Option A is recommended because Option B is not available. The decisive factor is not a trade-off 169 between the two but a platform constraint: MRT hosts only PWA Kit storefront bundles, so an 170 integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application at all. Once that is established, Option A 171 is the only option that satisfies the §2 constraints, and it satisfies them without migration cost 172 because it is the current state. 173 174 The recommendation is qualified in one important respect. Endorsing Option A is not an endorsement of 175 the status quo, because the status quo includes an isolation gap that is real and demonstrated: 176 today's arrangement has no isolation between integrations at any level, despite documentation 177 describing per-origin connection pooling as though it were in place. The recommendation is therefore 178 Option A **implemented as a modular single application**: one bundle, with integration code in 179 clearly separated modules, each with its own connection pool, timeout budget, and error boundary. 180 This is the "middle option" the originating ticket asked to be considered; it is not a third topology 181 but the correct implementation shape of Option A, and it is specified in §5. Adopting Option A 182 without that work would leave success criterion 1.4.3 unmet. 183 184 ### 4.3 Trade-offs Accepted 185 186 - **Shared-process failure modes remain.** Even fully implemented, in-process module boundaries do 187 not give memory, event-loop, or crash isolation. A synchronous CPU-bound operation in any 188 integration will block every other concurrent request on that process, and no connection pool or 189 configuration prevents it (demonstrated, §6). This is mitigated by a coding rule, not by 190 infrastructure, and is accepted as a permanent property of the chosen topology. 191 - **Coupled deploy and rollback granularity.** One immutable bundle per environment means the unit of 192 deploy and rollback is the whole application. A rollback triggered by one integration reverts every 193 integration in that bundle. Accepted; mitigated only by release discipline and small changes. 194 - **Coarse credential and access scoping.** All integrations' credentials share one flat 195 environment-variable namespace per environment, and MRT project roles are all-or-nothing: everyone 196 who needs deploy or variable access for any integration has it for all of them. Currently four 197 people, all Admin. Accepted for now; revisit if the team grows materially. 198 - **Isolation depends on convention.** Nothing in the platform or the current CI setup enforces the 199 module boundaries in §5. Accepted, with the mitigation in §7. 200 201 --- 202 203 ## 5. Technical Implementation 204 205 > Scope note: this section specifies the implementation of the chosen option. The work itself is 206 > deliberately **not** part of this spike. It is specified here so it can be picked up as its own 207 > ticket once §8 is signed off, and because §1.4 cannot be met by a recommendation that leaves the 208 > isolation gap undefined. Three of the files below are absolute Tier 1 (§2.1), so the implementing 209 > ticket must secure owner approval before starting. 210 211 ### 5.1 High-Level Sequence 212 213 1. A shopper request arrives at the MRT environment and is handled by the single Express app in 214 `overrides/app/ssr.js`. 215 2. The route handler for the relevant surface delegates to an integration module under 216 `overrides/app/ssr/` (one module per integration, as today). 217 3. The module issues its upstream call via `fetch`, passing the `dispatcher` option bound to **its 218 own** connection pool from `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`, so its connection usage is 219 capped independently of every other integration. 220 4. The pool applies that integration's own `connectTimeout` and `bodyTimeout`, bounding how long a 221 slow upstream can hold a connection, and keeping the request inside MRT's 20s/16s execution 222 ceiling rather than being terminated by it. 223 5. On success, the module returns typed data to the handler, which renders or responds. 224 6. **Error path:** if the upstream fails, times out, or returns a non-OK status, the module catches it 225 at its own boundary and converts it to an explicit outcome: an HTTP error response for a 226 dedicated endpoint, or a degraded-but-rendered result for a page surface per the graceful 227 degradation constraint. The rejection **must not** propagate out of the module. 228 7. **Error path:** the route registration awaits (or explicitly `.catch()`es) the module call, so no 229 integration failure can become an unobserved floating promise. Today two routes do not do this 230 (§5.2), which is why a Marketing Cloud failure currently produces no response at all rather than 231 an error response. 232 233 ### 5.2 Component / API Changes 234 235 | File / Endpoint | Change Required | Type | 236 | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | 237 | `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts` | Confirm pool definitions against real hostnames; resolve the two placeholder origins (`sfcc-payments`, `booxi`). Currently defines 7 pools but is imported nowhere. | Modified | 238 | `overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccScapiPool` on the JWKS `fetch` (line ~78, currently a bare global-dispatcher call). | Modified | 239 | `overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccPaymentsPool` on the metadata `fetch` (line ~42). | Modified | 240 | `overrides/app/ssr/marketingCloud.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: marketingCloudAuthPool` / `marketingCloudRestPool` on the two `fetch` calls (lines ~38, ~61). **Add a try/catch boundary**; this module currently has none. | Modified | 241 | `overrides/app/ssr.js` **(Tier 1)** | Await or `.catch()` the `sendMagicLinkEmail` calls in the passwordless-login and reset-password routes (lines ~150 and ~168). Both currently create an unobserved floating promise. | Modified | 242 | `config/default.js` **(Tier 1)** | Add a `proxyConfigs` entry per new MRT-mediated integration as each is built (MuleSoft, Google Places, Booxi). Only SCAPI and OCAPI exist today. | Modified | 243 | Runtime Admin, Environment Settings | Matching MRT-side proxy entry per environment. **MRT proxy config is a separate source of truth from the bundle's**; both must be updated together. | Modified | 244 | `.claude/rules/` (new or existing rule file) | Document the integration-module contract in §5.3 so it is enforced at review time. | New | 245 246 ### 5.3 Data Structures / Interfaces 247 248 The contract every integration module must satisfy: 249 250 ```ts 251 // Each integration owns exactly one pool, and every outbound call uses it. 252 import { mulesoftPool } from './connectionPools'; 253 254 // 1.
